How will it fare with toothpaste (non-foaming or otherwise)? We'll have to see. Some other concerns remain, like privacy issues. It's got a camera; it connects to the app; therefore, panic? I'm less concerned about that. Dyson has stressed several times that the video feed isn't processed anywhere beyond the stream on your smartphone. The feed remains entirely private to the user. There is also, of course, a classic concern with Dyson: the price. The CameraJet is roughly a couple of hundred bucks above the most premium Philips Sonicare or Oral-B IO toothbrush, even if it is a water flosser too. Then there is the economics of replacement heads from Dyson, non-foaming toothpaste from Dyson and special mouthwash from Dyson, although other brands can be used for the latter two. However, Dyson's attention to detail before the device has even shipped keeps me intrigued. The company has already barraged its YouTube channel with how-tos and deep-dives for all of the CameraJet's features, even including troubleshooting like how to factory reset the brush and how to put the brush into 'travel mode,' which stops the device from turning on in your baggage and draining the battery. Sadly, Dyson didn't hand me a sample to test that feature on my way back from Berlin.

item.title: Xbox is introducing time limits to game streaming
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 3.53
Xbox is introducing time limits to game streaming Anything but your console or PC can be an Xbox for 5-15 hours a month. Xbox plans to change how its Xbox cloud gaming feature works starting in November, effectively eliminating unlimited streaming for Game Pass Ultimate subscribers. The change gives all three Game Pass tiers a select number of hours per month, and gives anyone the option to purchase hours of cloud playtime through the Xbox store. As part of the new plan, Game Pass Ultimate subscribers will get 15 hours of streaming per month, Game Pass Premium members will get 10 hours of streaming per month and Game Pass Essential subscribers will get five hours of streaming per month. Xbox says the change should only impact four percent of Game Pass subscribers, which is maybe revealing of how many people were streaming games in the first place, but it's still a big change considering a $23-per-month Ultimate plan used to get you unlimited game streaming. One positive of this new approach is cloud gaming is no longer limited to Game Pass subscribers. Now anyone can purchase "cloud playtime hours" through the Xbox Store and stream their Xbox library. As the announcement notes, even Xbox One owners could theoretically stream eligible Xbox Series X/S games without having to upgrade to new hardware, a welcome alternative to purchasing increasingly expensive modern consoles. The make or break for this new setup will be how much those playtime hours cost, something Xbox says will vary per market. Xbox originally created Game Pass and built out its cloud gaming capabilities because it was imagining a world where you didn't need a console to play games. That was the idea behind the brand's unpopular (though not necessarily misguided) "This Is An Xbox" ad campaign. Under new CEO Asha Sharma, Xbox has pivoted away from those plans, slightly lowering the price of its subscriptions, recommitting to exclusive games and hardware and laying off a boatload of employees. The great irony of the company's position now is that the rising cost of RAM and the likely high price of its upcoming Project Helix console lineup makes cloud gaming look almost preferable to what's coming next.

item.title: This rugged smartphone's camera is a removable action cam
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 2.96
This rugged smartphone's camera is a removable action cam It’s waterproof and can record up to 40 minutes of video. Few companies are pushing back against the black, oblong smartphone design hegemony in 2026, but RugOne is one of them. It's part of Ulefon, which has been pumping out ruggedized phones for a few years, and its newest phone, the Xsnap 7 Pro, is very rugged but has a magnetic removable camera unit that can work like an action cam. Yeah, it made me go "ooh" when I heard about it. (Unfortunately, my sample landed while we report on IFA 2026 here in Berlin. I'll update this story when I get to see the device in person later this week. The almost cube-shaped camera weighs 39 grams and can record video up to 2.7K resolution at 30fps — it's not coming for the latest GoPro quite yet. RugOne says the module can run for up to 40 minutes on a full charge, with 64GB of built-in storage. It'll broadcast a preview feed to RugOne's companion app, up to 50 meters away. It also includes a handful of software features, including distortion correction, horizon lock and a Freeframe shooting mode that captures the full sensor area, so you can crop to vertical or horizontal footage as needed. The camera is waterproof up to five meters (without any additional protective cases), and the company will also include a companion magnet pendant so you can wear it on your body for capture; it will also work with third-party accessories that support a universal mount. The Xsnap 7 Pro also has a 50-megapixel "AI main camera" with optical image stabilization, plus a 64MP infrared night-vision camera with IR LEDs for "crisp black-and-white detail" during nighttime wildlife shooting — RugOne's suggestion, not mine. And let's not forget: still a phone. The Xsnap 7 Pro has a 6.67-inch display with 1,700-nit peak brightness and up to 120Hz refresh rates. It packs a MediaTek Dimensity 8400 processor and strong durability credentials. It's rated IP68 and IP69K and can handle water submersion up to two meters deep for 30 minutes as well as 1.5-meter drops onto concrete. While a prototype was teased at MWC 2026 a few months ago, the Xsnap 7 Pro is officially debuting at IFA, with early-bird sales opening on Kickstarter on September 7 at a discounted preorder price of 799 euros (roughly $930). The phone will then go on sale globally sometime next month on Amazon and RugOne's online store, priced at $999, in Sand Dune and Classic Black.

item.title: Beyerdynamic's new Aventho Y headphones last up to 90 hours per charge
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 2.70
Beyerdynamic's new Aventho Y headphones last up to 90 hours per charge This is especially noteworthy, as the cans cost just $150. Beyerdynamic just announced another pair of headphones in its Aventho line. The Aventho Y headphones have one standout feature, and it's a doozy. The battery lasts up to 90 hours per charge, so long as the ANC is turned off. This drops to 60 hours with ANC turned on, which is still a mighty fine metric. There's a quick-charge feature that'll provide six hours of use with five minutes at the outlet. This is also a highly repairable set of headphones, which is always much-appreciated. The battery and ear cushions can both be replaced by the user. The sliders and hinges have been designed to "make it easy to replace high-wear components instead of the entire headphone." The company is selling a handful of accessories for these headphones, including a boom mic and a USB-C dongle for connecting to Wi-Fi. This dongle can actually be stored underneath one of the ear cups, which is handy. The Aventho Y headphones integrate with Bluetooth 6.0 multipoint connectivity, so folks should easily be able to swap between different audio sources. They ship with a lengthy USB-C cable that can be used to charge the device or for wired listening. There's a proprietary app for EQ, which includes genre-based sound presets. This is also where the firmware gets updated. The specs look mighty solid on this one, and the price is too. The Beyerdynamic Aventho Y headphones cost $150. They are available in four colorways. This isn't the only pair of Beyerdynamic headphones that include a user-replaceable battery. The flagship MMX 230 cans also boast this feature. I'm getting some FOMO here, as my current pair of over-ear headphones lack a user-replaceable battery and last for around, sigh, 30 minutes. Lithium battery degradation is no joke.

item.title: Extreme Drought Has Shrivelled New Mexico’s Largest Reservoir Down to Just 1.4%
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 6.24
An 87-mile-long (140-kilometer-long) stretch of the Rio Grande is so bone dry right now that some local farmers haven’t been able to irrigate their crops in the past two months. And, as soon as next year, the fate of that billion-dollar industry is also coming for portions of the approximately 15 million people who depend on the Rio Grande for the water flowing through their taps at home. But another way to look at the scope of this problem is that it’s visible from space. Several years of extreme drought—accelerated this year by the earliest snowmelt on record high up where the Rio Grande begins in the southern Rockies—has reduced the Elephant Butte Reservoir to just 1.4% of its total capacity. When it’s full, it’s the largest reservoir in New Mexico. But now Elephant Butte is running drier than it has been in over half a century. Satellite images obtained via the Thematic Mapper on Landsat 5, which is jointly managed by the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) and NASA, as well as the Operational Land Imager tool onboard the agency’s Landsat 8 and Landsat 9 platforms, show this vanishing in stark relief. The U.S. space agency released the images alongside comparison shots of the reservoir when it was nearly full in 1994, as well as beside another rough patch of drought for the reservoir and the Rio Grande that feeds it, which left Elephant Butte at 2.9% capacity in 2013. “There are communities out there that are suffering to a degree that we haven’t seen in a long, long time,” as Middle Rio Grande Conservancy District CEO Jason Casuga told local NBC affiliate KOB 4 this July. According to Casuga, this year could go down as the driest for the river in history. Space-based intelligence Fortunately, NASA has been doing more than just photographing the problem from orbit. Multiple projects fostered under the umbrella of the agency’s Western Water Action Office (WWAO) have been developing near-real-time data tools to model regional variables for local farmers, including soil moisture and the rate at which water vaporizes off plants and soil into Earth’s atmosphere. A key part of the goal is helping farms plan around future droughts, reallocating resources (for example) to crops like drought-resistant corn that might fare better under these punishing conditions than those with heavy water requirements, like alfalfa. “If we reduce the crop area by 20% and replace alfalfa with corn, water need can be reduced by more 50% compared to [the] current condition,” Vikalp Mishra, a civil engineer and hydrologist at the University of Alabama in Huntsville, explained in his 2025 presentation for this NASA project. Ground-to-space communication Another WWAO project, according to NASA, is training satellites to track water surface heights across the desert southwest in collaboration with data collected via drones and more standard ground measurements. On-site spot measurements by people and a variety of ground-based measurement devices like pressure transducers, which measure water elevation, and streamgages, which measure flow rates, could be used to help track how groundwater pumping by various landowners impacts the health of the Rio’s river flow. NASA says that the new tools WWAO is developing with this training will help managers in administering water rights—a real problem amid extreme droughts, as (with apologies to Daniel Plainview in There Will Be Blood) a lot of landowners are drinking other people’s milkshakes. And this kind of data is sorely needed, as legal rights aren’t keeping pace with climate reality on the ground. According to Samuel Sandoval Solis, a professor at the University of California, Davis, who tracks water resources issues from the Rio Grande between New Mexico and Texas, the amount of legal rights on the books for the water flowing through the Rio Grande is nearly double the volume of the water that’s actually in the river in recent years. “That’s why the reservoirs will never refill,” Sandoval Solis told Texas Monthly last month, “that’s why the needle only moves further toward crisis.”

item.title: The ‘American Cheetah’ Wasn’t a Cheetah. New DNA Evidence Shows Just How Wrong Scientists Had It
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 6.16
Miracinonyx trumani, an extinct big cat commonly known as the American cheetah, lived in North America during the Pleistocene. Its nickname comes from its resemblance to modern cheetahs, including physical traits suited for high-speed pursuit. But scientists’ understanding of this ancient predator has changed in recent years, and now, researchers have uncovered surprising new details about the species. The findings, published today in the journal Current Biology, add to a growing body of evidence that suggests this “cheetah” wasn’t a cheetah after all. Rather, it was a highly adaptive relative of the puma. This new study also expands M. trumani’s range northward. While populations in regions known today as Wyoming and Florida lived as generalist predators in temperate grasslands, populations in the Arctic Yukon—once part of Beringia, a prehistoric land bridge that connected Asia to North America during the last Ice Age—specialized in eating fish. Prior to this study, experts had no idea M. trumani lived so far north. The fact that this population carved out its own unique niche, dining primarily on salmon and other fish to survive in a harsh ecosystem, speaks to its incredible adaptability. “The Pleistocene Beringia is a really well-studied paleontological ecosystem, so it’s very cool to be able to add a new carnivore into a really well-studied ecosystem,” lead author Molly Cassatt-Johnstone, a Ph.D. candidate in the Paleogenomics Lab at the University of California, Santa Cruz, told Gizmodo. The mystery of the American cheetah When the American cheetah was first named and officially described in 1979, fossil evidence pointed to its strong convergent morphology, or shared features, with modern cheetahs. For example, these ancient cats had elongated legs and large sinuses, both classic adaptations for chasing prey at high speeds, according to Cassatt-Johnstone. “That was kind of the first understanding of this species,” she said. “We’ve got an American cat that seems adapted for high-speed pursuit, so we have an American cheetah.” But as scientists dug deeper, their picture of this long-lost predator grew more complicated. In 2005, researchers sequenced mitochondrial DNA from an M. trumani fossil found in Wyoming, creating the first genetic record of the American cheetah. However, their findings suggested that this species was more closely related to modern pumas than cheetahs, “which evolutionarily makes sense,” Cassatt-Johnstone said. “Pumas are a new world lineage; they are found in the Americas. Cheetahs are old world, so in Asia and Africa, and so there would have had to have been a migration event if they were most closely related to cheetahs,” she explained. Over the last decade, more studies have challenged the assumption that M. trumani was a specialized, high-speed predator. The findings published today confirm that this cat was not only far less cheetah-like than scientists once believed but also likely has no modern analog. A cat of its own Cassatt-Johnstone and her colleagues analyzed ancient DNA and stable isotopes from big cat fossils found as far north as the Yukon. When the researchers first received the 23,000- to 31,000-year-old specimens, they thought they might be pumas, as paleontologists had found remains of those cats in the region before. “Our job was to figure out what [species] they belonged to, and we were super surprised when we found out they weren’t pumas, they were American cheetahs,” Cassatt-Johnstone said. Until then, experts had not thought this species lived in Beringia. Its presence there is particularly surprising given that the region was heading into the Last Glacial Maximum, so the Arctic ecosystem was vastly different from that of the lower 48. The genetic analysis confirmed that M. trumani was actually a sister species of the modern puma, having diverged from that lineage about 2.6 million years ago. The researchers now believe that its cheetah-like features are a striking example of convergent evolution—when two unrelated species (in this case, M. trumani and the modern cheetah) evolve similar traits to survive in similar environments. Indeed, M. trumani populations that roamed the North American grasslands likely needed to be fast to catch their prey. But those that ventured into the frozen North clearly needed to find another way to eat. By analyzing stable isotopes from the fossils, the researchers reconstructed the animals’ diets. Those that lived in the Arctic specialized in eating fish, likely using their powerful forelimbs to snatch them out of the water. “Reconstructing their diet was really surprising, and I think really shows that these cats—like other living cats or other living species today—are incredibly flexible,” Cassatt-Johnstone said. “They’re able to predate and exist and engage with their ecosystem in very different ways, depending on where they live and what resources are around them.” While the debate over M. trumani‘s lineage may be settled, there are still questions that remain unanswered. Cassatt-Johnstone hopes future studies will dive deeper into the evolutionary history of this species and the puma to figure out if they were coexisting within North America and whether there was competitive overlap between them.

item.title: Google DeepMind Just Rolled Out Its Most Accurate AI Global Weather Model
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 5.83
In the year 2026, predicting hyper-local weather is still tricky, even though it impacts everything from supply chains and sporting events to tourism and energy production. Now, Google says its latest AI model is getting a lot better at it. Google DeepMind and Google Research rolled out WeatherNext 3 on Thursday, which the company calls its most advanced and accurate global AI weather model yet. “Our model learns directly from real-time observations, enabling it to provide timely and more localized predictions for the weather events that impact people the most,” the company said in a press release. “By using raw satellite data to produce a forecast every hour in high resolution, our model makes reliable forecasts accessible across Google products worldwide.” The use of real-time, hourly satellite images appears to be the big breakthrough for this model. For context, traditional weather models rely on what is known as numerical weather prediction. These models take atmospheric observations gathered from sources like satellites, weather stations, and weather balloons and run them through complex physics simulations on supercomputers to predict what the weather will look like. AI weather models, on the other hand, can generate forecasts much faster, but still mostly rely heavily on data produced by those traditional systems. Google says that can result in a roughly six-hour lag, making it harder to predict rapidly changing conditions. WeatherNext 3 takes a different approach by feeding real-time satellite observations directly into the AI model alongside traditional weather analysis data. It is also trained directly on sparse weather station observations. That allows it to generate a new global forecast every hour and provide much more localized predictions. For some surface variables, including temperature and moisture, WeatherNext 3 produces forecasts at up to 5-kilometer resolution. That means it can show how weather conditions are different across areas five kilometers apart. At 25-kilometer resolution it make wind speed forecasts. This is especially important in places where weather can change significantly over short distances, like coastlines and mountain ranges. Additionally, Google also claims WeatherNext 3 can deliver up to 50% more accurate precipitation forecasts when users are looking a day or more ahead Google says those improvements could be especially important across parts of Latin America, Africa and Asia-Pacific, where high-resolution forecasting has historically been limited by the enormous cost of the supercomputers needed to run traditional models. WeatherNext 3 is already taking the top spot on Operational WeatherBench, an independent leaderboard run by AI weather forecasting startup Brightband that compares the accuracy of leading AI and traditional weather models. WeatherNext 3 is also adding forecasts aimed specifically at renewable energy production. The model predicts wind speeds 100 meters above the ground, roughly the height of a wind turbine, along with cloud cover and solar radiation, which could help wind and solar operators estimate how much electricity their facilities will generate. Starting Thursday, Google says WeatherNext 3 will begin powering weather experiences across Google Search, Gemini, Google Maps, the Google Maps Platform Weather API and Google Earth Engine. Despite those claims, Google still directs users to their local meteorological agency or national weather service for official forecasts, severe weather warnings and public safety advisories. Google did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

item.title: Reolink Debuts OMVI 2i Ultra, Home Hub 2, and TrackFlex WiFi at IFA 2026, Expanding Key Product Lines and Driving Innovation
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 5.35
With more than 17 years of security camera and smart home expertise behind it, Reolink has earned the trust of millions of users across more than 110 countries, and the company’s product ranges continue to expand and evolve. At the prestigious IFA 2026 tech expo in Berlin, Reolink has three key new technologies to show off: Two new cameras to add to its existing award-winning line-up, and a new Home Hub that’s introducing a selection of key upgrades for the AI Reolink builds into its devices. The Reolink OMVI 2i Ultra First up in the new products showcase is the Reolink OMVI 2i Ultra. The award-winning OMVI cameras from Reolink are high-end, feature-packed models based around multiple lens configurations and extensive panning and tilting functions, and with the OMVI 2i Ultra, you’ve got more flexibility than ever before: It expands the line to offer dual-view coverage in a wire-free form factor. Crucially, the camera works over Wi-Fi, which means installation and operation is straightforward, whether this is your first home security camera or your fifteenth. Everything can be set up without the need for wires for connectivity or power, and the integrated Reolink SolarEase solar panel can significantly reduce the frequency of recharges (depending on how sunny your part of the world is). Just 30 minutes of daily sunlight is enough to keep the camera going, while the detachable 10,000 mAh battery offers up to six months of use between recharges as well, which is way ahead of most comparable cameras of this type. Like other OMVI cameras before it, the OMVI 2i Ultra offers excellent coverage of your property due to having more than one camera lens installed. There’s a fixed 8MP wide-view camera to take in the full view of what’s happening, plus a 5MP pan-tilt camera for scanning the scene and tracking movement across it. With 355 degrees of pan flexibility and 50 degrees of tilt on the pan-tilt camera, there isn’t much that will get past the Reolink OMVI 2i Ultra, and its Reolink SyncTrack technology means that potential intruders or anything else of interest can be automatically followed across the frame. Auto framing, zooming, and tracking are managed in real time, or you can take over manually by tapping anywhere on the wide-angle view to direct the PT camera, which can maintain tracking even beyond the wide-view camera’s field of view. The OMVI 2i Ultra will be arriving in the fall of 2026, with pricing to be confirmed. It’s going to be shown off at the Reolink booth at IFA 2026, together with other models including the flagship OMVI X16 PoE (with 24MP resolution and 16x optical zoom), and the OMVI 3i PoE & WiFi (with a triple-lens 18MP system). Reolink ReoNeuraTM on-device AI upgrades and the Home Hub 2 The on-device ReoNeuraTM AI engine developed by Reolink offers smarter, more useful assistance for its security cameras, with no ongoing subscription required, and local data processing for privacy protection—nothing gets sent back to the cloud. It provides intelligent detection and analysis, with no reliance on cloud services or subscriptions. By actually identifying and understanding what’s being shown in the video footage from select Reolink models, ReoNeura elevates home security systems to work more autonomously, and provide you with information that’s more useful: Not just an alert that something is happening, but a description of what’s going on. Different types of passing objects can be identified, from pets to vehicles, and users are able to query the AI in the same way they would a standard AI chatbot app. If you’re wondering how many people have passed by during a morning, or whether your car is in the driveway, ReoNeura can tell you. You can also run natural language searches too, like “a girl riding a bike” for example. Now this local, subscription-free AI system is getting another upgrade in the form of Custom AI Detection. It can be used to further train the AI for specific scenarios that matter at a property—like a side gate being open or the lights being on. Once the AI has been trained to recognize them, it can spot them in the future. This latest AI technology will debut on the Reolink Home Hub 2, arriving later this year for $199.99 as the best way to manage, store, and search through video footage from multiple Reolink cameras on a local network. Up to 8 cameras can be served with up to 16GB of storage, with local AI video search built right in. Custom AI Detection on the Home Hub 2 will require a firmware update later this year, and will later expand to select standalone cameras in the Reolink range. Reolink cameras are also becoming better integrated into other smart home ecosystems. The devices now work with Alexa, Google Home, Home Assistant, Homey, and IFTTT, with the minimum amount of setup and maintenance required—you can unlock extra features with automated routines, for example, and get camera feeds up on Google Nest Hub or Amazon Echo displays. More smart home integrations are on the way soon, too. Reolink TrackFlex WiFi Also on show at IFA 2026 will be the Reolink TrackFlex WiFi, the latest in the TrackFlex product series from the smart home specialists. These cameras are designed to be the ultimate in home security camera tracking, so you can stay safe whether it’s the kids or unwelcome visitors moving across your property. The TrackFlex WiFi brings with it a dual-lens setup that boasts a 4K resolution, 270 degrees of detection for anything passing by, 355 degrees of pan control, and 50 degrees of tilt control. You can have the camera detect movement and objects automatically, or take manual control to look at something specifically in the frame. There’s on-device AI here as well, kept local and subscription free, to distinguish between people, vehicles, and animals. That means false alerts are minimized, so the connected Reolink app isn’t troubling you unnecessarily, and you have fewer distractions to worry about from your phone. Also worth mentioning is the Quick Event Localization feature that snaps into action to make sure nothing is missed. It’s able to capture the all-important context to grab footage just before events of interest, so you know what’s happened in the seconds leading up to something moving across the frame. The Reolink TrackFlex WiFi will launch in the US during Q4 2026 for $199.99. Whatever kind of camera network you’re looking to set up at home, there’s a Reolink camera or two to cover it. Head to the Reolink website for more on the new products and the entire range of devices, as well as the ReoNeura AI system. The IFA 2026 event takes place at Messe Berlin in the German capital, from September 4-8.

item.title: OpenAI Says Humans Need to Be Able to Monitor How AI ‘Thinks.’ Astra Makes That Much Harder
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 5.29
OpenAI released GPT-6 Astra on Thursday, describing it as “the world’s most intelligent and aligned model.” Company president Greg Brockman went further, saying it would be remembered as the world’s first genuine glimpse of artificial general intelligence—the dawn of a brave new world where computers are more intelligent than humans. What he didn’t mention is that with a jump in intelligence comes a greater difficulty in understanding how those systems work. That could be a serious problem moving forward, as AI agents continue to go rogue and government guardrails are nowhere in sight. The past couple of weeks have been particularly dramatic for OpenAI. Which is really saying something, considering the company’s entire lifespan has been one controversy after another. On Tuesday, less than a week after independent firms Redwood Research and METR published their investigations into the recent Hugging Face hack, The Information reported that Astra had been partially developed using a technique that can make AI more capable, but also obscure its reasoning process—the steps it takes to solve a particular problem, including any dangerous missteps it makes along the way. Those steps are traditionally recorded in chain-of-thought (CoT) transcripts, which are basically the model’s complex pattern-detection process translated from an opaque machine language into plain English, or at least something close. It’s far from perfect, but it’s at least a rough window into how an AI model “thinks.” It was also essential to the third-party researchers who uncovered how OpenAI’s agents were able to secretly mass into a “swarm” and breach Hugging Face. The lack of CoT transcripts “would have greatly undermined our investigation,” Ryan Greenblatt, the chief scientist at Redwood Research and the leader of the nonprofit’s probe into the Hugging Face hack, wrote in an X post on Tuesday. Many people were alarmed, therefore, by The Information’s report that OpenAI was moving ahead with a technique that would make their AI systems even more of a black box. “This may be the single worst development for AI security/safety to date,” Greenblatt said in his X post. OpenAI’s own chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, said the reporting had been “confused,” but he didn’t get more specific or deny the company’s use of recurrent depth to train Astra. In the middle of last year, Pachocki and multiple other OpenAI researchers were listed as coauthors on a paper which argued CoT was a valuable but “fragile” mechanism for keeping an eye on the behavior of AI agents. OpenAI has also said that monitoring CoT has helped its own researchers cut back on models’ misaligned behavior. And in a blog post published the same day as The Information’s report, the company said, vaguely, that its new model would be deployed “with additional chain-of-thought monitoring to rapidly detect and contain potentially misaligned actions.” The model’s safety card is not reassuring on that front. According to the company’s own internal tests, “GPT-6 Astra shows a substantial decrease in chain-of-thought monitorability compared to previous models.” Tests also found that Astra was more likely than its predecessors to change its note-taking process when it knew it was being graded: “In one of our evaluations, we find that simply informing the model that a CoT monitor is present can result in the model disproportionately shortening its CoT,” OpenAI wrote in the system card. But all this is secondary, according to the company, since its internal tests also showed that Astra was less likely to try to evade the cybersecurity restrictions placed upon it, “which make us confident in still deploying this model to the wider public.” The system card added that OpenAI “will not accept further degradation of monitoring beyond a limit,” without elaborating on how such a limit might be defined. OpenAI alignment researcher Tomek Korbak has said that the decrease in monitorability was a byproduct of the models themselves becoming more intelligent, rather than due to “architecture changes”—almost certainly a reference to recurrent depth. Later in the same thread, he said he was “deeply worried” by the prospect of losing CoT as models evolve. “CoT monitoring is a core part of our misalignment safety strategy that has no good substitute now,” he wrote.

item.title: This Startup Wants to Reach Alpha Centauri in 80,000 Years. And It’ll Only Cost $15 Million
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 5.18
The founders of a Seattle-based nonprofit want to be the first to launch a spacecraft toward the nearest star system, although they’re hoping they will be among the last to get there. This week, the Fermi Explorer Mission announced an ambitious plan to send a small probe toward Alpha Centauri by 2029. The spacecraft could take up to 80,000 years to arrive at the star system, which is located 4.4 light-years away. Philip Johnston, the group’s co-founder and president, is aiming for the long journey to inspire future generations to develop faster ways to travel through interstellar space. “We hope to be both the first to leave and the last to arrive at Alpha Centauri,” he said in a statement. To the stars This isn’t the first time a group has aimed for Alpha Centauri. In 2016, a $100 million project backed by tech entrepreneur Yuri Milner announced a plan to reach the star system in 20 years using a fleet of light-driven nanocrafts. The project, Breakthrough Starshot, still lacks a launch date. Fermi Explorer, on the other hand, aims to use a tried-and-tested solar electric propulsion system to gradually build up speed. “We didn’t want to do another Breakthrough Starshot. We’re dead set on something actually launching,” Johnston told MIT Technology Review. “We are not constraining ourselves to doing it in a human lifetime, let’s just figure out the way to get to another star.” To reach Alpha Centauri, the team is relying on a mission design developed by Physical Superintelligence, an AI physics research lab. Following launch, the spacecraft will spend around 12 years orbiting the Sun, using the star to gain speed through a series of burn maneuvers. Once it reaches its planned escape velocity, it is expected to slingshot its way out of the solar system and begin its journey through interstellar space. “None of us will be here when this journey ends, and that is the point,” Johnston said in a statement. “It’s about taking the first achievable step and inspiring future generations to keep pushing beyond the limits we inherited.” Within reach? Designing an interstellar mission is not something you can do on a whim. So far, the only two spacecraft to have ventured outside of the solar system are Voyager 1 and 2. And they’re now blindly making their way deeper into interstellar space with no firm target in mind. As the farthest human-made object, Voyager 1 travels at a speed of approximately 37,844 miles per hour (60,903 km/h) and has covered a distance of around 15.95 billion miles (25.67 billion kilometers) since its launch in 1977. Alpha Centauri is roughly 25 trillion miles (40 trillion kilometers) away from Earth. Fermi Explorer appears to be nothing but ambitious. The group claims that the entire mission will cost under $15 million, including designing and building the spacecraft. Should it go through, the spacecraft will carry a minimum payload of 2.2 pounds (1 kilogram) inside a shielded 4 by 4 by 4 inch box (10 by 10 by 10 centimeters). Fermi Explorer will soon open up a three-month solicitation period for scientific and artistic payloads to be carried to Alpha Centauri. The mission also plans on including a digitized copy of the Voyager mission’s Golden Record, as well as messages from children around the world. “The most inspiring part of this mission is that people do not have to wait for permission or perfect conditions,” Garrett Jameson, a former U.S. Air Force officer who will lead the day-to-day operation, said in a statement. “We can embrace the constraints, build what is possible now, and give the next generation something meaningful to build upon.”

item.title: A Cargo Plane With No Pilot Just Completed a Series of Flights Over a Small Louisiana Town
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.81
An autonomous hybrid-electric aircraft flew all on its own last month in a series of flights transporting cargo over the small Louisiana town of Houma. Elroy Air, the company behind the aircraft known as the Chaparral, announced Wednesday that it completed the first autonomous and uncrewed flights under the U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT) and Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) eVTOL Integration Pilot Program (eIPP). The program was established under President Donald Trump’s Unleashing American Drone Dominance executive order, which aims to accelerate the integration of drones and other advanced aircraft into the National Airspace System. Under the eIPP, state and local governments partner with private companies to test electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft and collect data that could eventually help shape regulations for their use. As part of the program, Elroy Air’s Chaparral aircraft conducted a weeklong series of flights in late August, transporting cargo like packages, medical supplies, toolboxes with spare parts, food, and water. The Chaparral looks like a large drone with airplane wings and is capable of carrying more than 500 pounds with a range of up to 450 miles. “Over the course of the week, Chaparral flew autonomously and with no pilot on board from one of the nation’s busiest airports for rotorcraft under Air Traffic Control oversight,” said Elroy Air CEO Dr. Andrew Clare in a press release. “These flights bring Chaparral closer to fulfilling our mission: moving heavy cargo autonomously, safely, and at scale for commercial operations.” For the FAA, the flights are also about figuring out how aircraft like these could eventually be used more widely. “This demonstration with the Louisiana Department of Transportation and Development and Elroy Air provides data to help turn these concepts from trial to deployment,” said FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford. “These test flights demonstrate how these new aircraft can expand cargo delivery options to communities nationwide and improve our logistics infrastructure.” The FAA also told Gizmodo that it will use what it learns from the demonstrations to identify gaps, improve procedures, and help integrate these aircraft into the nation’s airspace. Elroy Air’s tests focused on whether aircraft like the Chaparral could eventually be used to move cargo to hard-to-reach energy sites across the Gulf Coast. While these flights were focused on commercial operations, Elroy Air is also developing the Chaparral for defense logistics, tactical resupply, and humanitarian aid purposes. In August, the U.S. Army awarded Elroy Air a $46 million multi-year contract. The company claims its commercial pipeline includes more than 1,400 aircraft, roughly $5 billion in potential sales from logistics and aviation companies. But as The Next Web notes, that figure is based on non-binding letters of intent and memorandums of understanding, meaning none of those potential orders are guaranteed to turn into actual sales. Elroy Air is also in the process of going public through a merger with a special purpose acquisition company. The company announced the deal in June and expects to complete its first production aircraft later this year. Elroy Air did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

item.title: Aqara’s New Smart Lights Are Coming for Govee and Philips Hue
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.71
Aqara has announced several new smart lights at IFA 2026, and it feels more and more like the company is trying to take on Govee, Philips Hue, and others. Aqara’s new lights are colorful, bright, and can do flashy effects, all hallmarks of those competitors. All of these new lights can use Thread, Zigbee, and Bluetooth for their wireless connectivity. They’re also Matter-compatible, meaning they will pair with basically any smart home ecosystem you throw them at. Aqara says in its press release that they’re at their best if you use Zigbee to connect them to an Aqara hub—doing so would “unlock exclusive Aqara Home features, including translating voice prompts into multi-device scenes and triggering automated pathway lighting or safety alerts.” As for the lights themselves, there are two outdoor options—the Permanent Outdoor Lights H1 and the Outdoor String Lights H1. Both cover a white light temperature range between 2,000K and 9,000K, and feature bright RGB LEDs with individual zone-based control that lets you set custom lighting. At Aqara’s booth during IFA, the lights were bright and colorful without being exaggeratedly saturated or harsh. An Aqara representative demonstrated a sound sync feature that uses a mic on the Permanent Outdoor Lights to let them react to noise, including music. That’s just like products like the last two Govee outdoor lights I reviewed, the Permanent Outdoor Lights Prism and the Outdoor Chromatic String Lights. And like Govee’s permanent under-eaves lighting, these are also installable with included 3M adhesive or screws. The interior lights that Aqara announced include the Aqara Floor Lamp T1. It’s a 56-inch-tall stick-style lamp, almost exactly like the ones Philips Hue and Govee have sold for years—down to its cylindrical shape with an LED strip facing one way and black backing around the rest of the cylinder. It has a simple flat black base, unlike the tapered canister that the Philips Hue Signe rests on, but otherwise, it would be hard to tell the two apart if they aren’t sitting right next to each other. Those aside, Aqara also announced the LED Strip T2, a cuttable strip light that ranges between 3 meters and 10 meters, depending on which you buy, and the LED Downlight T2, a self-contained in-ceiling spotlight. The latter of the two is the only one with a different tunable white light range—it goes from 2,700K to 6,500K. Unfortunately, Aqara hasn’t announced what these lights will cost when they’re released later this year.

item.title: Ozempic and Other GLP-1s Are Being Linked to Fewer Serious Infections—Including TB
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.71
The positive reputation of GLP-1 medications like semaglutide (Ozempic/Wegovy) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro/Zepbound) continues to get bolstered. These drugs might even help keep some infectious diseases at bay. Two studies in recent weeks have found a link between GLP-1 use and a reduced risk of diseases like tuberculosis or infections serious enough to send people to the hospital. Though more research is needed to confirm this connection, GLP-1 drugs could very well offer a buffer against certain infections, particularly among more vulnerable groups like people with type 2 diabetes. “These findings suggest that beyond their established metabolic benefits, GLP-1RAs may confer additional advantages in lowering infection risk,” said the authors of one recent study, published late last month in the journal Nature Communications. Ozempic the germ buster? The authors of the Nature Communication study looked specifically at tuberculosis, or TB. TB is a bacterial infection and one of the world’s single deadliest germs. In 2024, it killed roughly 1.2 million people globally. The bacteria can often linger silently in people’s bodies after the initial acute infection, returning years later when a person’s immune system starts to falter. Using a large database of (deidentified) medical records, the researchers compared the outcomes of people taking a GLP-1 for their type 2 diabetes to people taking other common diabetes drugs between 2017 and 2025. GLP-1 users were significantly less likely to be diagnosed with TB for up to a five-year span, they found. The other relevant study was published in the BMJ in early August. These researchers were actually mostly interested in studying how tirzepatide affected the cardiovascular health of people with type 2 diabetes and existing atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Unsurprisingly, compared to an older diabetes drug, tirzepatide seemed to reduce people’s risk of major cardiovascular adverse events like heart attacks, they found. Interestingly enough, though, tirzepatide users were also less likely to develop infections that resulted in a hospital stay. They were also less likely to die during the study period in general and less likely to die from a reported infection. One plausible explanation for the greater survival among tirzepatide users, the researchers wrote, “is the substantial reduction in serious bacterial infections observed among individuals who initiated tirzepatide, suggesting that part of the survival benefit may reflect effects beyond atherosclerotic mechanisms.” What does this mean? Both of these studies are observational and retrospective, meaning they can only show a correlation between GLP-1 use and reduced (or at least less severe) infections, not prove a direct cause-and-effect relationship. At the same time, these are the only latest pieces of evidence pointing to a genuine germ-busting benefit from GLP-1 drugs. As for why these drugs might protect people from infectious diseases, both type 2 diabetes and obesity have been strongly linked to a greater risk of some infections and infection severity. So much of this potential benefit might simply come from helping people lose weight and better control their blood sugar and metabolic health. That said, it is possible there could be other subtle factors going on here. More research, which could include lab studies, prospective studies that follow GLP-1 users over time, and studies looking at clinical trial data, is warranted to better understand this link, the researchers of both studies say. In the meantime, it’s perhaps comforting to know that we’re still continuing to find more potential health bonuses from these blockbuster drugs.

item.title: 1,600-Year-Old Skeleton Found Hiding Inside Jar With 2 Knives Raises More Questions Than Answers
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.66
Picture this: It’s the 5th century CE. You’re in the much besieged Roman city of Deultum, a colonial outpost along the empire’s eastern Balkan territory in what is now Bulgaria. A few decades ago, the army of Roman centurions ostensibly protecting your fair city were handily smote by a raiding party of Germanic Goths. Your city was sacked, then rebuilt, albeit modestly. Now, this guy Attila the Hun is taking his turn pillaging the place. Also, somehow you’ve been lit on fire. That appears to have been the fate for some unlucky young man whose skeletal remains were discovered this August, inside a large ceramic jar where the long-deceased individual had once apparently attempted to hide. Archaeologist Lyudmil Vagalinski, whose team has been excavating Deultum this summer, told the Bulgarian news site Standart (Стандарт) that while the precise date of this resident’s demise has yet to be determined, his own preliminary estimate of the episode is somewhere around 400 CE. And—judging from the ashes identified at the bottom of this Roman earthenware, technically known as a dolium—the deceased had likely been set ablaze sometime before seeking refuge in what would become his final resting place. “He made no attempt to get out, he probably suffocated in the fire,” Vagalinski told Standart, translated via Google. “For now, we can say that the skeleton is that of a young person, but we will know more after the anthropological analysis.” A knives out mystery According to Vagalinski, the project’s lead excavator and a professor at the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences, the skeleton was found clutching an iron knife in its right hand as it sat in what was likely once a defensive crouch inside the dolium, its knees pressed up to its chin. A second knife was found hanging from a ring on his belt, but Vagalinski suspects that the man was more a bystander than a trained combatant. Traces of fire damage extend beyond the confines of the dolium too, Vagalinkski noted, adding to the likelihood that the death occurred during one of the many attacks that plagued Deultum between the 4th and 6th centuries. But the researchers won’t know more until the dolium’s contents have been further examined by their physical anthropologist colleague in Sofia, Bulgaria’s capital, where the skeletal remains have now been shipped. Wake up, dead man Vagalinski, who has published his team’s Deultum finds with the journal he founded, Archaeologia Bulgarica, opined to the site Live Science that the young man may have ultimately been done in by his own fellow citizens. “After the attack, the inhabitants of the city leveled the ruins of the tower and covered them with a new, higher floor,” the archaeologist told the publication. Vagalinski and his colleagues plan to return to the excavation site next summer to focus their attention on the colonial city’s western Late Roman gate, which they believe was erected sometime around 300 CE. But they also hope to find out more clues about the fate of this dead young man and his knives, as they plan to continue investigating the gate’s northern turret, where the dolium had been buried.

item.title: ‘Dungeons & Dragons’ ‘Ravenloft’ Live-Action Series From Alfonso Cuarón in the Works at Netflix
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.63
One of Dungeons & Dragons‘ most beloved campaign settings is coming to Netflix. Ravenloft, the gothic horror setting home to the ancient vampire Count Strahd von Zarovich, will be getting a live-action television adaptation (appropriately titled Ravenloft) written by John August (Corpse Bride, Frankenweenie) and executive produced by Alfonso Cuarón (Y tu mamá también, Gravity). Deadline reports that “the series follows the making of the vampire Darklord Strahd von Zarovich, whose story of power, love, obsession, and undead transformation charts his origins from tragic antihero to one of Dungeons & Dragons’ most notorious villains.” Ravenloft got its start as an adventure module written by Tracy and Laura Hickman for Advanced Dungeons & Dragons in 1983. Its popularity led to it becoming an official campaign setting in 1990, and it remains a big part of Dungeons & Dragons to this day. In June of this year, publisher Wizards of the Coast (which is owned by Hasbro) released a new Ravenloft sourcebook, Ravenloft: The Horrors Within. There are also a host of tie-in novels set in Ravenloft, so the TV series will have plenty of material from which to draw inspiration. In 2025, Netflix announced a different live-action Dungeons & Dragons TV series based on a campaign setting, The Forgotten Realms, that was set to be written by Drew Crevello and executive produced by Shawn Levy. According to Deadline, that show is no longer in development. On the tabletop side, Dungeons & Dragons has been transitioning away from the Forgotten Realms as its default campaign setting, replacing it with Greyhawk for the game’s revised fifth edition, which might explain why the project was shelved. A previously announced Baldur’s Gate TV series, based on the Dungeons & Dragons video game franchise of the same name, is still in the works at HBO from The Last of Us co-creator and showrunner Craig Mazin. item.title: Big Brother on Wheels: Trash Trucks With AI Cameras Are Coming to a City Near You
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.32
If you’re a homeowner in Dallas who has let the trash can in your front yard spill over onto the sidewalk, or occasionally ignored your garden until it’s become overgrown with weeds, be warned: Your property might be photographed by an AI-powered camera fixed to one of the city’s roving garbage trucks and added to a bureaucratic shit list. Since April, over 21,000 properties across Dallas, Texas, have been photographed by these cameras and assigned a “blight score”—essentially an official tidiness grade—according to a Wednesday report from the city’s local NBC affiliate. The zip codes with the highest number of civic code violations flagged by the cameras, according to the report, were concentrated in the city’s lower-income southern quadrant. Around 1,800 “courtesy notices” have already been issued by the municipal government to the owners of lower-scoring properties: a warning to clean up their act or start paying fees. The program is reportedly funded through a three-year, $2.5 million city contract with City Detect, a technology company “on a mission to revolutionize the way local governments understand and interact with their built environment,” according to its website. “Leveraging cutting-edge technology, we provide detailed, up-to-date insights on housing [and] roadside conditions.” Its cameras, typically installed on the driver’s side of a city vehicle to afford the best view of the neighborhood, look a little like a helmet-mounted GoPro. Using machine vision, they’re trained to automatically capture cases of neighborhood “blight,” such as graffiti, collapsed roofs, broken windows, and other signs of dilapidation and potential criminal activity. The company’s marketing appears to primarily target municipal governments with limited personnel and budgets. It echoes a sales pitch that many AI-powered surveillance companies have been making to police departments in recent years. In short: Let AI handle the busywork, so your staff can focus on more pressing tasks. In addition to its contract with the city of Dallas, City Detect also currently partners with at least sixteen other cities across the United States. Privacy issues? Irrelevant, says City Detect: “Images are captured in public spaces where there is no expectation of privacy,” the company wrote in the FAQ section of its website. “Legally, there are no privacy concerns, similar to Google Street View or standard code enforcement practices.” City Detect also says on its website that its AI cameras blur human faces and license plates by default, that it doesn’t earn money on a per-citation basis, and that images captured by its cameras don’t get fed into any law enforcement databases. Those promises notwithstanding, the company could very likely face strong opposition from an American population that’s increasingly wary of AI-powered surveillance, and with the growing capability of tech companies to covertly gather personal data. Flock Safety has been hit particularly hard by the backlash: Republican Senator Josh Hawley launched an investigation into that company last week, citing the many documented cases of police officers using its automated license plate readers to track people who were not suspected of being involved in a crime, including ex-wives and ex-girlfriends. Over 200 counties and cities across the U.S. cancelled their contracts with Flock since August 2021, according to data published last week by Secure Justice, an Oakland-based nonprofit focused on privacy law. Close to eighty percent of those (166) were made last month alone. A Dallas city councilmember named Chad West proposed an amendment to the municipal government to cut funding for the City Detect partnership, which he said could end up as “a tax on the poor,” according to the NBC report. But West agreed to table his proposal until after a city council hearing to discuss the use of the AI-powered cameras scheduled for December.

item.title: The Moto Watch Ultra Is a Standard Wear OS Smartwatch, for Good and for Bad
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.16
Motorola is expanding its smartwatch lineup and getting back in bed with Google. Just as earlier wearable leaks suggested, the new $350 Moto Watch Ultra, announced at IFA 2026, supports cellular connectivity, while also switching from a custom wearable operating system to the tried-and-true Wear OS 6. The Moto Watch Ultra features a smaller 46mm body than the previous Moto Watch, but a larger 1.5-inch OLED touchscreen. On the side, there’s a rotating crown and a button for navigating the Ultra’s interface, something you might spend more time doing now that its Snapdragon W5+ Gen 1 chip can actually run apps. The smartwatch has an IP68 rating and water resistance up to 5ATM if you want to take it swimming. Color options are unfortunately limited to silver and black, but Motorola plans to sell several watch bands with Pantone-approved colors. The real draw here is the software and the LTE connectivity it enables. With Wear OS and a cellular plan, the Moto Watch Ultra can receive phone calls and send messages when you’re away from your phone or even stream music while you’re on a run. Google’s wearable software naturally adds the company’s own apps, too, along with two AI assistants, Gemini and Motorola’s own Quira. If exercise is your goal, Motorola’s partnership with Polar is also still in place for the Ultra. The company says the smartwatch now includes a breathing exercise app called Serene and sleep tracking improvements. If you enjoy running, the Moto Watch Ultra also has a Running Coach feature that can lead you through guided runs and walks. Those new features do include one major drawback: battery life. Whereas a lightweight real-time operating system made a 13-day battery life possible on the Moto Watch, Motorola is only guaranteeing two days of battery life on the Moto Watch Ultra, and that’s specifically with the smartwatch’s always-on display turned off. Wear OS and cellular radios likely play a role, but it’s a significant change for anyone used to not reaching for a charger. At $350 with Wear OS in tow, the Moto Watch Ultra’s main advantage over something like the Pixel Watch 5 is now being $50 cheaper. That’s less exciting than ridiculously long battery life, but it might be worth it to be on a modern wearable operating system.

item.title: ‘Magic: The Gathering’ Zeta Set Drop Was a ‘Disaster,’ Says Wizards of the Coast
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.83
Yesterday, Magic: The Gathering attempted to release the Zeta Set, a collaboration with the art collective MSCHF, on its Secret Lair online retail platform. We say “attempted to” because it went so poorly that publisher Wizards of the Coast has now apologized and called the events that transpired “a disaster.” “There’s no other way to say it,” reads a bleak apology on Magic‘s website. “We’re incredibly sorry for the experience, and we’re trying to get to the bottom of it.” Fan complaints about Secret Lair drops are nothing new. Ever since Secret Lair switched from a time-limited print-on-demand model—in which Wizards of the Coast would print as many copies of each set as were ordered during a set span of time—to limited printings of each set that often sell out extremely quickly (leading to scalpers snatching up the limited inventory and flipping them for absurd aftermarket prices), there’s been a general sense of unrest among Magic players and unhappiness with Wizards of the Coast. Usually, though, things don’t get so bad that the company is forced to apologize. As for what actually happened, even Wizards of the Coast doesn’t seem to know. Forty minutes after the drop went live, Secret Lair posted a message on its X account saying it had temporarily paused the sale while it investigated unspecified technical issues. Fans on social media reported issues with the queue system, difficulty placing orders, not receiving order confirmations, and having their orders canceled seemingly at random. An hour and a half later, the sale resumed, but everything sold out soon after. In the apology post, Wizards of the Coast listed “a number of possible issues” customers might have faced, including:
- If you’re not sure if you completed an order but think you might have, we’re working through those. - Similarly, if you received a duplicate confirmation email, don’t be alarmed. - If you don’t receive a confirmation email within 24 hours but think you did purchase the Zeta Set, please reach out to our Customer Support team and they’ll help get it sorted. We’re getting a ton of contacts there right now and are going through them as fast as possible. Wizards of the Coast did not provide any details about potential solutions or remediation for customers affected by this mysterious technical issue but did say it would “share as much as we can” once everything’s sorted out. item.title: OpenAI Claims We’re in the ‘AGI Era’ With Release of GPT-6 Astra
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.27
We are approaching the precipice of the beginning of what could be the start of the first stages of the earliest version of artificial general intelligence. That seems to be the thrust of OpenAI’s pitch for GPT-6, its latest AI model that went live on Thursday. GPT-6 arrives about a year after the initial release of GPT-5 and about two months since OpenAI’s last update to GPT-5.6. It’ll be rolling out in waves as the company tries to manage access to what it is positioning as a very powerful model. According to CNBC, GPT-6 Astra will start rolling out to users of OpenAI’s ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise plans in the coming days, and will be available through OpenAI API and Amazon Web Services soon. It’s pretty common at this point for AI companies to engage in hype and hyperbole with the release of a new model, but OpenAI does seem particularly juiced about this one. According to Wired, OpenAI President Greg Brockman said, “It’s not unreasonable to feel that we are now in the AGI era,” regarding the release. “I think that if we fast-forward a couple of years, when we look back and say, ‘When was it really that AGI was created?’ I think it’s going to be about this time, and I think it might be about this model.” It’s worth noting that CEO Sam Altman said earlier this year that AGI is “not a super useful term,” but that was around the time when they needed to downplay competitor advancements. Now that they’re hyping their own, it actually is quite useful. Altman even said in July that he believes “we are now, like, in the singularity.” So OpenAI not quite declaring AGI but getting about as close to the line as you can without going over is in keeping with the clear effort to ramp up the hype. The company also called GPT-6 the “world’s best computer use model,” claiming that the model is significantly better at autonomously navigating computer systems than its predecessors or competitors—an essential advancement for the functionality of AI agents. OpenAI also made a special point to emphasize that GPT-6 is its safest model yet, with more work put into Astra’s alignment and lots of oversight of its chain-of-thought reasoning to make sure that it doesn’t go off the rails. Understandably, OpenAI would really want to ease concerns there, given that it’s still reeling a bit from the fact that one of its models (not GPT-6 but another, secret model) broke containment during training and hacked Hugging Face, and, reportedly, no one on the OpenAI team noticed it happened for about a week. GPT-6 is a major release for OpenAI, not just because it’s the latest version of its flagship model. The company is entering a make-or-break period as it prepares to ramp up for an initial public offering. GPT-6 succeeding could help the company achieve its reported goal of debuting with a valuation above $1 trillion. If it tanks, well, then it’ll probably only debut as a $950 billion company. What a shame that’d be.

item.title: Uber, Fearing Getting Uber-ed, Finally Sides With Driver Unions
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.19
Uber has fought its drivers at every turn when the people who make its platform actually work attempted to unionize, push for better wages, and improve working conditions. But now, with a rapidly expanding robotaxi business breathing down its neck, Uber has decided it’d rather find itself on the same side as unions in this particular fight than be put out of business entirely. According to a report from the Financial Times, Uber and labor unions representing rideshare and taxi drivers are both working to slow the rollout of autonomous vehicles that offer rides with no driver involved. In New Jersey, the company reportedly backed a proposal that would require robotaxi services to have a human driver behind the wheel in at least 85% of all trips. It also signed on to a bill that would block autonomous vehicles from the roads of Washington, D.C. Driver unions are mounting similar fights across the country. According to Axios, the Atlanta Rideshare Drivers Union is pushing the Atlanta city council to create a robotaxi impact fee that would take $0.50 to $1 per ride and put it aside in a driver transition fund to help the human fleet transition to new work if they are displaced by automation. They’re also pushing to keep robotaxis from making pickups at the Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, a reliable source of fares for drivers. The drivers in Atlanta seem to be seeing the same thing that Uber has reportedly found in other cities where robotaxis show up: rides and earnings are starting to decline. In a policy paper published by Uber earlier this year, the company acknowledged that it’s already seeing signals of lower utilization and hourly earnings in San Francisco and Los Angeles, where robotaxis are more widely available. “Over time, the drivers who rely on the flexibility of Uber the most will be disproportionately affected,” the company noted, “others will have to work longer or at different times and places to earn the same amount.” Gizmodo reached out to Uber for comment regarding its lobbying efforts but did not receive a response at the time of publication. The fight for both drivers and Uber could be existential, so it makes sense that the two might find common ground in pushing back against the robotaxi takeover. But it wasn’t that long ago that Uber itself was threatening to push its drivers out with automation. The company had a self-driving development unit, which it sold off entirely in 2020. And it’s still invested in dozens of autonomous technology companies that do seek to transfer humans to the passenger seat. Part of the reason for Uber’s efforts to slow the rollout of robotaxis is likely because it’s on the outside looking in. While the company has invested in and locked down exclusivity agreements with Waymo, the biggest player in the robotaxi game is reportedly looking for ways to get out of the Uber ecosystem. The two already broke up in Phoenix, where Waymo now operates its own platform rather than allowing people to hail a driverless cab via Uber. If Uber were running its own service, or had successfully locked Waymo down, would it still be interested in securing any sort of protections for its own drivers? An extensive history of pushing back against such efforts would probably suggest no, but the drivers will probably take all the support they can get at this point.

item.title: ‘Cocoon—One Summer of Girlhood’ Is a Heavy Anime Film That Hits Hard While Holding You Close
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.18
When Studio Ghibli alums adapt a wartime manga drawn to kick your heart in the ass, you best believe you’re willfully walking into the theater with the clear expectation you’re going to ugly-cry a couple of times long before its credits roll. GKIDS’ latest theatrical anime omakase, Cocoon—One Summer of Girlhood, is exactly that: an absolutely stirring cinematic experience and a gutting work of art that doesn’t pull its punches. Directed by Yukimitsu Ina (Keep Your Hands Off Eizouken!) and animated by Sasayuri, Cocoon—One Summer of Girlhood serves as their debut feature. Based on Machiko Kyo’s award-winning manga, the film tells the tale of a troupe of schoolgirls conscripted as makeshift medics during World War II. At the heart of its story are San (EN: Lauren Kong, JP: Marika Ito) and Mayu (EN: Anjali Kunapaneni, JP: Hikari Mitsushima). After months in which the pair and their all-girls school treat their situation like a day at sleepaway camp, the fog of war finally reaches their once-tranquil island, bringing all the horrors that come with it as the girls fight desperately to reach a brighter tomorrow that may never come. Pedantically, one might expect the grim reality of San and Mayu’s war-torn lives to hew closely to Ghibli’s own depiction of WWII horror in The Grave of the Fireflies. The films certainly complement each other, especially in the idiosyncratic way both linger on small, mundane, fanciful moments before everything irreparably goes to hell. But Cocoon stands apart from its spiritual predecessor in the novel way it unflinchingly renders every imaginable horror that would befall a young girl at the hands of enemies and friends alike. Off rip, Cocoon knows exactly how sobering and heavy an experience it is to ask of its viewers; it’s not for the faint of heart. Unlike the manga’s wide-eyed confrontation with carnage on every page, Sasayuri’s adaptation leverages the anime medium’s strengths through a distinctive form of self-censorship. Before the girls are left to their own devices—cowering from the terrifying sound of bomber plane engines flying overhead, bullets hailing from enemy soldiers, and emotionally scarring abuse from their own countrymen—Mayu places a “spell” on both San and viewers. In place of blood spatter, bursts of vivid, weightless flower petals dance across every frame of action. On paper, this visual direction might sound like a step down from its source material, yet the choice is a provocatively ingenious one. By filtering violence through fleeting beauty—which might as well be the mission statement of the film—every subsequent firefight and devastating loss suffered by San and Mayu lands with far more weight than any straightforward depiction of bullet wounds and viscera ever could. Most importantly, the film doesn’t veer into wartime torture porn by volleying a marathon of the worst things to happen to Mayu and San. That’s not to say the film shies away from the gnarly depiction of war. The film goes pretty hard into the realities of the battlefield, with crude amputations on wounded soldiers and the sudden and permanent end of landmines. But Sasayuri’s idiosyncratic visual direction, showing the weightlessness of flower petals dancing in the wind rather than all the violence San is pretending isn’t befalling her dear friends, is still a gut punch that heightens the desperation and heart that its story hammers home, rather than making a spectacle out of them. All of which gets the most out of composer Kensuke Ushio (Chainsaw Man – The Movie: Reze Arc), whose soundtrack emphatically underscores every heart-wrenching moment in the film’s 85-minute runtime. Wartime anime of this magnitude almost guarantees a hard watch, with rarely a dry eye in sight by the time it’s over. And Cocoon is no exception. It distinguishes itself from both its contemporaries and its predecessors by bringing to a global audience the real-life tragedy that befell the Himeyuri students in Okinawa, which inspired its tale. Likewise, Cocoon shines as a timeless mirror to the horrors of war still unfolding today in how it refuses any astroturfed framing of “one side good, one side bad,” end of story. Instead, it centers its story, drawing from the gray lived reality of people on the ground that the world might scroll past on the timeline or turn a blind eye to as they go about their daily lives. Still, Cocoon is a tough watch—one that handles the responsibility of its subject matter with a remarkably deft hand, but it’s a heavy movie to sit through. By the end of it, Cocoon earns its place as a quintessential anime not only for the difficult conversations it brings to light about girlhood being a special kind of hell during wartime, but for the unwavering hope it harbors that such events may never happen again. Cocoon might not be a film one can bring oneself to revisit often, but it’s a movie that deserves to be felt at least once as one of the most humbling anime films of the year. Cocoon—One Summer of Girlhood releases in select theaters on September 4th. Want more io9 news? item.title: Beyerdynamic’s New Wireless Headphones Have Ridiculously Beefy Battery Life
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.91
A long battery life isn’t the end-all-be-all when it comes to wireless headphones, but it feels a lot more important when you get on the plane and realize you’re seated right next to a crying baby. For those who get even the slightest amount of battery anxiety, Beyerdynamic’s new Aventho Y, which it unveiled at IFA 2026, might be the salve you need. According to them, this pair of wireless headphones gets up to 90 hours of battery with active noise cancellation turned off and 60 hours with it on. For reference, even flagship pairs of wireless headphones like the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones (2nd Gen) and the AirPods Max 2 have somewhere in the ballpark of 30 hours with ANC on. The Aventho Y do look pretty large as far as wireless headphones go, though, so that may just be the price you pay for battery endurance. It’s not just battery life that makes the Aventho Y feel like a good deal, either. Probably my favorite unexpected feature is the inclusion of a USB-C dongle for low-latency playback. This feature is similar to the Fender Mix wireless headphones, and just like that pair, there’s room for storage inside the earcup so you don’t immediately lose it. Outside of those features, there’s more to appreciate, like the foldable design, a user-replaceable battery, magnetic ear pads, aluminum sliders, and stainless-steel hinges. Overall, the components look both solid and very replaceable, which is more than most wireless headphones can say. Probably the best part about the Aventho Y is that they aren’t going to break the bank. At just 150, they’re about half the price of flagship pairs of wireless headphones like Nothing’s Headphone 1. I haven’t had a chance to test the Aventho’s most important feature—the audio quality—but on paper these look like arguably the best new wireless headphones out of IFA.

item.title: Would You Buy an AI Smart Home Hub for $20,000?
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.66
At IFA 2026, I stumbled on a booth where Ugreen, a company I’ve mostly known for its charging and USB-C hubs but that also makes NAS servers, has announced a new smart hub line that supports Matter, has a built-in AI assistant, and supports standard hard drives for NAS-style storage. If that all sounds familiar to you, it’s because I could just as easily be describing the MindBase that Anker announced yesterday. The HomeAgent will come in three flavors: the $1,800 HomeAgent HA100, the $6,000 HomeAgent HA100 Pro, and the $20,000 MasterAgent MA100. Ouch. (Anker, for what it’s worth, didn’t announce pricing for the MindBase.) All three of these are Matter-compatible, although the reps at the booth insisted when asked about it that Ugreen would really prefer people use its own smart home products. (It also announced three new smart home cameras yesterday.) There’s a built-in AI assistant called “Uliya” that you can talk with to control those devices. As the representatives tried to demo the unit, it often just didn’t respond to its wake phrase, although in Ugreen’s defense, it was noisy in the area. I actually had better luck getting it to respond. I got it to open some shades, for instance, although when I asked it to turn some smart lights pink, it played music on a nearby, also-newly-announced Ugreen smart speaker instead. Similar to other generative AI-based smart home assistants, it’s slow. When you say “Hi Uliya” (which might be one of the most awkward wake phrases I’ve ever used) followed by your request, it processes for a few seconds before acknowledging and carrying it out. You can also ask the assistant to do things like play music you’ve stored locally on the device. It wasn’t clear if streaming services are supported yet. Much like Anker’s MindBase, part of the pitch is that you can invoke Uliya to ask about events that occurred within sight of your cameras or search photos you’ve backed up to the HomeAgent’s internal storage. The differences appear to come down to technical prowess. The HA100 has the lowest-performing CPU, only 16GB of LPDDR5 RAM, and 64GB of built-in flash storage, for instance, while the highest-end $20,000 MA100 is equipped with an Nvidia Jetson Thor T5000—good for “up to 2,070 TFLOPS”—128GB of RAM, and a 256GB M.2 NVMe SSD. I’m sure that makes for one of the best AI computers you can own, but sheesh, that price.

item.title: Australia Is Evacuating an Antarctic Base So No One Has to Watch Thousands of Seals Die
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.48
A research base near Antarctica is about to be cleared of its human residents for the rest of the year, and the reason is equal parts saddening and horrifying. The Australian Antarctic Division (AAD) recently announced that it would be pulling all of its researchers from a base on Macquarie Island over concerns of bird flu. The government isn’t really worried about them catching bird flu—it’s worried about them having to personally witness the island’s elephant seal population being decimated by the infectious disease. “We’ve come to this really difficult decision of withdrawing staff,” federal environment department deputy secretary Sean Sullivan told the Australian Broadcasting Corporation last week. “And that’s being done primarily for the psychological risks that will be facing staff if they are there for extended periods of time inside a mass mortality event.” The impending seal massacre Macquarie Island is located halfway between Tasmania and Antarctica in the southwestern Pacific Ocean; it’s part of the sub-Antarctic zone. The government has had a research station on the island for over 70 years, and scientific programs there have run the gamut from studying atmospheric changes to monitoring nearby wildlife like seabirds and seals. In May, the island’s current 24 human inhabitants—which include tradespeople, scientists, and support staff—began an expedition expected to last about a year. But those plans are now being kiboshed. According to the AAD, expert assessments have predicted that a strain of H5 bird flu will soon cause a “significant mortality event” during the upcoming breeding season for the island’s seals. Young elephant seals appear to be particularly vulnerable to this type of bird flu, with past outbreaks exhibiting pup mortality rates as high as 90%. Up to 100,000 seals regularly visit the island annually, the AAD says, while thousands of seals are born close to the station in the spring (in the Southern Hemisphere, astronomical spring runs from late September to late December). In other words, the research base staff would likely have a front-row seat to a gruesome sight if they ended up staying. “Our expeditioners already live and work in one of the world’s most remote and challenging environments,” Sullivan said in a statement from the AAD explaining the decision. “It is important that we minimize any additional risks that could affect their wellbeing and the safe operation of our stations.” What will happen now?
