Australia’s icebreaking research and supply vessel, RSV Nuyina, is expected to pick up the staff and essential cargo sometime in late September or early October. No such evacuations will happen on other research stations near Antarctica since these aren’t close to wildlife that could be hit hard by bird flu. Unfortunately, the AAD says “active control measures” to help mitigate the likely outbreak among seals are not being planned due to the island’s remoteness and harsh conditions. “The Australian Antarctic Division is exploring options for monitoring the situation on Macquarie Island, with a view to returning expeditioners to the station in coming seasons,” Sullivan said. The possible silver lining here is that efforts to protect the island environment from invasive species and other disruptions have largely been successful. In 2014, for instance, the island was officially declared free of rabbits, rats, and mice. These efforts have made it easier for native animals like elephant seals to maintain robust populations, which should give them a fighting chance to bounce back from disasters like H5 bird flu, according to the AAD.

item.title: ‘Silo’ Season 3 Goes Out With a Bang
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.43
If for any reason over the past few years you ever felt like, “Man, it’s been hard to stick with Silo,” the season three finale made every second worth it. It was a shocking, brutal, excellent episode that perfectly paid off the season’s dual timeline story, while answering a bunch of questions and posing even more. To say more than that would be a massive spoiler, so let’s get into those massive spoilers for the season three finale of Silo, titled “Troy.” When we last left the characters in the previous episode, we saw the opening day of the silos and a mysterious nuclear explosion. Daniel and Helen, pregnant with their child, were separated and, we assume, forced to go into the silos they had been assigned: Number one for Daniel, number 18 for Helen. Unfortunately, the finale didn’t answer any of the questions about who set off the explosion, how everyone involved with the silos knew, or anything like that. But it did reveal the fate of most of those characters, in a way no one could have expected. The finale picks up hundreds of years in the future with Daniel waking up from some sort of cryo sleep. Only, they don’t call him Daniel. They call him “Troy.” And Troy is awakened by Victor (the doctor who helped his sister all those years ago) to help with a problem. There is an insurrection in silo 17, and Troy needs to figure out how to stop it. This is the event that Steve Zahn’s character experienced as a child, several decades before the events of the main timeline of the show. Instantly, as a viewer, we’re shook. How do all of those people we saw enter the silo hundreds of years before look exactly the same? Why is Daniel not Daniel anymore? We don’t know exactly, but apparently, Victor’s memory juice is not just working. It’s thriving. Troy goes to operations to try to fix the problem, and he runs into his sister Charlotte, though they call her “Susan.” He doesn’t recognize her. She doesn’t recognize him. And, eventually, Troy/Daniel is forced to dismiss Susan/Charlotte when she refuses to act out Troy’s plan to massacre almost 10,000 people. But he does it and is rewarded for it. Meanwhile, something is bugging Troy. Not the thousands of people he just killed to keep some silo secrets we don’t understand. He’s bothered by visions of a woman. A woman we know to be his wife, Helen. Troy asks Victor about her, and Victor says he doesn’t know what he’s talking about. However, we know Victor knew Helen, and we see that he has a file full of proof that Troy has asked him about her dozens of times. They are purposely keeping this from him. Speaking of Helen, though, we’re led to believe she ended up in silo 18, right? The same silo our show is set in? The same silo where the Pez dispenser Daniel gave her years ago shows up? The silo of Juliette Nichols, who sure seems to share that same rambunctious charm Helen had, doesn’t she? Hmmm. We wonder. Fast forward a few decades, picking up events from the end of the previous episode and finally bringing the two timelines from this season together. It’s revealed that Bernard and Camille’s suspicions from the penultimate episode are true. The all-knowing AI that gives them their orders is not a computer but a person. In this case, Victor, who is about to kill every single person in silo 18 for setting off some bombs. Camille begs him for time, which he gives, and ultimately we learn that Camille turned on her superiors and helped the rebels cap the failsafe pipe. It took all season to figure it out, but the pipe that would’ve allowed silo one to kill everyone with gas was finally located and capped, saving everyone’s lives. When Victor asks Camille why she turned her back on her superiors, she says it’s because she couldn’t answer a simple question. Why would they have the power to kill everyone? Victor doesn’t answer. Victor’s answer is to wake up Troy, which is how we learn it’s been 35 years since he killed all those people at silo 17. Apparently, silo one has a cryo process, and the people there go “on” and “off shift” every few years, which is how they age so slowly. Or, at least, that’s the implication. Senator Thurman, who runs the whole thing, looks a little older, but most everyone else is close to the age they were when it all started. Anyway, Troy is awake again and ready to figure out how to kill everyone in silo 18 when Juliette and her friends all approach the mysterious doorway down by the silo digger. This, apparently, is off limits, and Troy takes over the omniscient voice. He threatens the group, but eventually they reach a compromise—as long as they don’t try to contact any other silos, there will be no safeguard attempts. Everyone will be safe. Juliette agrees. But does she really? Of course not. This is Juliette we’re talking about, and she hatches a plan to not just save everyone in her silo, but all the silos. The one thing she feels silo one won’t be expecting is a full-on assault, and that’s what she wants to do. Meanwhile, we learn that Victor killed himself after the events earlier in the episode, and Troy gets a posthumous email from him. Victor reveals that he felt relief that the people of silo 18 stopped the failsafe, implying maybe he didn’t buy into their mission as much as he had for the past few centuries. That’s why he took his life. But before he went, he had one more piece of info for Troy—a name: Helen Drew. And, it seems, the name certainly triggered something. It would, considering she was your wife and the mother of a child you never got to meet. So the tables are set for the fourth and final season of Silo. Juliette Nichols is ready to take silo 18 out into the world and save the rest of the silos. The leaders in silo one, who have been around for centuries maintaining this mysterious balance, may have started to see some cracks. And there are certainly implications that Juliette, or someone, in silo 18 has some relation to Daniel, aka Troy, one of the top leaders. And yet, there are still so many questions that it’s almost silly. Who set off the explosion in the past? How did everyone know about it? Why did they do it? Why did they set up a system that they’d rather people die than communicate with each other? Can they repopulate the world at some point? Is there even a world left out there? What is the ultimate plan? Why isn’t this cryo sleep technology being used for better things? Again, so many questions. But this is Silo. And we’d have it no other way. The season three finale proved that even though Silo is always gonna have us asking questions, when we get the answers, it will be worth it. We just have to be patient. Here are a few other things we wondered: - The Senator says that Charlotte/Susan can’t be punished for her insubordination because her skills as a pilot will be crucial at the end of the mission. What does that mean? What is the ending? - The silos were the brainchild of Per Stensen (Colin Hanks) and Senator Rosalind Thurman, right? Well, the senator is still alive, kicking, and running the whole thing. But where is Stensen? And, yes, we know Silo is based on a series of books, and the answers are out there and accessible. But we’re talking about the show and prefer to experience the story that way. Want more io9 news? Check out when to expect the latest Marvel, Star Wars, and Star Trek releases, what’s next for the DC Universe on film and TV, and everything you need to know about the future of Doctor Who.

item.title: How to avoid paying a smart doorbell subscription fee
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.61
Are you hoping to avoid yet another subscription? Rather than opting for a Ring Protect or Nest Aware plan, buy a smart doorbell that gives you options instead. Here’s how to avoid the ongoing fees. Premium subscriptions are optional Accept fewer features Broadly speaking, most smart doorbells come with basic functionality out of the box. You’re able to answer the door on a smartphone or tablet, connect to the camera to view a live feed and get limited notifications of activity. Amazon’s Ring doorbells come with a 30-day trial of Ring Protect, while Google’s Nest doorbell has a 3-hour video history included for free but requires a premium Nest Aware subscription for longer. Some features like Ring’s Person Alerts and Google’s sound detection also depend on these services. If you want your smart doorbell to work more like a security system, you’ll need some way to save your recordings. Though many smart doorbell providers will try to tempt you into a monthly or annual subscription, there are other ways of doing it. If all you want is the basic functionality of being able to remotely answer the doorbell and not missing a package then you can ignore these options altogether. Store captured footage on an SD card You might miss out on some features, but you won't pay for video storage The most convenient way to avoid paying a smart doorbell cloud storage fee is to buy a smart doorbell that stores footage on a memory card instead. This is a cost-effective way to store recordings since flash memory is cheap and you can spend as little or as much on a card that suits your budget. Some of the cheapest doorbells on the market store footage on local memory, like the WYZE Video Doorbell v2 and the eufy Video Doorbell C210. Many of the more expensive ones have this option too. You don’t even need to manage space manually as most doorbells that offer this option will automatically remove the oldest footage and keep recording. In the event that you need access to your footage for some reason, you can simply eject the memory card and put it in a computer to copy the files across. There are a few downsides to this approach, the most obvious one being a lack of redundancy. Since all of your footage will be stored on a single memory card, if something happens to your storage medium the footage will be lost. This includes an intruder tampering with your doorbell. Though most doorbells that offer this option have a locking mechanism in place, these aren't infallible. If the intruder knows that your doorbell is a variety that uses a memory card for storage, they may feel inclined to break in and steal the card. On top of this, you might find yourself in a situation where you need to access recordings remotely. If the only place you have stored your footage is on local memory, you won’t be able to review the footage until you physically gain access to your doorbell. Of course, local memory card backup works great as part of a multifaceted approach to data storage. Get a HomeKit Secure video doorbell Let your HomePod or iPad do the heavy lifting If you happen to be an Apple user with an iCloud+ subscription, HomeKit Secure Video might be the best solution. For this to work, you will need a HomeKit hub such as an Apple TV 4K, a HomePod, or an iPad that remains home and acts as a local server. You'll also need a smart doorbell that is compatible with HomeKit Secure Video such as the Aqara Smart Video Doorbell G4 or the Logitech Circle View Doorbell. These aren’t the cheapest doorbells on the market, but since they can use Apple’s servers for data storage you’ll likely make your money back in the long-run. HomeKit Secure Video can be used to stream video live from your doorbell camera using the Home app on any Apple device connected to your Apple ID. Live feeds are encrypted end-to-end for security purposes. You’ll also get notifications of events detected by your camera, including people calling or packages being delivered. This footage is analyzed locally on your HomeKit hub rather than being sent to a remote server. This privacy-centric approach taken by Apple has been criticized in the past since it isn't as advanced as some of the alternatives that are processed in the cloud. You can use a single camera with a 50GB iCloud+ subscription, or you'll get up to five cameras with a 200GB plan. If you subscribe to the 2 TB plan, you can use as many cameras as you like. Footage stored on Apple’s servers is kept for 10 days and does not count towards your iCloud storage quota. The big benefit to using HomeKit Secure Video instead of solely relying on a memory card is that your footage will be available remotely, so you can view it from anywhere. Store footage on a local recorder Some doorbells are made for local storage Many “proper” home security systems use an NVR—or network video recorder—to store footage locally within the premises. This is overkill for a video doorbell system, though you can certainly find doorbells out there that support the necessary protocols. A better solution is to buy a smart doorbell that comes with a user-friendly solution like the eufy Video Doorbell S220. This doorbell uses eufy’s Homebase system, which acts as a hub for local recordings. There are no ongoing costs since captured footage is stored locally on the Homebase. eufy’s solution is user-upgradeable and works with the company’s other security cameras. Analysis takes place locally on the hub, with all footage encrypted. The fact that the Homebase remains inside your property means that tampering with the doorbell will not jeopardize your footage. You’ll pay a bit more for a bundle that includes a Homebase, but there’s no ongoing fee. Some doorbells include cloud or FTP support Build your own security camera server! If you avoid companies like Ring and Google, you might just find a doorbell that allows you to “roll your own” backup solution. This can require some work on your part, and there are very few models on the market that offer this option at present. Arguably the best right now is the Reolink Video Doorbell PoE or Reolink Video Doorbell Wi-Fi, depending on your needs. These affordable cameras can be had for around $100, use microSD storage, and automatically sync recordings with an FTP server of your choice. You’ll need to follow Reolink’s instructions to get everything working. Alternatively, the Netatmo Smart Video Doorbell offers up to 32GB local storage on a microSD card, with optional Dropbox or FTP upload. The big problem here is that this doorbell has been discontinued and can be hard to find. Use Home Assistant instead Own your own smart home Home Assistant is an open-source smart home platform that allows you to use devices from a range of different smart home ecosystems. In order to use Home Assistant, you’ll need to install it on a device such as a Raspberry Pi or spare computer that remains running on your local network. Since everything takes place locally, Home Assistant will record video captured by your smart doorbell (and similar cameras) to local storage. If you want to capture more footage, add more storage and scale up your Home Assistant server accordingly. The biggest hurdle you’re likely to encounter with the Home Assistant approach is finding a suitable doorbell and setting it up accordingly. There are many threads on the Home Assistant message boards asking for recommendations, with some members going as far as building their own solutions. If you aren’t already using Home Assistant, this approach will require a bit of work. You should search the Home Assistant Integrations database to see what options are available to you. Some manufacturers like Aquara have committed to providing support for Home Assistant through Matter support. On the upside, Home Assistant is completely free to download and install. You’ll lose nothing but an afternoon downloading and testing it out on an old piece of hardware, and you’ll likely discover just how powerful Home Assistant automations can be in the process. In some cases, a cloud subscription is just better and easier If money isn’t a concern and you’re happy to pay for a premium cloud backup and extra bells and whistles, premium subscriptions have their place. HomeKit Secure Video is another great option that doesn’t require too much setup.

item.title: 3 little-known Excel tools worth exploring this weekend (September 4-6)
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.40
Excel has plenty of features that can make everyday spreadsheet work easier, but some of the most useful ones are surprisingly easy to overlook. If you have a little time to experiment this weekend, try three of my favorite hidden gems. Custom Lists can teach Excel your own order Make Excel fill and sort the way you actually work Excel already knows that Monday comes after Sunday and February comes after January. But you can also teach it sequences that are specific to how you work. Custom Lists let you create your own order and then use it with Excel's fill handle or sorting tools. For example, a project tracker might use three priorities: High, Medium, and Low. To create this sequence: - Go to File > Options, then open the Advanced menu. - Scroll to the General section and click Edit Custom Lists. - Select NEW LIST. - Enter the items in the order you want them. - Click Add, then OK. Now type the first word in your list into a cell and drag the fill handle down. Instead of repeating that word, Excel continues with the next items in the sequence you created. You can also drag the sequence across a row if you want to create a set of column headings or another repeating structure. You might be thinking this is only useful for niche scenarios, but Custom Lists really earn their keep when you need to sort data according to your own logic. Excel's standard alphabetical sort would put these priorities in the order High → Low → Medium, but that's rarely useful. With a custom list, you can have Excel sort the data according to the order you've defined. Here's how: - Select your table. - Go to Data > Sort. - Select the column you want to sort. - Choose Customized List from the Order menu. - Select the custom list you created, then click OK. Excel sorts the entire table according to that hierarchy. You can also import a longer sequence from an existing worksheet rather than entering each item manually. Once created, the list is saved in Excel's settings, so you can use it again in other workbooks on the same computer. Excel's Camera tool can put live data anywhere Turn a range into a picture that stays up to date Copying cells from one part of a workbook to another is easy enough, but a normal copy can quickly become outdated when the original data changes. Excel's Camera tool creates an image of a cell range that stays linked to the original cells. Change the source data, and the picture updates too. This can be particularly useful when creating a dashboard. Suppose a detailed monthly budget sits on one worksheet, while a separate dashboard needs to display those figures. Instead of copying the cells and maintaining a second version, use Camera to display the original range on the dashboard. First, you'll need to add Camera to your Quick Access Toolbar (QAT): - Click the down arrow on the right-hand side of any tab on the ribbon. If you see Show Quick Access Toolbar, click it to activate your QAT. - Click the QAT down arrow and select More Commands. - Select All Commands in the Choose commands from menu. - Scroll to and select Camera, click Add to add it to your QAT, then click OK. You'll now see Camera in your QAT. Now, select the cells you want to display, click Camera, move to the destination worksheet, and click and drag to place the picture. The result looks like an ordinary image while remaining connected to the source range. If a budget figure or some formatting changes in the original cells, the corresponding figure in the image changes as well. The captured range can also be moved and resized, making it easy to position alongside charts, headings, or other dashboard elements. Camera works best with fixed ranges. If the source is an Excel table that regularly expands, newly added rows may not appear in the captured image. And if you want to capture a chart or another object, select the cells behind it rather than the object itself. Analyze Data can find insights without formulas Let Excel do some of the investigative work When you're working with a large table of records, finding useful patterns can mean building formulas, creating PivotTables, or manually sorting and filtering the data. Analyze Data (previously called Ideas) can give you a useful starting point much faster. If you're using Excel for Microsoft 365 and have an internet connection, you can use this tool to automatically examine a structured dataset for patterns and summaries. To use it, select a single cell inside your data, then click Analyze Data in the Data tab. In some versions of Excel, this button is found in the Home tab. Excel opens a pane containing automatically generated insight cards based on the information it finds. You can also type a question into the box at the top of the pane. For example, because this dataset contains "Genre" and "Rating" columns, you could ask, "What average rating does each genre have?" Excel analyzes the data and produces a result that may include a summary table or visualization. If the result is useful, click the contextual Insert button to add the generated chart, PivotTable, or PivotChart to your worksheet. You can also try one of the suggested questions Excel generates based on your data. Analyze Data works best when the source is properly structured. Make sure your data has a single header row and avoid unnecessary blank rows or columns. Formatting the range as an Excel table with Ctrl+T is also a good idea. There's always more to discover in Excel This weekend is as good as any to explore some of Excel's lesser-known features. Custom Lists can make Excel follow your preferred order, Camera can keep a live view of important cells elsewhere in a workbook, and Analyze Data can quickly uncover patterns in a table. There's so much hidden away in Excel that the discovery never really ends. So, if you still have some time to explore, take a look at some little-known Excel clicks that can further power up your spreadsheet skills.

item.title: I built an Excel job tracker that tells me more than where I applied
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.25
Once you've applied for more than a handful of jobs, keeping track of them can become a job in itself. You need to remember where you applied, when you applied, how you applied, who you spoke to, what the salary was, and whether you ever heard back. I built an Excel spreadsheet to keep all of that information in one place. Then I added a few features that make it more useful than a simple list of applications. You can download a free, editable copy of my job-search tracker at the bottom of this article. I wanted one place to keep track of every application Everything I need in a single worksheet I started with the information you'd expect in a job-search tracker: the position, company, industry, location, type (permanent, fixed term, temporary, contract), schedule (full-time, part-time, freelance), date applied, status, and notes. These are the basic details I want to capture for every application. I also included a few less-obvious fields: contact, salary range, application method, follow-up date, and a checkbox to indicate whether I've followed up. The result is a fairly wide spreadsheet, but that's intentional. A job application can involve a surprising amount of information, and I don't want to rely on my memory to keep track of it. I also turned the range into an Excel table, so adding a new application automatically extends the formatting and formulas. Above the table, four cards show the total number of applications, active applications, interviews, and urgent follow-ups. I can see exactly where every application stands A quick glance tells me what's happening The Status column is one of the most important parts of the tracker. It uses a data validation drop-down list containing "Applied," "Interview," "Offer," "Rejected," and "Withdrawn." Conditional formatting changes the appearance of each row according to the option I choose. Interview rows turn blue, successful applications turn green and bold, while rejected and withdrawn applications become gray and italicized. That means I can scan the spreadsheet and get a quick idea of what's happening without having to read the Status column for every application. I don't have to remember when I should follow up Excel keeps an eye on the calendar This is where the spreadsheet starts doing some of the work for me. The Follow-up column automatically calculates a date seven days after I apply. The formula is: =IF([@Status]="Applied", IF([@[Followed up]], "Done", [@Applied]+7), "-") If the application is still marked "Applied," Excel adds seven days to the application date. If I check the checkbox in the adjacent Followed up column, the corresponding Follow-up cell changes to "Done." If the application has moved to another status, it displays a dash. Finally, I used conditional formatting to make follow-ups due today or within the next three days orange, while overdue follow-ups turn red. That gives me a clear visual reminder of what needs my attention. I can see which applications are going stale Waiting is part of the process, too The Days column automatically counts how long an application has been sitting without progressing. Here's the formula: =IF([@Status]="Applied", TODAY()-[@Applied], "") An application submitted yesterday and one submitted three weeks ago are very different situations, even though both might still have an "Applied" status. This column makes that difference obvious. I can narrow down my job search in a couple of clicks I don't have to sift through every row The tracker has three slicers: one for Status, one for Type, and another for Schedule. I positioned them above the table, alongside the summary cards, so the main controls are always easy to reach. Because the slicers work together, I can combine them to create a much more specific view. For example, I could show only permanent, full-time positions that have reached the interview stage. I grouped the three slicers together so they stay aligned when I use them, then froze the top seven rows and the first two columns. This keeps the slicers, summary cards, column headings, and Position and Company columns visible as I scroll through the tracker. I can keep track of the details I'd otherwise forget The small details can matter later The less obvious columns are just as useful. I record the contact person's email address when I have one, and because Excel automatically turns email addresses into hyperlinks (unless you manually disable automatic hyperlinks in Excel Options), a single click opens up my email app with the recipient's email address already in the "To" line. The salary range makes it easier for me to sort the jobs by pay or compare like-for-like if I get two offers. The application method gives me a quick reminder of where to go to check the application status. It also gives me useful context if I contact a recruiter directly. I can tell them which position I applied for and where I submitted my application. I did consider adding a link to each job advert, but there's a problem: job listings disappear. Companies close applications, recruiters remove listings, and platforms eventually stop showing the original advert. The Notes column is there for everything that doesn't fit neatly elsewhere: someone recommending me for the role, something a recruiter mentioned, or a detail I want to remember if I eventually get an interview. I made a few changes to make it feel like an app The finishing touches matter Once the functionality was there, I made a few visual changes to make the tracker feel more like a dedicated job-search tool: - I turned off Excel's gridlines. The table already provides the visual structure, so the gridlines were just adding clutter. - I turned off the table's banded rows. I wanted the status colors to do the visual work, and the alternating row colors were competing with the conditional formatting. - I formatted the slicers to match the table. This makes them feel like part of the interface rather than objects I've simply dropped onto the worksheet. - I autofit the columns. I wanted enough room for the information to be readable without leaving unnecessary gaps between columns. With those changes, plus the frozen headers and grouped slicers, the finished spreadsheet looks surprisingly close to a dedicated job-application app. It's more useful than a list What started as a simple list of applications is now a tracker that tells me where I've applied, what stage I'm at, how long I've been waiting, and what needs my attention. A few formulas, checkboxes, drop-down lists, slicers, summary cards, and conditional formatting have turned a basic Excel table into something I can actually use to manage my job search. Download a free, editable copy of my tracker. When you click the link, you'll find the download button in the top-right corner. Open the file in Excel, replace "Start here" with your first application, and you're ready to go.

item.title: I turned my $15 ESP32 into a mini PC with this tiny OS
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.24
ESP32 boards are cheap and versatile, making them highly popular in the maker community. Setting them up isn't always that simple, but there's a tiny OS you can run on an ESP32 that allows you to use one as if it were a very small PC. An operating system you can run on an ESP32 A microcontroller you can use like a real PC Usually when you're building something with an ESP32, you flash dedicated firmware to the device that does one specific job. Tactility is a completely different approach. It's a tiny operating system designed to run on the ESP32 microcontroller family. Tactility supports a wide range of ESP32 devices, with the recommended models including the LilyGO T-Deck Plus, the Elecrow CrowPanel Advance 2.8", the M5Stack Tab 5, M5Stack Cardputer and Cardputer Adv models, and the Cheap Yellow Display 2432S032C. Tactility has a graphical interface, and as the name suggests, it's primarily intended to be used via a touchscreen. Once installed on an ESP32 connected to a screen, you can navigate the OS just as you would with a typical PC operating system. Getting it running was (almost) plug and play There were a few issues during setup I decided to try to run Tactility on my Cheap Yellow Display, a CYD 2432S028R. While this isn't one of the recommended devices, it is listed as supported, although it lacks the external RAM of some other devices. Installation and setup should be fairly simple, but I did hit a couple of bumps in the road. The simplest method is to use the web installer and connect your ESP32 device to the same computer. You can use the web installer to erase the current firmware and install Tactility. My first issue was that there are three different build options for the various CYD 2432S028R models, and I chose the wrong one on my first try. When the installation process finished, the CYD just displayed a green screen. I tried again with a different build, and the OS was up and running in under two minutes. The second issue was working through the initial setup screens. The OS requires a Wi-Fi connection to download additional apps, and I couldn't get it to connect to my Wi-Fi. The issue was that my CYD only supports 2.4 GHz, so I used a different SSID that operates solely at 2.4 GHz, and the Wi-Fi connected without any problems. You get a basic OS that can run small apps There are some fun apps and some useful apps Once I'd completed the setup, I was greeted with three simple icons. There's an app icon, a folder icon, and a settings icon. The file icon opens a file browser that lets you browse the internal or microSD card storage. The settings icon gives access to settings such as the display settings, Wi-Fi settings, and language settings. Tapping the apps icon brings up the list of preinstalled apps. These include the App Hub app (an app store for Tactility), a chat app for chatting with other local Tactility devices, an I2C scanner, a notes app, and a web server app. Using the App Hub, you can search for and download additional apps. The installed apps are mostly utilities, but you can install some fun apps via the App Hub. You can install a version of the 2048 number puzzle game, a Tamagotchi-like game, and even an EPUB reader. You can also develop and run your own apps in Tactility. Unsurprisingly, the OS is still very limited Without PSRAM, there's a lot you can't run Before you start unplugging your mini PC to throw it in the trash, you should be aware of the limitations. Unsurprisingly for an OS running on an ESP32, the apps that you can run are extremely limited. I wasn't able to run some of the apps from the App Hub because my CYD lacks PSRAM. Some ESP32 boards have additional RAM in the form of PSRAM that provides additional memory beyond the internal RAM of the ESP32 itself. Without PSRAM, my CYD can't run the EPUB reader app, which is a shame as I've become a little bit obsessed with tiny eReaders since getting one of my own. It means that I'm limited to what I can do with Tactility on my CYD, although some of the larger CYD variants do have PSRAM. I'm not going to be using Tactility on my CYD for any projects in the near future, as the limited resources of the device are better suited to dedicated firmware. Even so, it's impressive to see a genuine OS running on an ESP32. You can do a lot with an ESP32 Some people are put off experimenting with ESP32 boards because they assume you need to write complex code or get busy with a soldering iron to do anything useful with them. Tactility proves you can get an ESP32 running real apps with nothing but a USB cable and a browser.

item.title: 4 more excellent local LLM projects you can run for free on a slow laptop
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.24
An old laptop isn't the kind of device you think of when someone says "local AI," but as long as you pick the right AI, they can be pretty useful. Whatever device you use, it needs 8GB of RAM at a minimum, though 16GB is better. Luckily, even laptops from five years ago frequently had that much memory available. Cherry Studio is a local-first AI studio Don't upload sensitive documents to the cloud If you've ever wanted to use an AI to analyze a bank statement, medical records, or a tax document, but you don't want to upload it to the internet, you should try Cherry Studio instead. Cherry Studio is a free, open-source desktop app that acts as a front end for local AI models running with Ollama. It supports built-in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), so you can provide it with information to work with. You can load in PDFs, documents, spreadsheets, and then talk to an AI running on your local PC about the data. Some small AI models (4–12 billion parameters) will run reasonably well on a CPU, and if you have a GPU, you can run even faster models. It also includes a whole range of built-in tools and MCP, which allows you to connect it to most anything you want. Remember that RAG is only fully private if you use a local model. If you use a cloud embedding service, your documents still leave your PC. Jan is a polished chatbot It is similar to ChatGPT in many ways If you're not a fan of the command line, Jan is a pretty good option. It is a fully open-source desktop app that combines a model downloader, an inference engine, and a chat interface into one package. That means you don't need to work with the terminal to pull models with Ollama or anything like that. It is designed for convenience, and you don't get the granular customization with Jan that you do using llama.cpp directly, but that is a small price to pay for the simplicity. You also need to try and keep your model sizes and expectations in check. 8GB of RAM (or even 16GB) can't match the reasoning capabilities of a frontier, cloud-based model. Still, it can be useful for extracting data or discussing the contents of a folder. Transcribe audio for free with whisper.cpp Fast speech-to-text on a CPU If you ever need to transcribe audio to text, Whisper.cpp is a great option. It is a CPU-optimized variant of OpenAI's whisper models. On even a moderately capable CPU, you can get real-time or close to real-time audio transcription. That makes it suitable for simple voice recognition tasks for a voice assistant. If you have a low-power CPU, Whisper is still great for batch processing audio transcripts that you don't need done in real time. Your only costs are the laptop itself (which is often something you already own) and the electricity, The small or base models are accurate enough for most applications and will happily run in 8GB of RAM. Depending on your workflow, you may also need FFmpeg to handle file conversion first. However, with a little bit of setup, you get automated AI transcription that is completely private. Add a coding autocomplete to VS Code with Continue A small local coder model can do small, simple tasks well If you're a programmer working with an NDA, or just someone that values their privacy, you could try out Continue. Continue is an extension for VS Code that allows you to connect your IDE to a local AI server to provide inline autocomplete. You can also chat with the model about your code in a menu on the side. Typically, when you think of vibe coding you think of large, expensive frontier models, but they're not really necessary for simple things like generating regex and simple lines of code. You can find models in the 1.5B to 4B parameter range that are actually fairly capable. The only significant trade-off is latency. Completion on an older laptop CPU is not instantaneous like it is with a cloud service, and the larger your model, the worse that gets. I'd recommend using the smallest possible model for tab-autocomplete and only using a larger model for the chat panel to get the best performance-to-utility ratio. Sometimes a bit slow is completely fine Local AI on an old laptop when you can keep your projects focused, or you don't need it to run in real time. So long as you're careful about your application, it is an easy win for privacy and cost. If you aren't sure where to start, try Jan. It is very easy to get running and is useful "out of the box." Whisper.cpp is another favorite. It runs on almost anything, including a Raspberry Pi 4 or 5. That makes it suitable for a DIY home voice assistant that is completely private.

item.title: 5 hidden tricks hiding in your PC's headphone jack that beat Bluetooth every time
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.16
For many people, Bluetooth headphones are not and never have been a straight-up replacement for wired—they're just convenient to use on the go. But manufacturers have been trying to kill the 3.5mm jack for years now, stripping it from flagship phone models and even laptops. When this happens, however, you're losing more than just a headphone slot. Because this flexible little port is no one-trick pony. It can actually do quite a lot. And with its mere 5-10ms of latency, it can do those things very fast. Send lossless digital audio out through an optical cable Some 3.5mm jacks are secretly optical ports in disguise On some PCs—more often laptops and certain motherboards—the 3.5mm jack does double duty as a mini-TOSLINK optical output. A quick way to find out if this applies to yours is to darken the room and see if you can spot some red light emitting from around the jack. This is an emitter LED sending audio as pulses of light, sitting right alongside the copper contacts that handle your analog plugs. With this, you can run a clean digital signal straight to a soundbar, AV receiver, or external DAC using a cheap 3.5mm-to-TOSLINK adapter. However, there's no electrical power involved here, so the device you're feeding needs its own power and its own optical input. And, over optical S/PDIF, a PC will usually downmix to 2-channel PCM unless the sound hardware supports Dolby Digital Live or DTS Connect, which encode 5.1 on the fly for the cable. Turn it into an audio input to record from other gear Your output jack can be re-tasked as a line-in A 3.5mm jack is physically the same hardware whether it's pushing sound out or pulling it in, and on a lot of Realtek-based PCs, you can flip its role in software. Open the Realtek Audio Console, find Connector Retasking, and you can tell the driver what you actually plugged in. In plain terms, connector retasking lets the audio driver treat one physical jack as a different kind of connection—so a port that ships as an output can be reassigned as a mic or line-level input, if your codec and board support it. Suddenly you can record a synth, a mixer, or a cassette deck straight into your machine. As with most of the items on this list, however, whether you can do it or not depends on your hardware. Specifically, your codec, board, and driver version. And for laptop owners, it's even more complicated. A single 3.5mm combo jack on a laptop is usually TRRS, which only provides a mono microphone input, not a proper stereo line-in, so it's not suited to recording a stereo source like a synth or turntable at line level. Feed a bigger sound system Like an amp, powered speakers, or a soundbar Here's a good one—you can connect a 3.5mm-to-RCA or 3.5mm-to-3.5mm cable to the aux input on a stereo amp, a set of powered bookshelf speakers, or a soundbar. If you've been suffering through the tinny speakers built into your monitor, I bet you can hack together a better setup this way. There's a right way to do it, though. A PC headphone jack is an amplified output tuned to drive headphones, not a true fixed-level line-out. So when you feed powered speakers or an amp, start with the PC volume low and raise it gradually to avoid a hot, distorted signal. And if your gear offers a choice, remember how the two paths differ: the optical route sends digital audio for the receiver to convert, while the 3.5mm route sends already-converted analog—if your gear has both inputs, optical keeps the conversion (and any PC electrical noise) out of the signal path. Record real instruments by turning your PC into an interface Guitar, bass, or keyboard, straight into the jack Building on that input trick, the jack can become the front door to a home recording setup. With a small iRig-style adapter (or a retasked line-in), you can capture a guitar, bass, or keyboard into a DAW, and some of those adapters even let your PC stand in for a pedalboard as a multi-effects processor. Don't expect too much from this little hack, however. A guitar or bass is a high-impedance instrument signal, so it usually needs an interface or a Hi-Z input to be captured cleanly. Plugging straight into a mic jack often gives a weak, noisy result. Think of this as the cheap way to start rather than a studio replacement; a dedicated USB interface will always be quieter and lower-latency, and you'll still want a decent pair of headphones to monitor what you're capturing. But for laying down an idea at midnight, the jack you already have is more than enough. Split it so two people can listen at once One jack, two (or more) sets of headphones This is one of the most useful but also one of the best-known tricks for headphone jacks. We've had Bluetooth headphones for so long, and yet support for connecting multiple sets to one device has been so, so slow and patchy. With wired headphones, all you need is a three-dollar Y-splitter. It turns a single jack into two, so two people can share a movie on a laptop without huddling over one earbud each—and some splitters fan out to as many as six sockets. However, splitting literally divides the signal, so each pair can end up a little quieter, especially with harder-to-drive headphones. But for casual listening on a plane or a couch, though, you'll probably never notice. Not bad for a port everyone keeps trying to kill Some people will have a PC that can do just about everything on this list, while others will only be able to do one or two, but the point is—the 3.5mm jack can do lots of cool stuff, and manufacturers are wrong to try and sideline it. If you want to try any of these out, just remember to check if your hardware is compatible before buying any adapters.

item.title: Excel dashboards kept sending me down a rabbit hole. Gemini got me out
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.75
I'm forever creating dashboards in Excel, and while I get a lot of satisfaction from it, that's part of the problem. I end up going down a rabbit hole, adding more charts, and then wondering whether I left anything out. There's no handbook for creating a dashboard in Excel, as every dataset is different. So I decided to let Gemini do the decision-making for me. I gave Gemini my spreadsheet data and a single instruction I wanted it to decide what mattered I started with two CSV files containing a small library dataset: 40 authors and 180 books. I used CSV files rather than XLSX files because, in my experience, AI chatbots tend to handle datasets better when I strip out all the Excel-specific baggage. The files were linked by the AuthorID column, but I deliberately didn't explain this to Gemini—I wanted it to discover the relationship between them on its own. I kept my actual instruction surprisingly short. Instead of specifying a layout or telling it which charts to use, I simply gave it the data and asked it to analyze what it had been given before deciding what would make the standalone offline app useful. I did make sure it included the ability to add and manage authors and books, export the data, reset it, and keep my changes between sessions. Those were important because I wanted to test whether the finished app could actually replace the sort of ongoing spreadsheet workflow I had in mind, rather than simply produce a nice-looking demo. But that was essentially it. I was interested in seeing whether it could make sensible design decisions from the data itself, rather than simply following a detailed specification I'd written. Why Gemini? I've tested AI for various different projects in the past, and Gemini has often come out on top. For example, I found that Gemini was better than ChatGPT at turning my data into a dashboard in Excel. I've also compared how Gemini and Claude coped with turning a spreadsheet into an offline app, and Gemini's output felt more practical and usable. So I wanted to see whether Gemini could go one step further: take two separate CSVs, understand the relationships between them, and generate a standalone interactive app. Gemini built a dashboard I actually wanted to look at It didn't try to visualize everything The result was much more restrained than some of the dashboards I've built myself—but that's a good thing. Gemini built a clean overview with four summary cards that show key information from the library, including the number of authors and books, the number of pages read, and the average rating. Underneath, it used four straightforward bar charts showing books by genre, reading status, top authors by average rating, and authors by country. What impressed me most was what Gemini didn't do. It could have filled the screen with pie charts, percentages, and other visualizations simply because the data was available. Instead, it made a judgment about how much information belonged on the main screen and left the rest alone. It also gave the app a proper navigation structure. I could move between the overview, Book Explorer, and Author Directory, then drill into individual authors or books when I wanted more detail. Author information, for example, wasn't dumped onto the main dashboard. I had to click through to see an author's details and bibliography. In Excel, I'd have to make those decisions myself, then build the worksheets, navigation, links, filters, and supporting elements to make everything work together. Gemini simply made the choices for me. A good-looking app is useless if the data doesn't work I put Gemini's creation through its paces Once I liked the look of it, I wanted to see whether the app was actually usable. I opened the Book Explorer first, where I could search by title or author, filter by genre and reading status, and sort the results by title, rating, publication year, or page count. These controls worked together, too, so I could, for example, filter the library by a particular genre and reading status and then search within those results. Next, I made some changes to the data in the app to see how it reacted. First, I added an unread book to an existing author. The book count updated to 181 instantly, the new title appeared in the catalog, the author relationship was correct, and the author's bibliography reflected this change. I then added a read book for the same author and gave it a rating of 5. Gemini handled the rating logic correctly: the rating field only became active when I selected Read, while books marked Reading or Want to read could be added with the rating left blank. Next, I added a completely new author and then created a book for that author. The counts in the top-right corner updated, the new book was correctly associated with the new author, and the author's book count and other derived information updated accordingly. When I refreshed the page, my changes remained, and the same was true when I closed and reopened the HTML file. The whole thing also worked offline, which was one of my original requirements. And when I exported both the Books and Authors datasets as CSV files, the new records and their relationships were included. Finally, I reset the app, and everything returned to the original 40 authors and 180 books. Gemini made some surprisingly good decisions But there's one thing to be aware of I've run lots of experiments on making AI tools produce working code, so I wasn't surprised that Gemini could generate a working app from spreadsheet data. But what did surprise me was the quality of the decisions behind the app. The overview wasn't overloaded, the four charts were easy to understand, the summary cards gave me the headline figures, and deeper information was available when I needed it rather than being pushed onto the main screen. That restraint is probably the part I'd find hardest to reproduce if I started building the interface myself. Gemini effectively acted as the person saying, "That's enough." One thing I'd keep in mind, though, is the size of the dataset. In an earlier experiment with a much larger dataset of around 5,000 records, Gemini struggled to embed something of that size into a single standalone HTML app. That wasn't an issue with this 180-book library, but if I were working with a much larger dataset, I'd consider manipulating or reducing the data first rather than expecting Gemini to package everything into one file. Gemini gave me something that felt like a real app I set out to escape my usual Excel dashboard rabbit hole, where I would normally keep adding charts and tweaking the layout until I convinced myself everything was covered. This time, I handed those decisions to Gemini, and the result was an app that felt like it had been designed around my data rather than around Excel.

item.title: Google's new Pixel phone revives a classic feature that other phones already do better
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.73
The Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL bring back notification lights with a feature called HiLight. It's a nice touch, but Google isn't the first to modernize this idea, and its version currently trails what's already on the market. What is HiLight? A glowing ring built around the Pixel 11 Pro's camera flash HiLight is Google's attempt to revive the notification LED, a feature that used to be common on phones before AMOLED displays and always-on screens made it feel unnecessary. On the Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL, Google repurposed the LED built into the camera flash housing so it can glow in different colors and patterns, giving you glanceable information without lighting up the entire screen or requiring you to pick up the phone. The most visible use case ties into Gemini. When you prompt the assistant, the light shifts through different patterns to indicate whether it's listening, thinking, or responding, turning what used to be a purely audio or on-screen interaction into something you can register out of the corner of your eye. Google is also using HiLight for calls, letting you assign custom colors to specific contacts so you can tell who's calling without turning the phone over. Google frames this as a way to stay connected without distraction, especially when the phone is resting face down on a desk or nightstand. Instead of a buzzing, screen-lit interruption, you get a quiet pulse of color that only escalates to something more if you choose to engage with it. The company has also said more capabilities are coming, including notifications for messages from favorite contacts, suggesting HiLight is meant to grow into a broader notification system over time rather than launching as a finished one. It's a clever piece of hardware reuse, since Google didn't need to add new components to bring the feature to life. But as it stands today, HiLight is a fairly narrow implementation of an idea that other companies have been building out for years. Where does HiLight fall short? Limited to three phones and a small handful of triggers The first limitation is availability. HiLight is exclusive to the Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL, as well as the Pixel 11 Pro Fold, so anyone buying the standard Pixel 11 doesn't get it. That's a reasonable way to differentiate the higher-end models, but it also means the feature Google is using to market the whole lineup is unavailable to most buyers. The second issue is scope. At launch, HiLight only reacts to two things: Gemini's listening and response states, and incoming calls from contacts you've assigned a color to. It still doesn't support the kinds of notifications people rely on most, like messages, calendar reminders, or third-party app alerts. Google has said this is coming, but for now, HiLight functions more like a proof of concept than a fully useful feature There's also the matter of hardware design. HiLight uses a single LED zone wrapped around the camera flash, which limits how expressive the lighting can be. You get color and pulse patterns, but not the kind of segmented, multi-zone lighting that can represent more complex information at a glance, like a countdown or a progress indicator. Finally, HiLight only works when the phone is face down, which mirrors the same constraint that made old notification LEDs less useful once phones started living in pockets and bags rather than sitting screen-up on a desk. If your phone isn't positioned just right, the feature does nothing, and no companion app or settings menu lets you customize behavior beyond the contact colors Google has already built in. What are competitors doing? Nothing's Glyph interface set a much higher bar already Google isn't the first phone maker to bring notification lighting into the modern era. Nothing Phone has built its entire brand identity around the idea with its Glyph Interface, which debuted on the original Nothing Phone in 2022 and has been refined across several generations since. Instead of one lighting zone, Glyph uses (depending on the phone) multiple independent LED segments on the back of the phone, allowing far more expressive patterns than a single ring around a camera lens. Nothing also went further on functionality. Its Glyph Toys let you turn the lighting system into small interactive tools, including a visual countdown timer, a battery meter, and a flip-to-silence indicator, all controlled through light segments rather than the screen. Perhaps more importantly, Nothing opened a Glyph Developer Kit, letting third-party apps hook into the lighting system and trigger their own custom patterns. That means the feature isn't limited to whatever notifications the manufacturer decided to prioritize at launch, which is exactly where HiLight currently falls short.Other companies have experimented with similar ideas in different forms. Asus has used RGB lighting on its ROG gaming phones for alerts and ambient effects, and we've seen some phones do full-blown back displays. None of these approaches are identical to HiLight, but they demonstrate that the general concept of ambient, screen-free notifications has already had several years to mature elsewhere. Google Pixel 11 Pro - Brand - SoC - Google Tensor G6 - Display - 6.3-inch Super Actua display - RAM - 12 or 16GB - Storage - 256GB, 512GB, or 1TB - Battery - 4850 mAh The Google Pixel 11 Pro brings improved cameras, a faster Tensor G6 chip, and the HiLight notification LED to Android's official flagship phone. Compared to Nothing's approach in particular, HiLight looks like a first attempt rather than a fully realized feature. It's restricted to two phones, a narrow set of triggers, and a single lighting zone, with no way for developers or users to expand it. Google may well build HiLight into something more capable, but for now, it's playing catch-up to an idea the rest of the industry already validated. HiLight is a promising start, not a finish HiLight is a genuinely nice idea, and it's easy to see it growing into something useful. But in its current form, it's a narrower, less flexible take on a concept Nothing and others have already spent years perfecting.

item.title: 6 Intel CPUs that have aged like milk
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.30
Intel has had a colorful history over the years. While many people have made the switch to AMD Ryzen, plenty still remain loyal to Intel—and for good reasons. If you spent a lot of money on an Intel CPU years ago, it's reasonable to expect it to last a very long time. Or perhaps you're building a budget PC and found an older Intel chip that looks like a compelling deal. Whatever the case, be careful with the CPUs on this list, because they've long since outstayed their welcome. The Core i7-2600K has been living on borrowed time for years Time to retire Sandy Bridge for good The i7-2600K is a pretty old chip that came out way back in 2011, so even though it was one of the best consumer-grade processors when it launched, its appearance on today's list should hopefully come as a surprise to no one. This 4-core, 8-thread Sandy Bridge processor was beloved by enthusiasts for its powerful single-core performance in games and apps, which allowed it to stay relevant for many years. It was incredibly overclockable, with many users pushing the stock 3.8GHz Turbo Boost clock up to 4.5GHz with appropriate cooling. However, no amount of raw performance can save it from old age—not that it has a lot of it compared to modern CPUs anyway. This CPU and everything around it is simply too old for a modern machine. DDR3 offers a fraction of the memory bandwidth available from modern DDR4 and DDR5 platforms, and the CPU only supports PCIe 2.0. The ancient interface can become particularly limiting with some modern budget GPUs that rely on fewer but faster PCIe lanes, so you can't just drop in a budget graphics card to upgrade such an old system. If you're still rocking this chip, you're years overdue for an upgrade. The Core i7-4790K was a legend, but its time is up It earned its retirement The i7-4790K was one of Intel's best CPUs of all time. Like the 2600K, it held up incredibly well for years thanks to its excellent single-core performance, while its 4 cores and 8 threads kept it surprisingly competitive against CPUs that came out years later. Although it wasn't quite as overclockable as the 2600K, it was built on a much more efficient 22nm process and came with a respectable 4.4GHz Turbo Boost clock from the factory, which made it more than enough for most gamers. Unfortunately, the 4790K still falls victim to old age, as this chip is now 12 years old. Even entry-level chips have vastly superior IPC (Instructions Per Clock). Thanks to several generational leaps in architectural efficiency, budget chips can now run circles around the once-legendary 4790K. And although its PCIe 3.0 support makes modern graphics card upgrades more feasible (but far from ideal), its reliance on slower DDR3 memory makes it a poor choice for many modern applications and games. The Core i5-7600K aged much worse than anyone could've expected Four cores don't go far anymore The Intel Core i5-7600K came out during a transitional period. Depending on the motherboard, this CPU can support either DDR3L or the much faster DDR4 RAM that's still relevant today. However, that alone isn't enough to hide the fact that this CPU came out in early 2017. It's an old processor that performs about as well as you'd expect. The worst part of the i5-7600K's design is its 4-core, 4-thread architecture. It came out in an era when single-core performance was king in both apps and games, but now that things have shifted in favor of more cores and threads, the i5-7600K is being left behind. In short, you'd be wasting your hard-earned dollars if you combined DDR4, which is a hot commodity right now, with this old CPU that's worth less than a stick of 8GB DDR4 RAM on the used market. The Core i3-8100 was never great, but it's especially bad today Definitely time to upgrade The Intel Core i3-8100 is a generation newer than the i5-7600K, but that doesn't mean much when both CPUs were built on the same 14nm node and use a 4-core, 4-thread design. In fact, the i3-8100 is a bit weaker, but it was also considerably cheaper at just $120, making it a compelling pick for budget gaming and office PCs throughout late 2017 and 2018. Given that popularity, it's not surprising that some people are still running this old chip today. You can still encounter it relatively frequently in the wild. However, just because the i3-8100 technically meets the minimum requirement for running Windows 11 doesn't necessarily make it a good processor. Its lack of Hyper-Threading and measly 3.6GHz base clock with no Turbo Boost make it an extremely underpowered CPU for running modern apps, especially when you consider that its IPC is several generations behind that of modern Intel and AMD chips. The Core i7-8700K is still fast enough to fool you into keeping it This is a hard one to let go Okay, so the i3-8100 was a budget-oriented CPU from 2017, so it stands to reason that a flagship model from the same generation would be considerably better—and it is. On paper, the i7-8700K sounds like it should still be a fairly capable CPU to this day. It has a 6-core, 12-thread design that you can argue is still the sweet spot for many modern games in 2026, and it has a boost clock speed of up to 4.7GHz with some overclocking potential. It can also run Windows 11 and a wide range of modern games and programs, thanks to its extensive instruction set support, although it notably lacks AVX-512. However, even the i7-8700K isn't immune to aging, and after almost 10 years, it's getting harder to justify keeping it in your main machine when newer CPUs are considerably better. You'd need to pair it with an appropriate LGA1151 motherboard to get the most out of this chip, including features like XMP memory support and NVMe SSD support. When you put all those things together, the platform simply isn't worth investing the money these parts tend to go for on the used market, as you'd ultimately still end up with an outdated machine. The Core i5-11400 still looks modern, which makes it a trap for new PC builders Intel fumbled the transition At the surface level, the i5-11400 looks like a fairly compelling CPU for a budget build today. The i5-11400 is a 6-core, 12-thread chip that came out in 2021, making it only five years old. It's not exactly the latest technology has to offer, but a chip that's this old should theoretically still be a fine pick for an office or 1080p gaming PC. However, its age is somewhat misleading, as the Rocket Lake processors that the i5-11400 belongs to are ultimately built on the much-refined but ultimately mature 14nm node that dates all the way back to Intel's 6th-generation Skylake chips. AMD had already been building chips on TSMC's 7nm node for a couple of years by that point and was working toward 5nm, which makes the i5-11400 look like ancient technology by comparison. It runs surprisingly hot and gets inefficient when power limit restrictions are removed, which makes newer budget chips make way more sense. Aside from that, while the i5-11400 does support PCIe Gen 4, which should make it a bit more relevant when pairing it with budget GPUs and NVMe SSDs, the LGA 1200 socket is ultimately a dead end with a severely limited upgrade path. Intel's 12th-generation Alder Lake chips are a substantially better choice, with a couple more generations to upgrade to if you're on a very tight budget, and it's what I strongly recommend picking over the 11400 if you're dead-set on going with Intel. Some of these old CPUs can still make sense today, but context matters While most of the CPUs I've mentioned today don't make much sense in a modern Windows office or gaming PC anymore, that doesn't mean they're ready for the recycling bin. If you're running Linux, you can stretch this older hardware surprisingly far, and these chips can also make a great foundation for a low-cost home server built from old PC parts. Just be wary of their power consumption, because some of these aging CPUs can draw far more power than their performance is worth, making a cheaper, more modern alternative the better choice in the long run.

item.title: Google's new AirTag alternative fails to deliver the one feature I want from an Android tracker
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.16
The Pixel Tag gives Android users their first true first-party rival to Apple's AirTag, backed by Google's massive Find Hub network. But after looking into how it actually works, one omission stood out immediately, and it's the single feature I've wanted from an Android tracker for years. What it's lacking No simultaneous support for Find Hub and Find My Google's Pixel Tag ties itself exclusively to Find Hub, the crowdsourced network formerly known as Find My Device, and there's no other way to pair it. Outside direct Bluetooth range, the tag relies on nearby Android phones to anonymously relay its last known location to Google's servers, all end-to-end encrypted so even Google can't see exactly where the device sits. With Ultra-Wideband precision finding reportedly on board alongside IP67 water and dust resistance, the hardware itself is a legitimate answer to the AirTag, priced close to Apple's tag as well. What the Pixel Tag doesn't do, though, and what no first-party tracker from either company does, is broadcast to two networks at once. Once you set up a Pixel Tag on Find Hub, it reports only to that network. If you own an iPhone, or share a household with someone who does, that device is functionally invisible to your tag, since Apple's Find My network won't recognize or relay location pings from anything that isn't broadcasting the correct signal. This isn't unique to Google — and I'm not singling out Google here by any means. Third-party trackers that advertise support for "both" networks only mean you can choose one platform during setup, not that the tag talks to both at the same time; switching later requires a full factory reset and re-pairing. The Pixel Tag works exactly like every other single-network tracker already on the market, just with a Google logo on it. Why this is important Bigger networks mean faster, more reliable recovery The reason simultaneous network support matters comes down to simple math: a crowdsourced finding network is only as useful as the number of nearby devices that can detect and report your tag's location. Apple's Find My network runs by default on essentially every iPhone, while Android's Find Hub requires users to manually enable a setting called "Network in all areas" to unlock its broadest coverage, meaning fewer Android phones actively contribute than the raw device count suggests. For most people, this asymmetry is invisible until they lose something in a place their tracker's network doesn't reach well. Airports, mixed-ownership households, and cities with a heavier iPhone presence are exactly the scenarios where relying on a single network becomes a liability. If a Pixel Tag is attached to a backpack and it goes missing somewhere dominated by iPhones, the tag has no way of getting picked up unless an Android phone happens to walk by first. On top of that, that Android phone might not even have the specific toggle it needs to broadcast the tag's location. A tag that could broadcast to Find Hub and Find My at the same time wouldn't ask users to pick a side. It would draw on Google's stated figure of more than a billion Android devices and Apple's comparably massive iPhone install base at once, meaningfully raising the odds that a lost item gets spotted quickly. That's a different outcome than choosing the "better" single network and hoping for the best. There's also a practical convenience angle for anyone who switches phones or lives in a mixed household. Right now, moving a tracker from one ecosystem to the other means a factory reset and a fresh pairing process, not a toggle in a settings menu. Are there any alternatives that have this? A few trackers support both, but not at once A handful of trackers already market themselves as compatible with both Apple Find My and Google Find Hub, and they're worth knowing about if this feature matters to you as much as it does to me. Chipolo's Pop, priced at $29, is probably the best-known example, alongside Pebblebee's fifth-generation Clip, Card, and Tag Universal trackers, KeySmart's SmartCard Gen 3, and Rolling Square's AirCard Pro line. The catch is the same across all of them: compatibility isn't simultaneous. Each of these trackers connects to a single network at a time, chosen during initial setup, and switching between them requires a factory reset before re-pairing with the other app. Chipolo has been fairly explicit that this is a deliberate design decision rather than a technical limitation waiting to be patched, since a tag simply can't function on both networks at once as things currently stand. As of now, no consumer Bluetooth tracker from Google, Apple, or any third party genuinely broadcasts to both major finding networks at the same time. The Pixel Tag had a real opportunity to be the exception, given Google's control over both the hardware and the Find Hub software stack, but it chose compatibility with its own ecosystem over interoperability with everyone else's. For what it's worth, though, this probably isn't up to Google to implement either. Even if it could tap into Apple's Find My network, it'll probably have a hard time actually relaying Find My info to Android phones, or Find Hub info to iPhones — which is the scenario where it would become useful. This is one of those things where Google should go all-in and annoy Apple until it eventually opens up Find My, just like it did with RCS. It can be way more useful this way. One network still isn't enough The Pixel Tag is a solid AirTag alternative, but its refusal to bridge Find Hub and Apple Find My keeps Android users boxed into one crowdsourced network. Until a tracker broadcasts to both simultaneously, mixed households and travelers will keep losing out on faster, more reliable item recovery.

item.title: Samsung turned its old smartwatches into e-waste, and the FOSS community is struggling to keep them alive
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.12
Samsung spent over a decade building a smartwatch platform on Tizen, then walked away from it in under two years. Now open-source developers are racing to keep thousands of orphaned watches functional before batteries outlast the software. Why Tizen smartwatches are becoming e-waste Samsung's shutdown timeline leaves working hardware stranded Samsung previously confirmed that support for its Tizen-powered smartwatches would officially end in September 2025, just a year ago, closing out an era that began with the original Galaxy Watch. The wind-down actually started earlier, with Samsung notifying users it planned to sunset Tizen OS by the end of 2025 and immediately blocking new Tizen watch content from the Galaxy Store. The rollback traces back to September 30, 2024, when the Galaxy Store stopped offering paid content for Tizen devices, and purchases users had already made would stop being available for download, though existing downloads already on a device would remain there. This cutoff affects every Samsung Gear smartwatch and Galaxy-branded Tizen watch, including the Galaxy Watch, Galaxy Watch 3, Galaxy Watch Active, and Galaxy Watch Active 2. Devices released after the Galaxy Watch 3, starting with the Galaxy Watch 4 line, are unaffected because Samsung had already moved them onto Wear OS, the Google-backed platform it now builds its watches around. Not only is Wear OS the superior platform when it comes to ecosystem and adoption, but with Samsung's old watches being the only watches to use Tizen, users would run into trouble even if Samsung hadn't cut off downloads. For watch owners, then, the practical result is a watch that still boots and still tells time, but can no longer install new faces, apps, or updates. It isn't bricked, but it's frozen in place, and a frozen smartwatch with no upgrade path is, functionally, headed for a drawer or a landfill. The hurdles toward a second life Tizen's closed hardware layer resists the usual open-source playbook That doesn't mean that developers aren't trying to make something out of these watches, but it's hard. The most active volunteer effort here is AsteroidOS, an open-source, Linux-based smartwatch platform built on components like OpenEmbedded, opkg, Wayland, Qt5, systemd, BlueZ, and PulseAudio, originally developed by French programmer Florent Revest. The project has had real success reviving watches, but almost all of that success has come on Wear OS hardware, not Tizen hardware, and the reason comes down to plumbing. AsteroidOS typically relies on libhybris to port itself onto Android-based watches, a compatibility layer that lets Linux software talk to Android's proprietary hardware drivers. Samsung's Tizen watches were never built with that Android driver layer in the first place. That gap shows up clearly in AsteroidOS's own documentation. For the Samsung Gear S2 Classic, the project notes that the device's vendor kernel is a very old 3.4 build with no existing abstraction for the Tizen hardware layer, so developers are attempting a mainline Linux kernel port instead of the usual libhybris route. But even sourcing the code to work from is a hurdle: downstream kernel sources for that watch are hosted on a contributor's personal GitHub page because Samsung no longer hosts them itself. Flashing anything onto the hardware brings its own friction, since these watches take firmware either wirelessly through Samsung's NetOdin protocol or over USB through the standard Odin tool, sometimes requiring a cable soldered directly to internal pads. Yikes. The project's official porting tracker is candid about where things stand: the Samsung Gear S2, S2 Classic, and S3 might be supported by AsteroidOS eventually, but they will need more work than other watches on the list. This isn't unique to AsteroidOS or even to Samsung. Across the broader modding community, there's a long-running complaint that manufacturers satisfy the letter of the GPL by publishing kernel source that doesn't actually match what shipped on the device, which leaves developers reverse-engineering drivers instead of building from a clean baseline. Will it be done sometime? Progress is real, but it's measured in years, not months There's genuine momentum behind AsteroidOS, just not necessarily where Tizen owners need it most. The project released version 2.0 nearly eight years after its first stable release, and the new version expanded hardware support meaningfully. It now covers Fossil's Gen 4, Gen 5, and Gen 6 watches, the Huawei Watch and Watch 2, several Ticwatch E and Pro models, the Oppo Watch, and the 2015 Moto 360, alongside partial support for a handful of other models. Most of those, notably, are Wear OS devices where the libhybris approach already works. Still, there are signs the Tizen side is inching forward. The Samsung Gear 2 is now the project's first watch supported through a mainline Linux kernel, meaning it runs without needing libhybris at all, and the Asus ZenWatch 2 has picked up very basic support running on a mainline kernel too. That mainline-kernel approach is exactly the strategy being applied to the Gear S2 and S3, so every improvement made for one Samsung watch has a decent chance of transferring to the others. AsteroidOS remains, by most accounts, the only large-scale effort focused specifically on repurposing existing smartwatch hardware rather than building new devices around open software, which means its pace effectively sets the pace for the whole ecosystem. Keep in mind that none of this happens on a corporate roadmap. It's contributor time, old hardware datasheets, and a lot of trial and error on watches Samsung has already stopped thinking about. A working Tizen build on a Gear S3 is plausible within the next year or two based on current porting activity, but there's no firm date, and watches like the original Gear S2 may simply run out of willing contributors before they run out of battery cycles. An old platform's afterlife depends on volunteers, not Samsung Samsung's Tizen watches aren't dead, just abandoned by their maker. Whether they get a real second life now rests on a small, unpaid community reverse-engineering hardware Samsung never intended anyone outside the company to touch.

item.title: UGREEN's new "Ultra" NAS systems put your sluggish homelab to shame
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.61
UGREEN wants to be sure your home studio has network-attached storage that's always up to the job—even if you're juggling multiple tasks at once. The company has come to IFA 2026 with two NAS units, the NASync DXP6800 and DX8800 Ultra, that are meant for everyone from individual creatives through to fast-growing shops. The DXP6800 Ultra is a six-bay NAS that can hold up to 208TB of storage. Its Core 5 120U chip is fast enough for file access from mutliple people, performing backups, or running local apps.
