item.title: HTC's New Smart Glasses Offer a Few Imperfect Fixes for the Pervert Problem
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.28
Privacy and smart glasses should go hand in hand, and with the $499 Vive Eagle AI, HTC seems to realize that. It's clear the company wants to avoid the "pervert glasses" stigma that Meta's smart glasses have earned, and it's taking notable steps toward that end, though the built-in camera remains on the Vive Eagle AI. I'm currently testing them, and a full review is coming, but for now, here's what I see with HTC's "privacy-first approach." Addressing and Anonymizing AI Like all AI glasses, the Vive Eagle has built-in voice-activated AI. Interface functions, like activating different features, are handled by HTC's Vive AI, and HTC says your data will not be used to train its AI. Frankly, I think all AI data training should be opt-in, not the opt-out-and-good-luck-finding-out-how-because-we-won't-tell-you approach of a lot of AI systems. Including AI systems you weren't interacting with in the first place, like Twitch. If you want general information beyond the glasses' core functions, the Vive Eagle supports Google Gemini and OpenAI's GPT. They're much larger systems that have basically scraped the entire internet for training data, and will certainly use your interactions as well. Considering how much Google is tied to our internet footprints, there's a reasonable concern that every Gemini-related thing you do with the glasses will be linked to your Google profile. However, HTC says LLM requests through the glasses will be de-identified. The company pointedly says it makes it "harder" to build a profile, but not impossible. Sadly, that's the current reality we live in, and no privacy or security feature is completely bulletproof. Welcome to the data economy. The Vive Eagle is also ISO 27001 and ISO 27701 compliant, which means it meets international standards for securing personal data and ensuring some level of user-side privacy control. The Camera Problem The Vive Eagle has a built-in 12MP camera that lets you take photos and 3K video, and provides translations in 96 different languages. A camera is always handy to have, but it's also the main reason "pervert glasses" has become a common phrase. Creeps, stalkers, and general jerks use camera-equipped smart glasses to surreptitiously record and harass people. To address the problem, HTC added extra privacy and security features to the Vive Eagle. First, its recording light uses multiple sensors to ensure it's always visible when the camera is recording. It will adjust its brightness based on ambient light to be easily seen, and the camera won't work if the light is obscured in any way. A recording light that you can't disable has become standard on major smart glasses with cameras, including Meta's, but I'm skeptical that it can't be circumvented in some way. Second, the camera will not record unless the glasses are being physically worn. This means someone can't take the glasses off and set them to capture from a hidden position. There could also be a workaround there, but it's another good step. Third, the camera will turn off if anyone nearby says "stop filming." That's kind of brilliant in its simplicity. If you know you're being recorded, you can stop it. Again, in theory. The fourth feature is less an anti-pervert-glasses fix and more about general user security improvements. Photos and videos taken on the Vive Eagle stay on the glasses' on-board 32GB storage until you manually transfer them to your phone or another device, and that data can't be accessed if you pair the glasses with a different device. When combined with the ISO 27001 and ISO 27701 certifications, anything you capture on the glasses should be safe from other people. Privacy, Security, and Uncertainty It's good that HTC is up-front and highlighting its privacy and security measures on the Vive Eagle. They aren't remotely guaranteed, since no information security measure is, but it's a start. Still, in an ideal world, we wouldn't have to worry about this at all. Security to prevent individuals from stealing your data is one thing. Preventing unauthorized system access by bad actors has been a vital part of information security for as long as information has existed. Thieves will always exist, so we find ways to deal with the threats. But the concerns about AI glasses go beyond those bad actors to the devices' own manufacturers, service providers, and users. The Vive Eagle doesn't anonymize your AI prompts to keep some random hacker from tracking you; it does that to keep Google and OpenAI from tracking you. HTC comes out and says Vive AI won't use your data for training, even though every major AI firm is using it for training, whether you like it or not. The glasses don't have a "stop filming" kill switch to keep your photos and videos out of others' hands; they have it to keep you from being a creep or stalker with them. These privacy and security features aren't simply necessary to protect us from criminals. They're necessary to protect us from the very services we rely on, and from ourselves (or at least other people using the exact same devices). HTC seems to be doing what it can with the Vive Eagle (besides removing the camera entirely), but the fact that these actions need to be taken in the first place? Well, that really sucks. About Our Expert I’m PCMag’s home theater and AR/VR expert, and your go-to source of information and recommendations for game consoles and accessories, smart displays, smart glasses, smart speakers, soundbars, TVs, and VR headsets. I’m an ISF-certified TV calibrator and THX-certified home theater technician, I've served as a CES Innovation Awards judge, and while Bandai hasn’t officially certified me, I’m also proficient at building Gundam plastic models up to MG-class. I also enjoy genre fiction writing, and my urban fantasy novel, Alex Norton, Paranormal Technical Support, is currently available on Amazon.

item.title: Open and Neutral? Nvidia Says Don't Worry About Its Hugging Face Acquisition
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.16
Nvidia’s $13 billion deal to acquire Hugging Face might spark concerns about the future of the popular AI model platform, but both companies insist that Hugging Face will remain “open and neutral” for AI developers and enthusiasts. “We want to continue to work with all AI developers globally,” Nvidia’s VP for enterprise computing, Justin Boitano, said in a press briefing after the acquisition was confirmed this morning. “To make sure that they’ve got an open and neutral platform that interoperates with every cloud provider, every hardware company in the world.” “We think this operation, this announcement, will allow the world and AI to be more distributed all over the world, and to avoid too much concentration of power,” added Hugging Face CEO Clément Delangue. The concern is that Hugging Face hosts numerous open-source and open-weight AI models, effectively operating as the "App Store of the AI world" for over 200,000 companies, notes PCMag’s Brian Westover. Nvidia, on the other hand, is the top seller of enterprise GPUs to power AI models and is preparing consumer-focused chips with its RTX Spark line to drive AI use on laptops. Will the Hugging Face deal push the platform to favor Nvidia technology? Boitano says no. The priority is to keep the platform open and neutral so that it can grow, which requires maintaining trust with the software developer community. In turn, Nvidia will benefit as AI developers and businesses buy its chips to run AI models. Boitano also addressed whether the deal might face antitrust scrutiny from government regulators, saying Nvidia’s role is focused on helping Hugging Face “scale and expand access to AI globally," adding, “We think regulators are going to see this as overwhelmingly positive because it's going to infuse AI into every country, into every industry." Hugging Face’s Delangue also noted that “the vast, vast majority of what we do is open-source, open models, open datasets, that are by definition, neutral. Everyone can take them. Everyone can optimize them, everyone can fork our open-source if they are not happy about it.” He added that a major goal is to grow the platform’s user base to 100 million AI software developers over the next few years, up from the current 18 million. “We think that this announcement is really going to be fantastic and massively impactful for all the players in the ecosystem, not just Nvidia, but all the players,” Delangue said. Still, analysts at research firm Forrester noted that the deal gives Nvidia significant influence over the AI ecosystem, including a potential competitive edge over other GPU designers. "Nvidia gains visibility into customers' preferences and the AI models they use. They can see which models are trending, what datasets customers are downloading, and the architectures that are gaining traction weeks before they hit mainstream tech news,” says analyst Naveen Chhabra. "Nvidia also gets data-driven foresight into what next-generation chip architectures they need to build based on developer habits.” About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. I got my start as a schools and cities reporter in Kansas City and joined PCMag in 2017, where I cover satellite internet services, cybersecurity, PC hardware, and more. I'm currently based in San Francisco, but previously spent over five years in China, covering the country's technology sector. Since 2020, I've covered the launch and explosive growth of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, writing 600+ stories on availability and feature launches, but also the regulatory battles over the expansion of satellite constellations, fights with rival providers like AST SpaceMobile and Amazon, and the effort to expand into satellite-based mobile service. I've combed through FCC filings for the latest news and driven to remote corners of California to test Starlink's cellular service. I also cover cyber threats, from ransomware gangs to the emergence of AI-based malware. In 2024 and 2025, the FTC forced Avast to pay consumers $16.5 million for secretly harvesting and selling their personal information to third-party clients, as revealed in my joint investigation with Motherboard. I also cover the PC graphics card market. Pandemic-era shortages led me to camp out in front of a Best Buy to get an RTX 3000. I'm now following how the AI-driven memory shortage is impacting the entire consumer electronics market. I'm always eager to learn more, so please jump in the comments with feedback and send me tips.

item.title: DLSS 5 Spikes Power Consumption
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.13
DLSS 5 doesn't just tank frame rates and weather faces; it might also spike power consumption on GPUs. Tom's Hardware tested various games with high-end graphics cards running DLSS 5 and found that, in some cases, power consumption jumped by hundreds of watts when the card had headroom. Where it didn't, performance fell further, suggesting the already fire-happy 12v-2x6 connector may be limiting performance with DLSS 5 enabled. DLSS 5, which brings AI-powered photorealism to PC games, launched today on NBA 2K27. Whether it actually makes games look better is still up for debate. It's more efficient than when we first saw it, but the RTX 5090 still loses nearly half its FPS. When running Hogwarts Legacy at 4K with ray tracing and DLSS set to Performance mode, Tom's Hardware found that the RTX 5090 FE jumped from 417 watts without it to 547 watts with it. For the RTX 5090 Lightning Z, with a much higher power limit, it leaped from 480W without DLSS 5 to 720W with it. In comparison, the Founders Edition 5090 performance dipped by 49% with DLSS 5 enabled, while the Lightning dropped by just 42%, and its 1% lows were much less impacted. You can argue the Lightning Z is the more powerful card, but it was only 3fps higher than the FE card without DLSS 5, so DLSS 5 has the biggest impact here. The same story was true in Cyberpunk 2077, where the Lightning Z version went from 580W to 723W, losing 39% of its overall FPS in the process. The 5090 FE went from 482W to 551W but lost 42% performance, dropping below 60fps even with DLSS on Performance. Control had the highest power consumption and, therefore, the greatest limitation on the FE card. The Lightning Z version went from 691W to 802W, while the standard 5090 pulled 563W and only 575W with DLSS 5 enabled. While both cards saw their frame rates drop by 42% with DLSS 5 enabled, the Lightning Z still held above 60fps average, while the 5090 fell to just 51fps. So, DLSS 5 appears to benefit most from the latest tensor cores and greater power limits. Like the original DLSS release, it is likely to be a multi-generational technology that will be far more useful in the years and generations to come. More powerful cards with faster tensor units, with greater power limits, may be needed to take full advantage of it. But Nvidia will have to address that connector if it tries to push even more power through these things. Maybe something extra stealthy like the BTF method? About Our Expert Jon Martindale is a tech journalist from the UK, with 20 years of experience covering all manner of PC components and associated gadgets. He's written for a range of publications, including ExtremeTech, Digital Trends, Forbes, U.S. News & World Report, and Lifewire, among others. When not writing, he's a big board gamer and reader, with a particular habit of speed-reading through long manga sagas. Jon covers the latest PC components, as well as how-to guides on everything from how to take a screenshot to how to set up your cryptocurrency wallet. He particularly enjoys the battles between the top tech giants in CPUs and GPUs, and tries his best not to take sides. Jon's gaming PC is built around the iconic 7950X3D CPU, with a 7900XTX backing it up. That's all the power he needs to play lightweight indie and casual games, as well as more demanding sim titles like Kerbal Space Program. He uses a pair of Jabra Active 8 earbuds and a SteelSeries Arctis Pro wireless headset, and types all day on a Logitech G915 mechanical keyboard.

item.title: Move Over, DJI: Hohem's Eyepic 4K Vlogging Camera Has a Massive Twist
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.03
Vlogging cameras are the hot ticket right now, and the space just got a brand new player. Hohem, a brand best known to date for its iSteady smartphone gimbals, is bringing its first-ever camera to IFA in Berlin. The Eyepic is a tiny 4K video camera that can be handheld, worn, or magnetically mounted to a three-axis gimbal—making it a true triple threat for content creation. A Pocket Gimbal That Snaps Apart for Underwater Action The Eyepic draws inspiration from the DJI Osmo Pocket series, which has proven to be the go-to choice for vloggers who want to record handheld video and has inspired competitors such as the Insta360 Luna Ultra. Like others in the class, the Eyepic has a long, skinny body that fits comfortably in your hand, a touch screen, and a small joystick to control its powered gimbal. The gimbal promises to keep footage smooth and steady, even for walk-and-talk shots, and the Eyepic camera records clips at up to 4K60 quality. That's not as ambitious as some competitors—the DJI Osmo Pocket 4P and Insta360 Luna Ultra both support higher frame rates for slow motion and include dual lenses for wide and telephoto views, while the Eyepic is a single-lens device. But the Eyepic does one thing that DJI and Insta360 can't—its camera works separately from the gimbal. It pops on and off with a quick magnetic attachment, so you can go between handheld vlogging and mounting the camera to an object in a snap. That makes the Eyepic the first gimbal camera that's also a waterproof action camera, one that works down to 32.8 feet underwater. It also makes it easy to switch between widescreen and vertical video—the camera mounts to the gimbal in either direction. Pro Audio Upgrade: The AI-Powered Hohem Mic 2 Kit Vloggers know that a video is only as good as its soundtrack. Built-in mics tend to sound hollow and pick up a lot of background noise, so the company is releasing a wireless mic kit for the Eyepic: the Hohem Mic 2. The kit ships with a receiver and two body mics, and supports up to four mics in total. It supports 48kHz/24-bit audio, has AI-powered noise cancellation, and promises an incredible 984-foot transmission range. Availability: Targeting CES 2027—And an Opening in the US Market Like many of the products making their debut at IFA, the Eyepic isn't quite ready to ship to customers, so we don't know how much it will cost or which regions it will be sold in. Hohem says it plans to release a general version in the first quarter of 2027, and we'll be sure to have more information closer to that date. The early 2027 timing is conspicuously timed with CES, which takes place in Las Vegas and is a traditional launchpad for the coolest consumer tech, so we're hopeful that the Eyepic makes it US debut then. On paper, it looks like a great choice for US-based vloggers and content creators who can't get the latest DJI Osmo Pocket models because of the FCC's ban on new DJI products. Stay tuned to PCMag for more information as it develops. About Our Expert Images, and the devices that capture them, are my focus. I've covered cameras at PCMag for the past 15 years, which has given me a front row seat for the changeover from DSLRs to mirrorless cameras, the smartphone camera revolution, and the emergence of drones for aerial imaging. I have extensive experience with every major mirrorless and SLR system, and am also comfortable using point-and-shoot and action cameras. As a Part 107 Certified drone pilot, I’m licensed to fly unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) for commercial and editorial purposes, and am knowledgeable about federal rules and regulations regarding drones.

item.title: Microsoft: Sorry, But Time Limits Are Coming to Xbox's Cloud Gaming
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.89
If you like Xbox’s cloud gaming feature, prepare to pay more. Microsoft is introducing time limits on Xbox Game Pass plans. The service currently touts “unlimited cloud gaming,” letting users stream Xbox games on other devices, including phones, PCs, and smart TVs. Starting in November, however, subscribers will face a cap that ranges from a rather measly 5 to 15 hours each month. - Game Pass Ultimate: 15 hours - Game Pass Premium: 10 hours - Game Pass Essential: 5 hours Microsoft explains: “We’re introducing this model because the cost of providing cloud gaming grows as more people use it and play for longer. Moving to monthly limits allows us to keep offering the service while continuing to invest in its reliability and performance. We understand that for some players, the practical result is a higher cost.” Despite the rising use of Xbox’s cloud gaming feature, the company also suggested most Game Pass subscribers won’t be affected. “We recognize that introducing limits is a meaningful change, particularly for players who regularly spend more time gaming through the cloud. We expect this upcoming change to impact 4% of Game Pass subscribers,” Microsoft wrote. To exceed the monthly cap, customers will need to pay an extra fee through the Xbox Store. “Available hours, purchasing options, and cloud gaming features may vary by market. We’ll share pricing and further details before the changes take effect,” the announcement adds. The decision isn't sitting well with Xbox gamers. "Jeez this is awful for anyone who uses cloud gaming. 15 hours is nothing," wrote one user on Reddit. The news is also surprising, considering Microsoft has boasted about Xbox's cloud gaming as a major feature in years prior. In the meantime, Xbox owners without a Game Pass subscription will also be able to buy hours for cloud gaming, letting them stream “eligible games they own on supported devices.” The new option will also arrive in November. “This will provide another option for people who want occasional access to cloud gaming or do not want a recurring Game Pass subscription,” the company said. Microsoft has also been testing an ad-supported version of cloud gaming. This comes a few months after Microsoft dropped the price of Xbox Game Pass Ultimate from $29.99 to $22.99 a month and PC Game Pass from $16.49 to $13.99 a month. However, gamers will have to wait "about a year" for future Call of Duty titles on Game Pass. About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. item.title: Anthropic Fixed Fable 5.1's Worst Problems...So Why Am I Staying With Opus?
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.85
Fable is perhaps the most intriguing AI model to date. Anthropic positioned it as the world’s most powerful LLM, comparable only with its big sibling, Mythos, which was too powerful for a public release. Then the US government banned it almost immediately, only to allow it to return in a less capable state. Now, Fable 5.1 is here. I’ve tried it, and I find it far more compelling, thanks to its friendlier pricing, relaxed censorship, and more. Here are the top five things Fable 5.1 gets right—and why all of these massive upgrades still aren't quite enough to change my daily routine. 1. Fable 5.1 Is Cheaper, Unlocked, and Here to Stay Previously, a cutoff date when Fable would only be accessible with purchasable credits rather than a regular Claude subscription loomed large over the experience, but that’s no longer the case. Now, you can access Fable via Enterprise, Max, and Team plans for up to 50% of your weekly usage. Of course, you still have the option to buy credits to keep using Fable beyond those limits. Fable 5.1 is also cheaper if you buy credits. According to Anthropic, you can expect savings of up to 25% in general and up to 45% for highly agentic work. This comes courtesy of reduced prices on cache reads, “where the model reads inputs that have already been processed and stored.” If you want to use Fable 5 heavily, these savings could potentially become significant. Just keep in mind that Opus 5 is still significantly cheaper per token and is available on all paid Claude plans. 2. Generous Usage Limits (With a Fine-Print Catch) Anthropic is currently (and has been since May) running a promotion that lets you enjoy 50% more weekly usage with Claude Code. However, when that promotion expires, Anthropic promises a permanent 25% increase to weekly usage across Enterprise, Max, Pro, and Team plans. So, although this means you can expect a 25% usage decrease versus what you’re getting now, that’s a permanent 25% bump over the baseline. Every bit of Fable usage counts, given the weekly usage limits. 3. Goodbye, Overly Aggressive Censorship Fable 5’s censorship was incredibly aggressive. Previously, when I asked benign questions such as, “What happened with Fable and the US government?" or “What’s new in chemistry?”, Fable bounced me back to Opus. And I couldn’t ask about potential exploits to any coding projects I was working on, either. Now, Fable 5.1 handles all of these prompts without issue. Safeguards are still in place, though, so don’t expect to hack into any mainframes with it. When Fable 5 came back online after its ban, Anthropic noted that it might falsely flag coding tasks. That tendency limited the LLM as a coding tool, but the company promised to continue refining its classifiers behind the scenes. It seems to have followed through on this initiative, as I haven’t encountered any issues with Fable 5.1 blocking coding-related prompts. Of course, your mileage may vary, but I no longer have any meaningful concerns about censorship. 4. Surprisingly, You Don't Need an ID Check When Fable 5 returned after its prohibition, Anthropic also updated its privacy policy to include a new section on ID verification. Considering the US government’s Fable ban focused on its use by foreign nationals, it seemed possible that you would soon need to provide ID to use Fable. However, this hasn't been the case. Although Anthropic notes that “a few use cases…might see a verification prompt when accessing certain capabilities,” this isn’t standard policy, and you can safely use Fable without the need to upload a picture ID. 5. Fable Reclaims Its Benchmark Crown From Opus Fable 5 was only briefly Anthropic’s most capable model. Opus 5 quickly outpaced it not just in efficiency but also in performance across Anthropic’s benchmarks for a variety of use cases, from agentic coding to biology. Since you could use Opus 5 with any plan to the full extent of your weekly usage limit, Fable 5 became difficult to justify. Now, Fable 5.1 tops Anthropic's list. So, if you actually need best-in-class performance, you should consider using Fable 5.1 first. That applies to everything from agentic coding tasks to complex business workflow development to scientific research and more. Why I'm Still Sticking With Opus Fable 5.1 is objectively much better than the original. If you have a tough task that Opus 5 just can’t handle, you can confidently turn to Fable 5.1 without spending extra money (or as much if you opt for credits), verifying your ID, or worrying about censorship. However, chances are that you won’t notice much of a difference versus Fable 5 or Opus 5 for simple coding projects or web searches. As always, I plan to keep testing Fable to see if any aspect of it could convince me to switch from Opus, but I haven't found one yet. About Our Expert I’ve been writing about consumer technology and video games for over a decade at a variety of publications, including Destructoid, GamesRadar+, Lifewire, PCGamesN, Trusted Reviews, and What Hi-Fi?, among many others. At PCMag, I review AI and productivity software—everything from chatbots to to-do list apps. In my free time, I’m likely cooking something, playing a game, or tinkering with my computer.

item.title: Sweep Up These Early Labor Day Dyson and Robot Vacuum Deals
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.66
With Labor Day marking the unofficial transition from summer to fall, it's probably a good time to give your house a thorough cleaning, and a new vacuum can help. Lucky for you, there are currently plenty of vacuum cleaners on sale right now, from top Dyson models to mighty-but-affordable robot vacuum and mops. Below, take a peek at the best Labor Day weekend robot vacuum and Dyson vacuum deals. Plus, follow our coverage for even more Labor Day tech deals from Amazon, Walmart, and Best Buy. Dyson Vacuum Labor Day Deals When it comes to cordless stick vacuums, the Dyson V15 Detect is one of our favorites, having earned a rating of "Excellent" in testing. Despite its relatively small and compact size, it boasts stronger suction than any of its predecessors, plus whole-machine HEPA filtration. The laser-equipped cleaner head shows dust, dirt, and debris you'd otherwise miss, like lingering pet hair, and the numerous accessories make it exceptionally versatile. The Dyson V8 is the brand's base model, but it still gets the job done exceptionally well. Compared to your average vacuum cleaner, the suction on the V8 is much stronger and more efficient, capturing 99.99% of particles as small os 0.3 microns. Plus, it's a jack-of-all-trades, working as a handheld vac or easy-to-maneuver stick vacuum cleaner. It also tends to be one of the cheaper stick vacuums in the Dyson line-up, even on sales events like Labor Day. The Dyson V11 Origin is a highly capable stick vacuum, with 60% more suction power than the base V8 model. It also has a particle-counting LCD and a special Boost Mode for intensive spot cleaning. Naturally, various attachments (including one that detangles hair) allow you to clean easily almost anywhere and everywhere. The Dyson Ball Animal 3 is specifically geared towards homes with big misses and pets. The extremely powerful suction easily tackles stubborn dirt build-up, while the brush roll automatically detangles hair as it cleans. Plus, the stair tool and combination tool help ensure a deep clean in every nook and cranny of your house. Eufy Vacuum Labor Day Deal The Eufy Robot Vacuum 11S Max is an affordable robot vacuum that doesn't sacrifice performance for price. It's one of our favorite budget-friendly models, offering strong, efficient cleaning across various floor types in a quiet, compact machine. In fact, it's small enough to fit under most furniture in your home (where most dust tends to collect). You won't find many fancy features, but at a sale price of just $169.99, it gets the job done well without requiring a major investment. Ecovacs Vacuum Labor Day Deal The Ecovacs Deebot X9 Pro Omni is a sleek robotic floor cleaner that delivers excellent vacuum performance thanks to its redesigned air intake system, Blast. At the same time, it boasts the same innovative roller mop of its predecessor, which cleans itself as it works. It scored among the highest marks we've seen in our suction power stress test and earned a rating of "Excellent" in our 2025 review. iRobot Vacuum Labor Day Deal The iRobot Roomba 105 helps you spend as little time as possible on chores with an auto-empty dock that can hold up to 75 days' worth of dirt. That's roughly 15 days more than most other self-emptying robot vacuums. Combine that with efficient mapping, four strong suction levels, and a $200 discount, and it's hard to go wrong. Roborock Vacuum Labor Day Deals You'll be hard-pressed to find a more capable combo robot vacuum and mop at this price. It boasts strong, efficient suction power that can suck up embedded dirt and debris from carpets, as well as an anti-tangle design that can easily handle homes with pet (or human) hair. Plus, it can vacuum and mop simultaneously, ensuring that no crumbs or dust particles are left behind. While it's not self-emptying, it will still save you lots of time and energy. Check out more Labor Day tech deals and keep checking back for the latest sales of Dyson and robot vacuums!

item.title: Apple's Sept. 9 'Surprise and Shine' Event: What to Expect, Including iPhone 18, iPhone Ultra, Watch Series 12, and More
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.49
Apple’s Sept. 9 “Surprise and Shine” event isn’t exactly aptly named. Details about the company’s upcoming products have been leaking for months, and I doubt there will be a single jaw left hanging by the time John Ternus—its new CEO—leaves the stage. But if there’s one rumored product poised to steal the spotlight, it’s the iPhone Ultra, Apple’s first-ever foldable. Cupertino is also tipped to unveil the new iPhone 18 Pro series, updated Apple Watches, improved AirPods, and more. With plenty of new hardware on the way, here’s a deep dive into everything Apple is expected to show on stage during the Sept. 9 event. How to Watch Apple's Sept. 9 Event The Surprise and Shine event will take place on Sept. 9 at Apple’s headquarters in Cupertino. It will kick off at 10 a.m. PT / 11 a.m. MT / 12 p.m. CT / 1 p.m. ET. If you didn't get an in-person invite, you can still watch it across a number of different platforms, including the Apple TV app, the Apple Events page, and the company's YouTube channel. Before the show starts, tune in for live coverage from PCMag's Executive Producer, Iyaz Akhtar, and CNET Editor at Large, Bridget Carey, starting at 9:30 a.m. PT / 12:30 p.m. ET. Unfolding the 'iPhone Ultra' First, here's what you shouldn't expect at Apple's Surprise and Shine event. While you may be hoping for a refreshed entry-level iPhone 18 reveal, and perhaps a new-generation iPhone Air, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, Apple won't be announcing these products on Sept. 9. Instead, the company is shifting the spotlight toward the iPhone Ultra, Apple's long-rumored foldable. It's expected to have a short-and-wide form factor similar to the Galaxy Z Fold 8, but it won't feature Apple's best-in-class camera system because it will lack a telephoto lens. However, knowledgeable sources claim that it will have a rival-beating, nearly creaseless display, as well as impressive durability, thanks to an advanced Liquid Metal hinge. iPhone Pros Only Although we supposedly won't see the base models, Apple is broadly expected to unveil the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. According to The Information, the Pro models will feature an under-display Face ID sensor, relocating the selfie camera to the top-left of the screen. The Pro models will also reportedly include a “mechanical aperture,” allowing users to control how much light enters the lens. Finally, Apple may move the devices’ memory chips closer to the core processor, potentially helping the iPhones process AI requests more quickly while keeping their reliance on cloud servers to a minimum. The phones will also come in a new batch of colors that don't include traditional black or white. More Wrist Computers Gurman claims that Apple’s modest upgrade trend for its smartwatch line will continue with the Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Both will reportedly get a major performance boost, along with a handful of new health and fitness-related updates. One of those features is an updated heart-rate sensor that continuously tracks your heart rate throughout the day rather than only detecting intense activity. Plus, the company is reportedly considering a ceramic case option, as well as new colors and bands. Fresh Budget Buds The new AirPods 5, an upgrade to Apple's entry-level earbuds, are also expected to make their debut at the Sept. 9 event. Gurman didn't say much about the rumored AirPods 5, but in an X post, he revealed that they'll continue to come in two flavors: one will feature active noise cancellation, while the other will not. There have been whispers about new camera-equipped AirPods coming down the pipeline, but Gurman says that's more of a 2027 conversation. Then There Are the 'Maybes' Of course, there are always products that are much more of a wild card. Gurman says Apple’s new TV set-top box and an updated HomePod mini are expected to launch this fall, but he isn’t sure whether either will show up at the Sept. 9 Surprise and Shine event. The new smart home hub, which will reportedly feature facial recognition to identify users, is even more uncertain: Apple could preview it during the event, but Gurman says its actual launch could come anytime between October and early next year. We won't know for sure about these rumored products until we hear about them directly from Apple. Stay tuned for PCMag’s coverage of the Surprise and Shine event, as we’ll be on the ground bringing you all the latest announcements, hands-on impressions, and analysis straight from Apple Park. About Our Expert I’m PCMag’s Senior Writer for Mobile on the Consumer Electronics team, diving into the latest phones, tablets, Bluetooth speakers, audio devices, and other portable gear. I’ve been covering consumer technology for six years. Before joining PCMag, I contributed my tech expertise to Laptop Magazine, Mashable, Tom’s Guide, Esquire, Good Housekeeping, and more.

item.title: iPhone 18 Pro Expected Next Week. Here Are the Rumors That Look Legit
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.46
Tim Cook is out, and John Ternus is in, and he'll introduce himself to Apple fans on Sept. 9, when the company hosts its "Surprise and shine" event. It's set to be a packed presentation. What can we expect? And how much more expensive will Apple's latest and greatest be, given the memory crunch? Apple already raised prices across several major product lines in June, but iPhone pricing has remained steady, helping drive iPhone 17 sales during the last quarter. However, "For September, we expect to pay even higher memory costs,” Cook said during a recent earnings call. With Apple's foldable expected to cost north of $2,000, the iPhone 18 Pro is probably the more economical choice if you're looking to upgrade this fall. To help you know what to expect, we've rounded up the biggest iPhone 18 Pro rumors we have heard so far. iPhone 18 Pro: Revised Lineup The biggest rumor around the iPhone 18 lineup is its release timeline. Unlike previous years, where Apple released four phones in the same series in one go, Bloomberg reports Apple could take a two-pronged approach to ensure consistent revenue throughout the year. Flagship phones, such as the iPhone 18 Pro, 18 Pro Max, and the foldable iPhone, will be unveiled in September, while the base iPhone 18, iPhone Air 2, and the iPhone 18e could be launched in spring 2027. We discuss the foldable iPhone in detail in a separate rumor roundup, so we’ll just stick to the Pro models here. iPhone 18 Pro: Design and Colors The iPhone 17 Pro models brought a major overhaul to Apple’s smartphone design language, with a new camera “plateau” and two-toned color scheme. This year, Apple isn’t expected to drastically change the device's appearance, but it could add a few bold colors and return to a more uniform color scheme on the back. Several leakers, including Sonny Dickson and Instant Digital, claim that Apple could go with a never-before-seen cherry red and a new light blue, alongside the regular dark gray. Dickson also shared pictures of potential dummies, including one in light gray. In a fresh leak this week, Fixed Focus Digital backed dark cherry, sky blue, and dark gray colors for the new models, but noted that light gray or white/silver was highly unlikely. While the appearance of the rear is expected to remain the same, the in-hand feel could be a lot different. Ice Universe says the battery could get slightly larger on the iPhone 18 Pro Max, contributing to increased weight and bulk. More precisely, the leaker expects the device to be 0.25mm thicker and 7 grams heavier. iPhone 18 Pro Display On the front, we might see one significant change. The Dynamic Island, or the camera cutout, could be reduced by 35%, Ice Universe says. This won’t shrink the feature's overall functionality, but it could move the Face ID sensor’s illuminator to one corner below the screen. When it comes to display sizes, the consensus is that the iPhone 18 Pro will come in its usual 6.3-inch screen, while the Pro Max will have a 6.9-inch screen. Apple, however, has reportedly been pushing suppliers to provide much brighter displays and could use the more power-efficient LTPO+ display tech. iPhone 18 Pro Cameras The iPhone 17 Pro lineup bumped all three cameras to 48MP. For the iPhone 18 Pro, the biggest camera-related rumor we have heard is around variable aperture. While the iPhone 17 models had a fixed aperture, the iPhone 18 Pro may introduce a variable aperture. ETNews reports that the modified system has already entered production and would help the cameras deliver more light to the sensors in dark conditions and reduce light in bright conditions. Apple may also modify its relatively new Camera Control button. Introduced with the iPhone 16, the capacitive button at the bottom right of the phone lets you quickly launch the Camera app, take pictures, and adjust settings for zoom, exposure, depth, and other controls. Mastering the capacitive button, however, has proved difficult, with users noting that they have been accidentally launching the Camera app. Apple may finally fix the problem by removing the touch-sensitive components of the button and delivering a more user-friendly experience, 9to5Mac reports. iPhone 18 Pro Performance The iPhone 18 Pro is likely to receive a performance boost with the A20 chip. It will use TSMC’s 2nm technology, an upgrade from the previous generation’s 3nm tech. The transition will allow more transistors on each chip but also raise chip costs by 50%, MacRumors reports. The chip is also rumored to have TSMC’s Wafer-Level Multi-Chip Module (WMCM) technology, which infuses RAM into the same wafer as the CPU, GPU, and Neural Engine. Overall, it is expected to be 18% faster and 30% more power-efficient than previous generations, according to leaker Fixed Focus Digital. Apple usually reserves the base variant of its chip series for the standard iPhone models, while the Pro models get the corresponding Pro chip. With the iPhone 18 series, Apple is reportedly considering offering just the high-end variant across the lineup. Another expected upgrade is for the modem. The iPhone 17 Pro models had an unspecified third-party modem, but the iPhone 18 Pro could get the company’s proprietary C2 modem. It will support 5G satellite connectivity and reduce the scope of location data retained by networks, according to MacRumors. iPhone 18 Pro Battery Apple never reveals its battery capacities, but multiple leakers have indicated a larger and more efficient battery for the iPhone 18 Pro Max. According to Digital Chat Station, the top variant will have a capacity of up to 5,200mAh, slightly better than the 5,088mAh capacity of its predecessor. With a more efficient modem and processor, the battery life could be significantly longer. The iPhone 18 Pro, on the other hand, could see a minimal bump from 4,252mAh to 4,288mAh. More recently, leaks posted on Korean and Chinese social media sites tip a US iPhone 18 Pro Max model with a 5,567mAh battery, a nearly 10% increase over the iPhone 17 Pro Max, MacRumors notes. iPhone 18 Pro: Pricing and Release This is what much of the decision-making hinges on. According to The Wall Street Journal's estimate, rising component costs would push the iPhone 18 Pro to start at $1,299. If you couple that with recent Apple trends, the iPhone 18 Pro Max could be priced $100 higher, taking its starting price to $1,399. In comparison, the iPhone 17 Pro starts at $1,099, while the 17 Pro Max starts at $1,199. When asked on a recent earnings call about potential price hikes for the iPhone, Cook said it's "too early to come to a definitive conclusion of what happens there. Because it takes a little while for the channels to adjust since there's channel inventory, it takes a while for the consumer to respond. We'll understand that more in the weeks ahead." With the event scheduled for Sept. 9, preorders will likely begin a few days later, ahead of the launch the following week. About Our Expert Jibin is a tech news writer based out of Ahmedabad, India. Previously, he served as the editor of iGeeksBlog and is a self-proclaimed tech enthusiast who loves breaking down complex information for a broader audience.

item.title: Nvidia's Hugging Face Buyout: A Brilliant Move or an Antitrust Nightmare?
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.39
It's official: Nvidia has agreed to buy Hugging Face for $12.9 billion, as formally announced in a blog post by CEO Jensen Huang this morning. While multi-billion-dollar AI acquisitions have become commonplace, a lot of people are scratching their heads over this particular deal. With an estimated annual revenue of around $150 million, Hugging Face is not a cash cow, so why is Nvidia willing to pay 86 times as much to own it? Nvidia is not buying a ready-made income stream. Instead, it's leveraging its own massive war chest to gain strategic control over a key player in AI development. You may have never heard of Hugging Face before, but in AI circles, this is stunning news. What Is Hugging Face? Hugging Face started as a simple chatbot app back in 2016. Its odd name is actually derived from the Hugging Face emoji 🤗 (Unicode U+1F917), which was also adapted as the company logo. However, the chatbot was not particularly successful and never had a large user base. In 2019, the company pivoted. After open-sourcing the chatbot model, Hugging Face became a platform for sharing AI models and datasets—still relatively niche in the early 2020s. But since the advent of ChatGPT, interest in open-source AI has exploded, and Hugging Face has become the premier platform for open-source AI models, large and small. By the time I started writing about open-source AI in 2023, Hugging Face was the de facto central repository for these models. Hugging Face has become the App Store of the AI world.
The open-source aspect is perhaps the most important thing here. In addition to hosting millions of AI models, datasets, and developer tools, its position as a community platform in the open-source world essentially made it the neutral public square in the biggest boomtown of modern technology. Because it shared models largely for free, without being beholden to a single hardware provider, it has grown into a key player in AI development, most comparable to GitHub. Put simply, Hugging Face has become the App Store of the AI world, providing access to the models that power AI features for millions of enthusiasts, businesses, and end users. How Did a Gaming Company Become an AI Giant? If Hugging Face is like the App Store, it's because Nvidia is the iPhone in this analogy, building out the hardware that made the AI boom possible. Though Nvidia started as a gaming company making GPUs, CEO Jensen Huang made a prescient move in 2007 by introducing CUDA (Compute Unified Device Architecture), unlocking the parallel processing capabilities of GPU hardware for general-purpose mathematical programming. Researchers and academics began using GeForce GPUs for data science and machine learning, resulting in a 2012 breakthrough when they used the gaming hardware for AI training. This positioned Nvidia at the center of AI years before ChatGPT and generative AI went mainstream. In the years since, Nvidia has scaled beyond basic GPUs into specialized AI acceleration, high-speed networking, server hardware, and full supercomputer racks, becoming the world's leading AI hardware maker and riding that infrastructure to massive profits. Not Just a Software Play: Why Nvidia Needs Hugging Face As AI technology continues to develop, it has become massively more competitive across every layer of the tech landscape. While closed-source labs like OpenAI and Anthropic push to develop their own proprietary hardware, Nvidia relies on a thriving open-source ecosystem to sustain GPU demand and maintain its hardware dominance. Nvidia has been consolidating its position in this new competitive landscape by expanding its chip production and becoming more involved in the development of AI models. But its developer outreach has mostly been a sandbox for teams already using Nvidia server infrastructure and developer units like the DGX Spark. Control of Hugging Face would give Nvidia gatekeeper power over the software side of AI.
The investment in Hugging Face is a strategic play to expand beyond that sandbox. By offering an accessible model directory, an active community, and smooth deployment tools, Hugging Face has become the primary hub for the open-source AI ecosystem. Control of Hugging Face would give Nvidia gatekeeper power over the software side of AI. It would have influence over visibility and discovery of new models, potentially shaping key standards such as default execution pipelines, software environments, and performance benchmarks. By embedding Nvidia toolchains directly into standard open-source workflows, the company can build deeper ecosystem lock-in, sustaining hardware demand while blocking rival chipmakers from gaining traction. This move also accelerates Nvidia’s enterprise and cloud ambitions. Acquiring Hugging Face instantly provides an established developer base, a deep portfolio of enterprise clients, and a seamless model-to-production pipeline that could be tightly integrated with Nvidia’s cloud services. Potentially, buying Hugging Face would allow Nvidia to buy a level of influence in the software development world that matches its dominant position in AI hardware. Echoes of Microsoft and GitHub Hugging Face is frequently described as the GitHub of AI models, and Nvidia's purchase of Hugging Face has significant parallels to Microsoft's acquisition of GitHub. When Microsoft purchased GitHub in 2018, the company paid $7.5 billion. But it wasn't purchasing the IP for any code hosted on GitHub; instead, it was buying the hub where the code lived—essentially, a dev community. Similarly, Nvidia is not buying proprietary AI model weights; it's trying to purchase the platform where millions of AI developers collaborate. Though GitHub is still central to the open-source community, the purchase has funneled millions of software engineers to Microsoft's Azure cloud ecosystem. There is a legitimate fear that Nvidia is executing a similar move here, wanting to steer the open-source AI community toward its infrastructure hardware, such as DGX Cloud. Reasons to Cheer and Fear the Deal Obviously, reaction from the open-source community is varied. Among the concerns is the risk that Hugging Face will favor Nvidia GPUs and back-end technology, influencing search rankings, default configurations, and model optimizations across the platform. For a community built on free access and hardware-agnostic support, there are fears that competing back-ends (such as AMD ROCm, Intel GPUs, and custom ASICs) will be deprioritized. Seeking to allay those fears, Nvidia is already making big promises about maintaining neutrality. "Hugging Face will remain an open platform for the entire AI ecosystem," Huang says in today's blog post. "Developers will choose the models they want, the frameworks they want, the clouds and inference service providers they want, and the computing platforms they want. Nvidia compute will not be required to build on or deploy through Hugging Face." But even if Nvidia plays it straight and keeps its thumb off the scale, the mere potential for undue influence may reshape the open-source movement. Erosion of trust can occur based on perception alone, and developers on Reddit and other communities are already discussing forking the platform to host models, weights, and tools on an independent, neutral alternative platform. On the other hand, there's some hope. A major injection of capital and world-class hardware engineering could provide a huge boost to open source, improving out-of-the-box optimizations and making open models cheaper and faster to run on ubiquitous Nvidia hardware. Hugging Face CEO Clement Delangue is also bullish on the merger, seeing it as a strategic move to strengthen the open-source ecosystem. "They’ve committed to strongly supporting Hugging Face and our mission while keeping the platform open, independent, and compute agnostic," he tweeted today. "The founders and the team are all staying to keep pushing this mission forward." Finally, while Nvidia may be the 500-pound gorilla in hardware, there are perks to having that gorilla on your side: stronger enterprise-grade security, improved industry compliance, and robust infrastructure support. Regulatory Questions Linger Just as Microsoft’s acquisition of GitHub serves as the strategic blueprint for this deal, Nvidia’s failed attempt to acquire Arm provides the roadmap for the challenges ahead. Now that Nvidia and Hugging Face have confirmed the acquisition, the regulatory battle begins. When Nvidia tried to buy Arm for $40 billion, the deal collapsed under global pressure from the FTC, the UK Competition and Markets Authority, the EU, and China. The core issue was platform neutrality: Arm was considered the "Switzerland of hardware," thriving precisely because it licensed chip architecture equally to hundreds of competing companies. Competitors and antitrust authorities successfully argued that Nvidia's proposed purchase opened the door to destroying that independence and granting unfair access to sensitive rival data. There is an immediate parallel to Hugging Face, which occupies a remarkably similar position as the "Switzerland of AI software." The massive repository of open-source AI models and datasets is used by virtually every developer, researcher, and tech company around the world. Merging the dominant AI hardware vendor with the dominant open-model distribution channel raises real concerns about platform neutrality that are likely to turn into similar regulatory challenges. Competitors like AMD, Intel, Google, and Amazon all run models on Hugging Face, and have legitimate reasons to fear that Nvidia might degrade performance or accessibility for non-Nvidia hardware. Those same tech giants that use Hugging Face to host, test, and fine-tune their models also worry that Nvidia would gain direct visibility into the traffic, downloads, and developer trends around those models. That sort of telemetry surveillance would give the hardware maker inside information on every competing AI project. Additionally, Hugging Face is a global ecosystem, adding a geopolitical angle to the conversation. Chinese AI research labs are responsible for roughly 41% of the models on the platform. Regulators in both the UK and China may balk at a US-based company gaining control of the open-source hub used by most foreign research labs. That's all to say that Nvidia has a steep, complex uphill battle before this agreement ever reaches final approval. The End of Neutral AI Infrastructure? Obviously, there are major questions about whether this deal will proceed from agreement to final closure. Both major tech competitors and the entire open-source movement are rightfully questioning what this acquisition would mean as the AI ecosystem consolidates behind major hardware makers and cloud giants. The leadership at Nvidia and Hugging Face are obviously positive about the deal, with Jensen Huang stating, "AI advances faster when people can build together." And Hugging Face's Delangue highlights that open-source AI offers a strong alternative to the closed approach of most frontier AI companies. "Together, we think we can make open source the default way to build AI, with the goal of empowering 100 million AI builders to own their intelligence rather than rent it." Nvidia's best move to survive regulatory challenges and maintain the platform is to follow Microsoft's lead and more or less leave that community alone. Purchase Hugging Face, but keep it strictly independent, let it remain committed to its open-source mission, and keep it fully open to rival chips and cloud providers. For the moment, it looks like that's exactly the plan. Ultimately, Nvidia's capital, expertise, and influence could either accelerate open-source AI development or fracture it, driving the developer community away from the most established platform for AI models and datasets. About Our Expert From the laptops on your desk to satellites in space and AI that seems to be everywhere, I cover many topics at PCMag. I've covered PCs and technology products for over 15 years at PCMag and other publications, among them Tom's Guide, Laptop Mag, and TWICE. As a hardware reviewer, I've handled dozens of MacBooks, 2-in-1 laptops, Chromebooks, and the latest AI PCs. As the resident Starlink expert, I've done years of hands-on testing with the satellite service. I also explore the most valuable ways to use the latest AI tools and features in our Try AI column.

item.title: Flossing Just Got Easier. I Tried Dyson's New $500 Camera Toothbrush, and It's Worth the Hype
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.33
BERLIN—I floss daily, but if you don't, you might want to consider Dyson's new camera- and water-jet-equipped toothbrush. At $499, the Dyson CameraJet is extremely expensive, yes, but this isn't your average toothbrush. I got to try it out at IFA (on a fake set of teeth, not my own), and it's easily the most advanced oral hygiene product I've ever experienced. It uses the camera and a water jet to automatically blast plaque, food, and debris from the gaps in your teeth, and also dispenses mouthwash. Moreover, it gives you a close look at all the nooks and crannies inside your mouth, and works with an app to teach you how to brush properly. Dyson engineer Guy Turner tells me it's designed for the "9 out of 10 people" who don't floss as much as they need to. During my demo, I saw how the tiny camera on the toothbrush sends a real-time view of your teeth to an app on your phone. As I slowly moved the brush over the fake set of teeth, tiny gaps I could barely notice with my eyes were suddenly magnified on the phone screen. The demo unit I tried didn't actually have any liquid inside, but Turner explained that when the camera detects a gap between your teeth, it shoots out a conical (cone-shaped) burst to clean out any debris, and it all happens within milliseconds. A charging base holds water for the flossing feature and mouthwash, and automatically refills the liquid tanks as needed. The toothbrush features three oscillation modes and a light on the end so you can look deep into crevices, which I think could come in handy if you're afflicted by tonsil stones. Some Dyson long shots turn out to be little more than a gimmick (ahem, the Zone), but the CameraJet appears truly useful. And considering the cost of dental work, it definitely seems like a justifiable purchase. You can buy the Dyson CameraJet now for $499. About Our Expert I'm PCMag's managing editor for consumer electronics, overseeing an experienced team of analysts covering smart home, home entertainment, wearables, fitness and health tech, and various other product categories. I have been with PCMag for more than 10 years, and in that time have written more than 6,000 articles and reviews for the site. I previously served as an analyst focused on smart home and wearable devices, and before that I was a reporter covering consumer tech news. I'm also a yoga instructor, and have been actively teaching group and private classes for nearly a decade. Prior to joining PCMag, I was a reporter for SC Magazine, focusing on hackers and computer security. I earned a BS in journalism from West Virginia University, and started my career writing for newspapers in New Jersey, Pennsylvania, and West Virginia.
