item.title: Final Fantasy Resonance: How Square Enix Turned a Dead Gacha Game Into a Must-Play Console RPG
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.17
I was genuinely excited when Square Enix announced Final Fantasy Resonance ($49.99), an upcoming RPG for PC, PS5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch, and Switch 2 boasting stunning Octopath Traveler-style graphics. That excitement took a hit, though, when I realized it was a revival of Final Fantasy Brave Exvius, the defunct mobile title. How could Square Enix convert a gacha game into a premium console RPG without dragging along its predatory microtransactions and bloated design? More importantly, how could it translate passive screen-tapping into gameplay that satisfies classic RPG purists? After a hands-on preview, I walked away once again excited. Resonance isn't a sloppy cash grab or an asset flip; it's a cleverly designed remake that preserves the original story while radically enhancing the gameplay mechanics. By distilling a decade of live-service fluff into a tight, unlockable roster, Square Enix has crafted a thoughtful console and PC experience that feels every bit like a mainline, classic Final Fantasy game. From Gacha Bloat to FFV-Style Glory: The 26-Vision Job System On paper, the math behind this adaptation is shocking. Brave Exvius ran for more than nine years and ballooned to more than 2,500 characters. It did this by churning out numerous duplicate characters (like five different Cloud Strife units), introducing hundreds of original units, and, of course, various crossover events with popular performers and brands, such as Arianna Grande, Deus Ex, and Fullmetal Alchemist. For Resonance, Square Enix is trimming the legacy lineup to a tightly curated, highly balanced roster of exactly 26 hero characters, called Visions. Losing fan favorites like Auron, Tifa, and Vivi will inevitably cause a stir, yet playing the game convinced me that this radical downsizing is precisely what gives Resonance its quality feel and gameplay depth. Instead of the characters taking up individual party slots like in the mobile version, the 26 Visions function as a deeply flexible and highly strategic Job System, much like the mechanics in the beloved Final Fantasy V. The core demo party consisted of the game's protagonists: Fina, Lasswell, Lid, and Rain. However, I could freely equip them with any Vision I had available to alter their stats, elemental affinities, and supplementary skills. For example, slapping Cloud on Lasswell gave the latter hard-hitting melee and lightning attacks, while equipping Lid with Zidane opened invaluable stealing and speed-based abilities. Due to the newly condensed roster, the power creep that plagued the mobile game has been virtually erased. As a result, every unit has value and utility. And since the gacha elements are no more, I could acquire Visions via overworld shrines, boss battles, and curious trivia quizzes rather than the swipe of my credit card. This gave Resonance an exploration-driven reward system that took me back to the old Final Fantasy games. Rebuilding Combat: Timeline Turns, Staggers, and Brutal Boss Battles Resonance's combat loop is one of its most radical changes. The mobile game's screen-tapping play system has been replaced by a deliberate, timeline-based turn order that captures Final Fantasy X's intense, tactical weight. Firstly, Resonance uses a stagger meter. This mechanic has become a staple in modern Final Fantasy titles, and it works the same way here. With it, all attacks do a certain amount of stagger damage, which depletes the gauge beneath the enemy’s health bar. When the stagger gauge empties, the enemy enters a stun state, loses its upcoming turn, and becomes vulnerable to attacks. Targeting elemental weaknesses and using special heavy attacks rapidly deplete the stagger gauge, so there's a strategic advantage in capitalizing on vulnerabilities to dominate the field. The character that staggered the enemy receives a bonus turn, too, giving you an extra advantage on the field. Unique to Resonance is the Sweeping Stagger system. Depleting the stagger bars of all enemies on the battlefield during the same turn triggers this state, which creates a bonus attack phase that lets your party unleash unique and powerful finishers. This felt like a direct nod to the Valkyrie Profile series's Soul Crush mechanic. To trigger the finisher, you tap the corresponding directional button to chain together attacks from each party member. During the demo, Sweeping Stagger added a dynamic, action-like element to an otherwise entirely turn-based system. I found it tremendously rewarding to use it and every possible advantage to shut down the opposing enemy party so they can't take turns. My demo session peaked with a brutal dungeon run through the Wind Temple, where I squared off against a boss, Veritas of the Heavens. Veritas didn't pull punches; he routinely summoned minions and pummeled my party with potent wind-based attacks. In fact, a Square Enix rep started that my party had been overleveled because Veritas was so brutal; Japanese players who got their mitts on it before me couldn't finish the fight. Still, with efficient use of the Sweeping Stagger system when minions were on the field, I ultimately prevailed. Final Verdict: A Defunct Mobile Title Transformed Into a New Classic By forcing you to engage with tight, meticulously balanced tactical mechanics instead of brainless screen-swiping, Square Enix has done something truly remarkable. The company has successfully rescued a defunct mobile title and transformed it into a console and PC RPG that looks great on all fronts. When Final Fantasy Resonance launches on Oct. 22, 2026, it won't just be a must-play for classic RPG fans—it will be a new blueprint for video game preservation. About Our Expert In 2014, I began my career at PCMag as a freelancer. That blossomed into a full-time position in 2021, and I now review email marketing apps, mobile operating systems, web hosting services, streaming music platforms, and video games as a senior writer. I'm a graduate of Hunter College, a hard-core gamer, and an Apple enthusiast.

item.title: Microsoft Defender is falsely flagging Google links as malicious
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.71
In summary: - PCWorld reports that Microsoft Defender for Office 365 is incorrectly flagging legitimate Google search URLs as malicious, causing false security alerts for users. - The issue stems from the Safe Links feature, which is mistakenly blocking valid Google URLs instead of protecting against genuine threats. - Microsoft has identified the cause and is working on a fix, though no timeline for an official patch has been confirmed yet. Even though Microsoft Defender is more than enough security on its own, its reputation has taken a bit of a hit this year. Over the last few months, vulnerabilities like RedSun and RoguePlanet were discovered (and later patched), while just last month Defender was showing false warnings that it was disabled even when it wasn’t. The latest Defender issue to crop up is that it’s now incorrectly classifying Google links as malicious, reports Neowin. Specifically affecting Microsoft Defender for Office 365, and confirmed by Microsoft, this bug shows an “Opening this website might not be safe” warning when trying to open legitimate Google links. Microsoft says it has identified the cause of the issue, clarifying that it isn’t an actual security threat with Google links: Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Safe Links may block the opening of Google search links (URLs), identifying them as malicious. In addition, admins may receive related alerts and incidents in the Microsoft Defender portal and Microsoft Sentinel as a result of these detections. We’ve determined that an inaccurate security classification is causing legitimate Google search URLs to be incorrectly identified as malicious, resulting in Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Safe Links blocking access to affected links. We’re working to correct the misclassification to remediate impact. Microsoft says it’s working on a fix, but hasn’t given a specific timeline regarding when the fix will be released.

item.title: How ad-free streaming became so much less affordable
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.52
Ad-free streaming used to be one of the biggest benefits of cutting the cable TV cord. Now it’s become a luxury. Inspired by some new research into the growing price gap between ad-supported and ad-free streaming, I decided to calculate how much the cost to avoid commercials has increased over time. Depending on which services you have, you could be paying an extra $42.50 just to skip ads, up 60 percent from a few years ago. Not all hope is lost for affordable ad-free TV, but you might have to get a bit creative to get it. The increasing ad-free tax My impetus for writing this is a new report from Ampere Analysis about the growing gulf in price between ad-free and ad-supported streaming. The study found that globally over the past three years, the ad-free tiers of Netflix, Amazon Prime, and Disney+ have increased by $1.61 on average, versus $1.21 per month with ads. Those results actually understate the problem. When you look at the United States in particular, which includes more streaming services, the ad-free tax becomes even bigger. Let’s say you’re a subscriber to Netflix, Amazon Prime, HBO Max, Disney+, Paramount+, and Peacock. At the end of 2022 (when both Netflix and Disney launched ad-supported tiers), the total cost would have been roughly $44 per month with ads, or $70.50 without ads, for a difference of $26.50. Those same six services now cost roughly $63 per month with ads, or $105.50 per month without ads. While the overall price has increased on both sides, the difference between ad-free and ad-supported plans has jumped by 60 percent, from $26.50 to $42.50 per month. Here’s a closer look at how the price gap has grown over the years: | | Dec. 2022 (ads / ad-free) | Sept. 2026 (ads / ad-free) | Ad-free fee increase | |---|---|---|---| | Netflix (Standard) | $6.99 / $15.49 | $8.99 / $19.99 | +$2.50 | | Amazon Prime Video | $8.99: Ad-free only | $8.99 / $13.98 | +$4.99 | | HBO Max | $9.99 / $14.99 | $10.99 / $18.49 | +$2.50 | | Disney+ | $7.99 / $10.99 | $11.99 / $18.99 | +$4.00 | | Paramount+ | $4.99 / $9.99 | $8.99 / $13.99 | $0.00 | | Peacock | $4.99 / $9.99 | $12.99 / $19.99 | +$2.00 | | Total | $43.94 / $70.44 | $62.94 / $105.43 | +$15.99 | Amazon is the biggest offender. At the start of 2024, it started including ads in Prime Video and charged $3 per month to remove them. The ad-free price then jumped to $5 per month last March, with a plan that Amazon now calls “Prime Video Ultra.” Other companies were more subtle in pushing ads on users. Disney initially indicated that its ad-supported tier would cost less than the ad-free plan. When that plan arrived in late 2022, Disney raised the price of for ad-free streaming and slotted in its new ad-supported plan at the old price. Netflix, meanwhile, phased out its “Basic (Ad-Free)” plan in 2024, making the jump to ad-free streaming more drastic. And Peacock has raised prices so aggressively that even its ad-supported plan costs more than the ad-free version once did. In all cases, the dynamic is the same: As Ampere points out, subscription growth is leveling out in the United States, and streamers are increasingly relying on advertising to boost their revenues. While ad-free streaming becomes more of a luxury, the streamers still need to keep ad-supported prices low so they can bring in new subscribers and scale up their advertising businesses. Ad skipping still remains alive and well in the realm of live TV streaming services such as YouTube TV, Sling TV, and Fubo. Those services include cloud-based DVRs, so you can record live TV and skip the commercials. But as more viewers opt for cheaper standalone streaming services, the streamers are now ushering the DVR toward obsolescence. What you can do about it In some cases, bundling services together may provide price hike relief, even on ad-free tiers. Disney, for instance, has actually shrunk the price gap for its bundle of Disney+ and Hulu. That package cost $10 per month with ads or $20 per month without ads a few years ago. Now it’s $13 per month with ads, but still $20 per month without ads. The bundle of Disney+, Hulu, and HBO Max has also maintained the same $13 per month upcharge for ad-free over the past couple years, even as the overall cost has increased. (It’s $33 per month for all three without ads.) The growing price gap may also create an opportunity for more affordable ad-free services. I keep writing about how YouTube is taking over TV viewing in the United States, and it now has 125 million subscribers on its Premium or Music plans. If you just want to skip ads on YouTube, Premium Lite for $9 per month can look like a pretty good value compared to traditional streaming services. Keep an eye on Roku’s Howdy streaming service as well. At $3 per month with no ads, the catalog is heavy on B-movies and forgotten reruns, but has some hidden gems that remind me of Netflix’s early days. It reportedly topped 1 million subscribers in less than a year, and it continues to grow its catalog with new licensing deals. If you’re up for a more adversarial approach, you can also take ad-skipping into your own hands. I’ve previously written about PlayOn, which records video from ad-supported streaming services and lets you skip the commercials. Using it can be a hassle, as it requires either pay-as-you-go cloud recording credits or a Windows PC to run the recording engine, but the savings can be significant. If you’re willing to watch through a web browser, the Multi Skipper extension will attempt to fast forward through commercials on major streaming services for free. I’ve been using this on my still-experimental living room PC setup with great success, and while relying on a computer for streaming has its own trade-offs, it’s one of the last ways to retain some control in a system that’s increasingly stacked against its viewers.

item.title: Best of IFA 2026: 10 hot PC products and tech on the horizon
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.25
Like CES in Las Vegas, the IFA technology tradeshow that takes place every year in Berlin gives technology vendors and taste makers an opportunity to show off their latest and greatest wares, and consumers a chance to start planning their next purchases and saving their shekels. From a PC user’s perspective, the category that got the most love this year was monitors, and we’re here for it as innovations include esports-caliber OLED and truly affordable Mini LED. There are also some tasty laptops coming down the pike, some intriguing developments for consumer AI, and a few very promising hardware concepts that we’re praying will make it to market. Without further ado, here are the 10 products and innovations from IFA 2026 that have us most excited. Acer Vero 16 Acer IFA is generally a showcase for laptops, and this year the big news is those RTX Spark models due in October. But I’m wary of new Arm chips, and doubly wary of Nvidia. For my money (what little it buys in a laptop these days), Acer stole the show with its revamped Vero 16. Granted, Acer is mostly cribbing on Framework here. In addition to recycled components that were a highlight of previous Vero designs, this one allows tool-free access to the primary laptop component bay, replaceable hinges, replaceable battery, all while keeping at least some durability. You can swap out the SSD, too…but not the RAM, like most Core Ultra Series 3 laptops. With a standard OLED screen and a base Core Ultra 5 322 processor (up to Core Ultra X9 388H at the top end), respectable Arc B390 graphics, and a 71-watt-hour battery, this looks like a pretty good option for a mid-range, all-rounder laptop…though who knows how much all that extra engineering will add to the price. I can’t say I’d prefer the Vero to a Framework without getting my hands on it, but I’m happy to see more companies incorporate repairable designs. – Michael Crider Lenovo’s Project AeroBlade concept Mark Hachman / Foundry PCWorld was the first to break the story on the Frore AirJet cooling chip, and we’ve been following the technology for years. Now the Lenovo Project AeroBlade concept finally looks like it could bring the AirJet chip to store shelves inside a new 14-inch laptop. Fortunately, Lenovo concepts often end up as products — I’m guessing in 2027. Why is this important? An AirJet laptop stands to be both quiet (no fans, remember) as well as light — 1.83 pounds, in this case. It’s literally as heavy as a full 24oz water bottle. Lenovo is using Intel’s Core Ultra 200 chip inside it, so it stands to be moderately powerful as well. I can’t wait until I can take something like this on a business trip. – Mark Hachman Alienware AW2527HX 560Hz OLED esports monitor Alienware For me, the biggest story coming out of IFA was the deluge of fantastical new monitors, and the Alienware 25 560Hz QD-OLED Gaming Monitor (AW2527HX) captured my attention like no other. The upshot here? OLED is finally ready for the high refresh rates that esports sweats clamor for. That means that in addition to the blistering 560Hz refresh rate, this 24.5-inch 1080p display also offers all of OLED’s benefits, like luscious contrast, vivid colors with wicked accuracy, fast gray-to-gray pixel response times, and inky VESA DisplayHDR True Black 600 certification that ensures blacks deeper than the darkest soul. Typical esports monitors use ancient TN panel technology instead, which is fast but suffers in visual quality and viewing angles. You won’t find that here. Add in physical design feedback from the esports pros at Team Liquid — I dig the height markers on the stand for easily repeatable setup — and the Alienware AW2527HX looks ready to turn heads when it launches in the first quarter of 2027. – Brad Chacos Acer Nitro XV275U Z2 OLED isn’t the only big dawg in the display junkyard. Mini-LED offers many of the same benefits of OLED, but offers higher peak brightness and better text clarity at the slight expense of slower gray-to-gray response times. Bottom line? Mini-LED monitors look great — and now they’re shockingly cheap. Case in point: Acer’s Nitro XV275U Z2. It will cost just $329 when it launches later this year, giving you a stunning 1,000 nits of HDR brightness powered by 1,152-zone mini-LED backlighting, along with a Dynamic Frequency and Resolution feature that starts at 275Hz at its default 1440p, 360Hz at 1080p, and 520Hz at 720p (ick). Mini-LED doesn’t suffer from the pixel burn-in concerns like OLED, either. Look for the Acer Nitro XV275U Z2 to land before the holidays. – Brad Chacos Alienware 32 4K OLED Gaming Monitor (AW3226Q) Dell Mini-LED may have historically offered superior text clarity to OLED, but thanks to new “RGB Stripe” OLED technology debuting this year, those days may be over. And Dell created a killer-looking 4K monitor for work and play that leverages the bleeding-edge feature. The Alienware 32 4K OLED Gaming Monitor (AW3226Q) offers everything gamers could want, from its pixel-packed resolution and 165Hz running speeds to its stunning 1,000-nit peak brightness and VESA DisplayHDR True Black 400 and Dolby Vision certifications. The panel is factory-calibrated for Delta E<2 color accuracy and covers 99 percent of the DCI-P3 color space, which should make it appealing to creators and visual pros as well — especially paired with RGB Stripe’s improved text clarity. Heck, Alienware even packed in HDMI 2.1, so the display plays nice with consoles, too. Is this the One Monitor To Rule Them All? I’m drooling at the idea of testing this display when it launches for $699 — a shockingly low price tag considering what the AW3226Q offers — later this fall. – Brad Chacos Acer DualPlay Mini concept Acer Why would you spend $2,000 on a PC gaming handheld instead of a gaming laptop? Aside from the size and the controls, everything else is a compromise. But what if you could have…both? Acer’s DualPlay Mini concept answers that question, with a transforming handheld that flips up to reveal a mini-laptop. High price and a lack of utility for most buyers are what makes me lose interest in high-end gaming handhelds. But this one could make a solid value argument, albeit for a small group of users. It’s basically cramming a netbook into a handheld, albeit a very powerful Arc G3 one. You could even say it’s more portable than a conventional gaming laptop, while preserving a full keyboard…though an eight-inch screen and no touchpad mean you’re still making compromises. I don’t think this is a practical or realistic design, and frankly I’d be shocked to see it come to market. But I’d love to be proven wrong. – Michael Crider Acer SFF RTX Spark Mini Workstation Acer Acer’s SFF RTX Spark is bigger than a mini PC, smaller than a desktop PC, with more than enough power for at-home AI work. Built on Nvidia’s new RTX Spark platform, it features a Blackwell RTX GPU with up to 6,144 cores, an Nvidia Grace CPU with up to 20 cores, up to 128GB of unified memory, and up to 1 petaflop of AI compute. Why pay for expensive tokens when you can run language models and image generation locally? That’s what this mini-workstation is geared for. The appeal here is obvious: a quiet, compact box that can handle modest AI tasks without involving a subscription or data center. Better privacy, no usage caps, and greater potential than running those same local models on less-well-equipped laptops. As one of the first with Nvidia’s RTX Spark, the Acer SFF RTX Spark is on the cutting edge—and what I appreciate most is how much power it packs into an unassuming box. It’s form and function, not mere novelty. Acer hasn’t announced pricing or availability yet, so for now we’ll just have to wait and see what comes of it. – Joel Lee Nvidia RTX PAIR Nvidia Nvidia teased out some more details about its forthcoming RTX Spark processor at IFA, but I’m more intrigued by some free software meant to tease more AI performance out of the hardware you already own. Nvidia’s RTX PAIR – an acronym for “Personal AI Router” — is a free app for Windows, MacOS, and Linux that you install on every PC you own with a GPU inside. Once you do, they’re added to a collective pool of resources. Once you spool up tasks for local AI agents in Ollama or LM Studio, RTX PAIR springs into action, dynamically assigning subtasks to the various GPUs in your home to complete AI inference faster. In Nvidia’s example, a “weekly Sunday tasks” chore took more than 18 minutes to complete on a single PC, but RTX PAIR dropped that to just 9 minutes by splitting agents between three computers. It’s a clever way for Nvidia to augment its already ferocious-looking RTX Spark chips, using the RTX gaming and creator laptops you already own to create an AI supercomputer inside your home. RTX PAIR is available now. – Brad Chacos Lenovo Project Swan concept Mark Hachman / Foundry Look, I’m a sucker for ultrawide monitors. Lenovo’s Project Swan concept turns a traditional 14-inch ThinkBook into a widescreen productivity beast at the simple push of a button. That’s all I need to know. I’m sold. Please make this real Lenovo. Please. – Brad Chacos Acer Swift Blade 14 Acer Acer’s Swift Blade is actually lighter (1.76 pounds) than the Lenovo AeroBlade (1.83 pounds) not to mention Acer’s older TravelMate P6 14 AI (2.2 pounds). What all these numbers say, though, is that ultralight laptops are back in a big way, and that the Swift Blade may be the lightest 14-inch laptop on the market. There are still questions: How long will its 50Wh battery last, attached to an 1800p OLED? Will its Wildcat Lake processor deliver the goods? Sure, there are those who don’t mind shouldering a 3- or 4-pound laptop for some additional performance. However, there’s also a viable market for consumers who just want a lightweight computing solution that’s not a phone or a tablet. And did we mention that the Swift Blade 14 is about a pound lighter than a MacBook Air? – Mark Hachman

item.title: Nvidia wants to turn your house of gaming PCs into an AI supercomputer
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.11
Nvidia and its partners are ready to roll out new RTX Spark-powered devices in October, shoving the GPU goliath into the CPU spotlight with a beastly first processor that’s augmented by powerful integrated graphics. It’s all to chase the allure of local AI. And to set the stage, at IFA Berlin 2026, Nvidia is introducing new software designed to turn your RTX-powered gaming household into a miniature AI factory of its own. Nvidia Dubbed Nvidia PAIR (short for “Personal AI Router”), the free application takes all the GPUs in your local network and dynamically shoots AI agents and subagents to the best available resources during inference tasks. Better yet, Nvidia says it should work with rival GPUs as well, not just GeForce or Nvidia’s pro graphics cards. Nvidia The idea is simple: Install RTX PAIR on every GPU-equipped PC on your network. The software will automatically detect and pair devices over your LAN, so note that hardwired Ethernet connections are key here. RTX PAIR will intelligently and dynamically shift tasks from AI agents and subagents to the GPU on your network that’s able to handle it first. RTX PAIR will initially support Ollama and LM Studio, two popular local AI options with support for multiple open models. In a demo, Nvidia showed Ollama running a person’s typical “Sunday morning” checklist of tasks side-by-side with RTX PAIR. You could see PAIR dynamically allocating agent tasks across the network as they spawned. Nvidia Spreading the load across a trio of RTX-powered PCs on a network helped the task complete in just over 9 minutes with RTX PAIR, compared to over 18 minutes running on a single PC. Nvidia Nvidia It’s a thoughtful move by Nvidia. There’s no question that RTX Spark PCs are built for AI-native workloads, and the early adopters who buy them likely already have big local models running on home PCs, gaming or otherwise. RTX PAIR lets AI fanatics unleash their entire home’s collective GPU compute on tasks, rather than singular devices alone. It’s a smart pairing (ha ha) with the RTX Spark announcement… …especially if the cloud AI bubble ever bursts. If ChatGPT and Claude keep raising token rates, or circular funding deals make the AI bubble pop in spectacular fashion, local AI will still be around and ready to kick ass on the hardware you already own. Nvidia says it has tested RTX PAIR on up to 18 devices on a local network, but there’s theoretically no limit to the number of connected PCs, so this could be a powerful tool that pushes local AI farms even deeper into CUDA’s arms, despite its compatibility with rival GPUs. To quote Robert Muldoon in Jurassic Park: Clever girl. Nvidia is launching RTX PAIR as a free download today, and you can use it to start distributing AI tasks among gaming and AI PCs ahead of RTX Spark’s October launch. The app will be open-source under the Apache 2.0 license and available on Windows, Linux, and macOS.

item.title: Is your USB port slowing down your Wi-Fi adapter? Here’s the answer
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.94
A Wi-Fi USB dongle is the easiest way to add new Wi-Fi hardware to a computer. Wi-Fi 7 and Wi-Fi 6 adapters promise data rates of well over one gigabyte per second. This is why many users wonder whether the USB port on their PC or laptop might be slowing down their Wi-Fi connection. To answer that, it helps to understand the speed specifications for Wi-Fi USB adapters–as with Wi-Fi devices in general–aren’t particularly reliable. The packaging often features a value such as AX1800 for a Wi-Fi 6 dongle or BE6500 for a Wi-Fi 7 dongle. This is what’s known as a pseudo-class–this speed rating is a marketing invention that has nothing to do with real-world speeds. First, manufacturers simply add up the maximum data rates for each frequency band supported by the adaptor. For example, AX1800 combines 1,200 Mbit/s on 5 GHz with 574 Mbit/s 2.4 GHz, which rounds up to 1,800 Mbit/s. However, as a Wi-Fi transmission always runs on just one frequency at a time, these combined figures can never be achieved. With Wi-Fi 7, this would theoretically be possible, provided that both the dongle and the router support the MLO MLMR (Multi-Link Operation with Multi-Link-Multi-Radio) function. However, no Wi-Fi 7 dongle is capable of this. The manufacturers’ specifications for the individual frequencies are gross figures that can never be achieved in practice. This is because, even at short distances between the router and the dongle, the data rate is reduced due to signal errors. You can assume that, in the best-case scenario, a Wi-Fi connection will achieve 60 to 70 percent of the specified data rate. A Wi-Fi 7 USB dongle ideally achieves a real-world data rate of around 2 Gbit/s. The maximum data rate for USB 3.0 (USB 3.2 Gen 1) is 5 Gbit/s. Here, too, there are some losses: USB speeds are reduced by overhead, poor-quality cables, high CPU load, faulty drivers, and other USB devices connected to the computer. Nevertheless, USB 3.0 should deliver 2.5 to over 3 Gbit/s in practice, which is sufficient even for the fastest Wi-Fi 7 dongles. Asus This means the interface is also fast enough for Wi-Fi 6 adapters, with the fastest models offering speeds of 1.5 to 1.8 Gbit/s. You should, however, avoid Wi-Fi dongles with USB 2.0 for Wi-Fi 6 or Wi-Fi 7 if you don’t want to slow down the connection. That said, these models – such as the Asus USB-BE92 Nano – offer other advantages. They are usually very small, which means they can stay plugged into your laptop and are unlikely to get lost. Furthermore, under good wireless conditions, they achieve speeds of around 200 to 300 Mbit/s, which is sufficient for the bandwidth offered by most VDSL internet connections. There is a pitfall to watch out for with USB Type-C. Unlike Type-A, where a 3.0 port can usually be distinguished from a 2.0 port by its blue color, with Type-C you’ll have to check whether the port on your computer is labeled accordingly. If it isn’t, the only solution is to consult the manual.

item.title: Windows 11’s next security feature may cost you gaming performance
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.93
Next month’s Patch Tuesday falls on October 13th, and with that update, Microsoft will be enabling “Memory Integrity” on all Windows 11 systems that are still receiving updates, according to this Windows IT Pro blog post. Memory Integrity (also known as Hypervisor-Protected Code Integrity, or HVCI) has been around for some time, but it hasn’t been enabled yet on many PCs. Starting October 13th, 2026, all supported Windows 11 PCs will enable Memory Integrity by default. While Memory Integrity is primarily intended as a security feature, gamers may find it a hindrance. What does it actually do? Well, Memory Integrity ensures that only verified kernel-mode code is loaded on the PC, blocking unsigned rootkits and raising the barrier to driver-based kernel attacks. The goal is for Windows 11 to be better protected against malware attacks. Before Windows enables this feature, it will check eligible computers and verify whether the machine is ready for it. According to this support page, Memory Integrity requires the following hardware: - 8th-generation Intel processor or newer - AMD Zen 2 or newer - Qualcomm Snapdragon 8180 or newer - At least 8GB of RAM on x64 systems - A 64GB SSD with firmware-enabled virtualization - Drivers with confirmed compatibility with Memory Integrity However, this feature has a major drawback: Memory Integrity can apparently slow down games. Tom’s Hardware measured years ago that HVCI combined with VBS (Virtualization-Based Security) causes games to run up to 15 percent slower. VBS is also enabled as part of this update, providing additional security features. According to Tom’s Hardware, Microsoft confirmed in 2022 that “Memory Integrity and Virtual Machine Platform could affect gaming performance on some Windows 11 configurations, and advised gamers prioritizing performance that they could temporarily disable these protections while playing, warning that doing so reduces security.” Gaming performance losses are most likely to be noticeable on computers with older hardware. Tom’s Hardware continued, saying that Microsoft’s guidance for gamers recommended “temporarily disabling Memory Integrity and VMP where they interfere with gaming performance.”

item.title: Windows 11’s August update broke Teams and Outlook on Arm PCs
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.83
It’s been nearly a month since Microsoft released its Patch Tuesday update for Windows 11—known as KB5121003—but problems are still cropping up and being reported by users. The latest issue affects Arm-based computers like the Surface Laptop 7 and Surface Pro 11. According to a recent Windows health update (spotted by BleepingComputer), Microsoft acknowledges that “Microsoft Teams and Outlook might fail to launch on Arm-based devices.” That’s referring to the new Outlook app, not the classic Outlook app. In fact, classic versions of Microsoft’s apps seem unaffected by the issue at hand: After installing Windows security updates released on or after August 11, 2026, (KB5121003), Microsoft Teams and the new Outlook for Windows might fail to launch or might close unexpectedly on Arm-based devices, such as Surface Pro 11 and Surface Laptop 7. Classic Outlook, Word, Excel, and other applications are not known to be affected. This issue is most likely to occur on new or freshly imaged PCs that have not yet installed any Microsoft Store updates. Microsoft says the issue affects Windows 11 versions 24H2, 25H2, and 26H1, and that the company is working on a fix that will be made available with a future Windows update. For now, if you’ve installed the KB5121003 update and you’re experiencing instability with Microsoft Teams and new Outlook, Microsoft’s provided workaround is to open the Microsoft Store, select Downloads → Check for updates, then install the latest update for the Auto Super Resolution Package (version 1.0.19.0 or later). This problem is just one more in a long line that traces back to the August Patch Tuesday update. In recent weeks, users have also reported that the update breaks printers and PDFs on Windows 11 and crashing games and causing other PC instability issues.

item.title: Never defragment your SSD. Do this instead to keep it in tip-top shape
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.72
Remember when you had to defragment your hard drive regularly? With traditional HDDS, this made sense because files could become fragmented into small pieces over a period of time. The mechanical read head then had to jump across the magnetic platters to find all the pieces of a file, which slowed the system down. Defragmentation programs reorganized the data and ensured that files were stored contiguously again. With SSDs, however, data storage works differently. Instead of moving parts, they use flash memory chips that are accessed electronically. As a result, whether a file is stored in a single block or across many fragments has little impact on performance. Samsung Fragmentation plays virtually no role on SSDs. On the contrary, defragmentation can actually be harmful here. Flash memory cells have only a limited number of write cycles. During defragmentation, large amounts of data are rewritten, even though this brings no performance benefit. As a result, the process unnecessarily consumes write reserves and can shorten the drive’s lifespan over time. Instead, modern operating systems handle SSD maintenance automatically. The TRIM command is particularly important here. It informs the drive which data blocks are no longer required after files have been deleted. The SSD can clear these areas internally and rewrite them more quickly later on. In Windows, TRIM is usually already enabled. However, if you still wish to check the status of this function, type cmd into the Windows Start menu and then launch the Command Prompt as an administrator. You can then use the command fsutil behavior query DisableDeleteNotify to check whether the TRIM is active. A 0 confirms that it is enabled, while a 1 means the function is disabled. If it’s disabled, enter the command fsutil behavior set DisableDeleteNotify 0 to enable the TRIM. It’s also a good idea to leave sufficient free space on the drive. A reserve of around 15 to 20 percent of the total storage capacity is a good rule of thumb. In addition, you should occasionally remove old programs, large files, and temporary data. The most important thing to remember: an SSD does not require traditional defragmentation. If you keep the TRIM enabled, make sure you leave sufficient free space and you’ll also want to occasionally tidy up the system. The drive should continue to operate quickly and reliably for a long time.

item.title: Lenovo’s fanless laptop makes AirJet feel real at last
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.05
In 2022, I broke the story on Frore Systems and its AirJet Mini and AirJet Pro, two solid-state cooling solutions that could replace traditional fans in laptops. Since then, readers have been grumbling: “Where are they? Is the AirJet just vaporware?” Apparently not, as Lenovo has built them into its Project AeroBlade concept that will ship, at a guess, in 2027. Here’s what the AeroBlade concept means: By using Frore’s solution, Lenovo can eliminate traditional fans and therefore shave off weight (from the traditional heat pipe) and reduce noise. It’s also a critical validation of Frore’s tech as a viable laptop cooling mechanism. Solutions like the AirJet should usher in a new wave of truly thin-and-light laptops, and that matters. This is Lenovo—not every prototype comes to market, but the majority of them do. This is a transformative technology. So, Lenovo’s Project AeroBlade promises to be the lightest 14-inch laptop on the market, right? Well, no. But it may be the better device. Mark Hachman / Foundry This week at IFA, Acer announced the Swift Blade, a 14-inch laptop weighing 0.8kg (1.76 pounds). Lenovo’s AeroBlade concept weighs “under 830g [1.83 pounds],” according to the company. Put another way, that’s about the weight of a full 24oz refillable water bottle. There’s a key difference, however. Acer is basing its Swift Blade on Intel’s “Wildcat Lake” processor, the Core 7 350, which performed capably but not competitively in my review of the Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 3i, which used the same chip. Lenovo’s AeroBlade will be based on Intel’s older Core Ultra 200 (“Lunar Lake”) chip, which outperforms all other x86 chips in terms of battery efficiency, based on my tests of the Snapdragon X2 Elite. We don’t know which Core Ultra 200 chip Lenovo will eventually include, but the Lunar Lake architecture includes four performance cores to Wildcat Lake’s two, and it can reduce the total core count. Based on numbers alone, the AeroBlade is likely to be more powerful and power-efficient. Since it’s just a concept, Lenovo isn’t revealing much. I was able to wave the AeroBlade around and marvel at how easy it is to carry. The keyboard felt solid, though not especially great, and we weren’t able to power the device on to check the processor or even if the device sounded “fanless” even under load. Mark Hachman / Foundry What’s neat is that the sub-10mm-thick chassis had to expand outward to accommodate traditional laptop ports like USB-C. Impressive! And while Wildcat Lake doesn’t have Thunderbolt capabilities—those laptops use a generic 10Gbps USB-C port instead—Lunar Lake is fully Thunderbolt capable, which will give users access to more powerful peripherals. Frore nears its coming-out party The Frore-Lenovo solution is called the Lenovo Active Flow Thermal Solution, and it implements the latest version of the AirJet Mini inside the laptop. Frore’s Airjet technology uses a vibrating membrane to suck in and expel air, all through vents mounted inside the AeroBlade’s hinge. (My late colleague Gordon Mah Ung walks you through AirJet in this video.) According to Frore, the Airjet Mini is 27mm wide and 41mm long, and each of the current AirJet Mini devices dissipates 7.5W. Lenovo told me there are four modules inside the AeroBlade, which should accommodate the 17W thermal power of a Core Ultra 5 or 7 Lunar Lake chip, but whose combined 30W of cooling won’t quite handle the maximum 37W of cooling power those chips are designed for. In short, the AeroBlade could still thermally throttle down under load. Mark Hachman / Foundry Still, it’s a win for solid-state cooling, which has had a surge of competition. While xMEMS seems content to use its MEMS diaphragms to power earbuds and other small speakers, Ventiva has its own fanless cooling solution waiting in the wings with partnerships between Intel and Dell, though there hasn’t been any public movement recently. By the way, Acer’s laptop apparently doesn’t include any similar fanless cooling solutions. When asked how Acer achieved its low weight inside its Swift Blade, a representative indicated that Acer had designed it around a carbon-fiber chassis and used the simpler Wildcat Lake package for its laptop design alongside a 51Wh battery. There’s nothing wrong with that. Competition benefits everyone, no matter how a laptop is architected. Still, just pushing thin-and-light laptops to new extremes of size and weight means that thin-and-light laptops actually matter, and are carving out new niches for users. Mark Hachman / Foundry

item.title: Oukitel’s new rugged laptop charges via sunlight and survives water jets
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.04
Oukitel, a Chinese consumer electronics company with a 10-year pedigree, just unveiled its new RG14-P laptop at IFA 2026 in Berlin. What makes this laptop unique is that it’s not only exceptionally durable but can also charge its own battery using solar power, reports Notebookcheck. According to Oukitel, the laptop’s solar panels can generate up to 15 watts. That should be enough to charge the 95 watt-hour battery from 0 to 50 percent in around six hours. The laptop’s battery also consists of a built-in 3,000mAh section and a removable 5,200mAh section, making it possible to carry and swap in spare batteries. The laptop has a 14.1-inch touchscreen with 1,000 nits of brightness, a 14th-generation Intel Core i7 processor, a webcam that can be directed both forwards and backwards, NFC, a fingerprint reader, and several ports including HDMI and Ethernet. The downside is that it weighs 3.7 kilograms (8.16 pounds), which is seriously fat and far from everyday portable. The Oukitel RG14-P also has an IP69K rating, which is the highest level of ingress protection, meaning it’s completely sealed and protected against water and dust infiltration. It can even survive against water jet cleaning. Oukitel has not yet announced pricing or availability.

item.title: Lenovo’s IdeaPad Vibe laptops combine color, chatbots, and computing
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.02
Lenovo’s IdeaPad Vibe is here to answer the question: What am I going to buy as a cheap, productive PC this holiday? If you can spare $699.99, Lenovo has the answer: Either 14-inch or 15-inch Vibe laptops, with attractive colorways, available initially with either first-gen Snapdragon X processors or the new AMD Ryzen AI 400 series processors. Intel processors will be supported at a later date, Lenovo said, but the company didn’t provide specifics. Remember, Lenovo has three brands: ThinkPad business notebooks; ThinkBooks, aimed more at a small business owner; and IdeaPads, Lenovo’s consumer brand for laptops. With skyrocketing prices across the board, Lenovo has to offer a consumer model that’s priced attractively. The problem, of course, is that only the base configuration will carry that $699 price tag; how quickly prices climb when you add different configurations isn’t known. (A Lenovo spokesman suggested that $1,500 would be on the higher end of the price spectrum.) Lenovo To be honest, I’m not particularly sold on either platform. Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X processor is the budget offering from its first-generation lineup, as opposed to the X2 chips that Qualcomm announced last fall and are shipping now. Qualcomm’s problem here is branding: Early discussions of the Snapdragon X1 Elite platform used the term “Snapdragon X” to describe them, but in 2025 Qualcomm added the “Snapdragon X” brand, which has fewer cores (eight) than the Snapdragon X Elite (12). AMD’s Ryzen AI 400 processors are current, though Ryzen AI 400 tests I ran weren’t particularly fast, and the battery life under load was pretty lousy. It’s perhaps one reason that you haven’t seen too much of either chip in the laptop market. What both chips do offer, however, is a full-fledged NPU, and Lenovo is shipping its Qira AI software as part of the onboard software package to help you take notes. You may not like so-called “AI slop,” but Qira does offer automated transcription as well as RAG document analysis, where you can upload a document and then ask questions about it. Finally, you can ask Qira to write for you, based upon what the software knows of your style. I wouldn’t use Qira to write for me, but to transcribe? Sure. Since the Vibe is a consumer platform, the most noticeable feature is the new colorways: Chill Blue, Zen Green, Spicy Gold, Radiant Coral, Dreamy Violet, Lowkey Grey, and Moody Blue. They’re attractive and eye-catching, a far cry from the very functional basic black of the business ThinkPads. Another twist: You’ll be able to mix and match keycaps in those colors, too. The Vibe series is uniformly based upon OLED, with the 14-inch models topping out at 1920×1200 resolutions and the 15-inch options equating to a “2.1K” display. All are 100 percent DCI-P3 compatible, with touch options. The 14-inch models weigh about 2.87 pounds, while the 15-inch models weigh 3.31 pounds. Memory options — a key limiter in 2026 — will vary, too. All of the Ryzen laptops are upgradable, with up to 32GB of DRAM available. The Snapdragon X versions, with their integrated memory, are not — you’re left with choices up to 24GB, but they can’t be adjusted. Storage options are identical, with up to 1TB of storage. I was also a little surprised to see the Ryzen AI 400 laptops shipping with either 50Wh or 65Wh battery options, while the Snapdragon laptops were limited to 50Wh versions. Lenovo All of the laptops appear to share the same port combination: two 5Gbps USB-A ports, two 5Gbps USB-C ports, microSD, audio, and an HDMI 1.4 port. There is no Ethernet jack. All of the laptops use WiFi 7 and Bluetooth 5.4. I had a chance to touch and feel the laptops at a press event in advance of IFA, and they’re fine. The real answers will lie in the intersection of their price and performance. It’s still a tough question to answer until the Ideapad Vibes begin shipping in October (AMD’s Ryzen AI 400) and November (the Qualcomm Snapdragon X).

item.title: Buying a USB-C cable? Beware these 6 hidden traps
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 3.67
It’s been a few years since USB-C first hit the scene. And while we still love how reversible it is and how powerful it’s become, we’re also more aware of the potential pitfalls around this high-powered cable. There have been plenty of stories of poor-quality cables frying components, shorting chargers, or even catching fire, so we’ve gone to great lengths to test many options, including some of the best USB-C cables you can get and some of the most hazardous to avoid. Here are some key gotchas you need to be aware of before buying a USB-C cable these days. Learn how to spot the bad ones and what you can do to end up with one that’s fast, durable, and priced well. Further reading: Laptop makers, I’m begging you for this one simple feature Don’t buy from no-name brands This tip is true for most electronics, but it’s especially important for USB-C cables. You might think a USB-C cable is just a bit of wiring in a sheath, but actually there are several safety features — at least, there should be — that ensure safe power delivery. Of course, just because safety regulations exists doesn’t mean that all manufacturers follow them, especially manufacturers who don’t have a reputation to uphold. That tends to be the case for manufacturers on the other side of the world who sell to the international market through sites like Temu, AliExpress, and Amazon. Although sticking to recognizable brands isn’t an entirely foolproof method of securing a high-quality USB-C cable, it does eliminate a lot of the risk as far as safety transgressions are concerned. There’s also more likelihood of recompense if something does go wrong. USB-C cable brands we recommend include: - Anker - Apple - Aukey - Belkin - Cable Matters - Dockcase - Microsoft - Ugreen Avoid USB-C-to-USB-A cables Gordon Mah Ung / IDG If transfer speed is important to you and if your devices and chargers support it, always prefer to use a USB-C-to-USB-C cable rather than a USB-C-to-USB-A cable or converting it from one to the other with an adapter. USB-A is limited in data transfer speed to 10Gbps and limited in charging speed to just 15W. Although there are some USB-C-to-USB-A cables that claim to handle up to 100W, these are typically based on proprietary charging technologies and only reach those rates when paired with appropriately compatible devices and chargers. In comparison, modern USB-C-to-USB-C cables can handle up to 40Gbps of data transfer and up to 240W for fast charging. (That said, 100W and less is still the most common.) You don’t need to buy a cable with the highest specifications, but higher-spec cables are usually higher quality, and that can help ensure that you’re getting a good USB-C cable. So unless you’re powering legacy devices that only support USB-A, you’re better off moving to end-to-end USB-C for both data transfers and charging if performance is a priority. Buy Thunderbolt or USB4 if you can Mark Hachman / Foundry Thunderbolt (3, 4, or 5) and USB4 cables offer the highest charging and data transfer speeds possible for USB-C as of this writing. But most people don’t exactly need those tip-top specs, right? Even so, there’s another good reason to buy one of these cable types: they must adhere to stricter specifications to earn their Thunderbolt or USB4 labels, especially Thunderbolt. A USB-C 3.2 cable isn’t just slower and less capable than a USB4 cable, it’s actually built to a weaker standard and probably isn’t as high-quality. Thunderbolt 3, 4, and the newest Thunderbolt 5 standard have far higher minimum requirements and taller ceilings on potential quality. All of this means that you’re way less likely to purchase a dangerous or underperforming USB-C cable if you stick to Thunderbolt or USB4. Just make sure you get whatever’s supported by your devices. (I mean, if none of your devices support Thunderbolt 4, you might as well save a bit of cash and opt for Thunderbolt 3 instead.) Check the cable’s weight Marcus Urbenz / Unsplash Weighing cables before you buy them might seem like some old-timey superstition, but it’s as legitimate as anything else on this list. Higher-quality USB-C cables are built with a thicker wire gauge, and that thicker copper wiring delivers a cleaner signal. Although some of a thicker cable’s heft and weight comes from its sheath, some of it comes from the wire itself — and more of that means a better cable. We have the receipts to back this up, too. We previously tested whether all USB-C cables are the same and compared a $9 USB-C cable to a $19 alternative. Both measured six feet in length, but the cheaper one was much thinner and lighter. (The $9 one weighed 38 grams while the $19 one weighed 86 grams. A significant difference.) Now, I know it’s not always easy or possible to weigh a cable before you buy it on the internet, but you can usually find weight in the cable’s technical specs. A little variation is okay, but if one cable is substantially lighter than others, consider axing it as a potential buy. Avoid third-party magnetic adapters Michael Crider / IDG You may have seen magnetic tip adapters that attach a USB-C cable and turns one end into a magnetic quick release, much like what we saw in Apple’s defunct MagSafe cables. But you should steer clear of these because they pose a significant risk of hardware damage. Many third-party magnetic USB-C cable adapters don’t offer protection against environmental damage to exposed pins. Others aren’t protected against debris shorting out the pins. There’s even the possibility of electrical arc damage when unplugging the connector. That last point is particularly dangerous, and it happens because the USB-C standard was designed with the idea that a USB-C cable would be plugged into a USB-C port, providing ample time to cut power when the cable is removed. However, magnetic connections are much faster to detach, so there’s a chance that power delivery is still going on even after detaching, leading to electrical arcs and potential damage. Stop using old USB-C cables James Barber / Foundry After all this advice, you might be thinking that it’s not worth the trouble and you might as well just use whatever old USB-C cables are lying around your home. But be wary of doing that! USB-C standards have continued to improve dramatically over the years, and many of those older USB-C cables from years ago weren’t just slow — they were dangerous. We performed an extensive test on older USB-C cables and found that most actually had the potential to provide too much power, which can damage ports and even fry devices. Do you really want to risk shorting your expensive laptop because you didn’t want to toss that old USB-C cable that’s been sitting in your drawer? Spending a few bucks on a new USB-C cable can protect you from all sorts of headaches and make life more convenient with faster data transfer and charging speeds. Further reading: The best USB-C cables worth buying

item.title: Lenovo made a ThinkBook that literally stretches sideways
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 3.37
At CES 2026, we saw a Lenovo gaming laptop that slowly unrolled into a widescreen laptop. At IFA, we’re seeing a second: a ThinkBook prototype that Lenovo is calling “Project Swan.” Let’s face it: Lenovo seems to have this rollable laptop concept sewn up. Lenovo’s ThinkBook Plus Rollable from last year was all about productivity: the $3,299 laptop included a screen which extended upwards from 14 inches to create a 16.7-inch display. Now Lenovo has gone in the opposite direction. Since Project Swan is a prototype concept, details are somewhat scarce. The basics, however, are here: Lenovo is taking a 14-inch laptop and unrolling the display to create a 17-inch laptop instead, via a 16:9 aspect ratio. It’s a simpler, more productive version of the Legion Pro Rollable that Lenovo showed off at CES 2026, which unrolled in two segments: from 16 inches to 21.5 inches, and then to 23.8 inches. The Legion’s functions were controlled by the function keys at the top of the keyboard, just like the new “Project Swan” ThinkBook. More precisely, the ThinkBook “Project Swan” laptop unrolls from an effective 2,258×1,672 screen to 2,850×1672, which is “almost” a 4K display, according to a Lenovo representative. (It’s actually about 57 percent of the pixels you’d see on a 3840×2160 “4K” display. The Legion Pro Rollable, however, was about a “3.6K” display.) Mark Hachman / Foundry Personally, I liked how the ThinkBook Plus Rollable created what was essentially a pair of 4:3 displays sitting virtually on top of one another. Lenovo’s representatives had another take: the widescreen rollable isn’t top-heavy, sits more ergonomically and better reproduces a traditional form factor. Moreover, as a gaming laptop the Legion widescreen rollable was heavy, with no real portability to it. “It’s the Legion technology with a productivity bent,” I was told. Lenovo didn’t reveal whether Project Swan would use a traditional IPS or OLED display. The Legion Pro Rollable, however, used the latter — a good sign that the Swan will do the same. Mark Hachman / Foundry I still think that actually arranging windows on the vertical rollable would be more productive than the widescreen “Project Swan” prototype Lenovo showed, but Lenovo’s team made a strong case in the Project Swan’s defense. We’re going to have to see what the future holds: the price, configuration, and the ship date. All those remain unknown. The next showcase will be CES 2026, where “Project Swan” may become a shipping product.

item.title: AI helps kids do better in school. That doesn’t mean they’re learning
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 2.33
The best way for us grownups to prepare for AI is to use AI, I’ve frequently argued. But when it comes to the benefits of kids using AI, there are far more questions than answers. New York City’s just-announced AI “moratorium” for elementary and middle-school students is among the most striking manifestations of the growing worries over AI’s growing presence in classrooms. Yet there’s also concern it may be too little, too late. According to a 2026 Pew Research survey, 54 percent of students reported using AI for help with their schoolwork, with 12 percent saying they got AI help with all their assignments. A 2025 report from the Center for Democracy and Technology goes even further, estimating that 85 percent of teachers and 86 percent of students used AI in the 2024-25 school year. OK, so what’s the lowdown about students and AI: Does it help them perform better in school, or does it harm their ability to learn? Actually, it does both, according to the latest research. Welcome to another edition of Prompt Mode, your weekly AI newsletter. I’m your host, Ben Patterson. Each week on Prompt Mode, I’ll be serving up analysis of the AI trends that matter to everyday users like you and me. Stay tuned for practical AI tips, hands-on experiences with the latest AI tools, and–you guessed it–prompts to help you get the most out of your AI assistants. Thanks for reading, and if you like what you see, just sign up right here. A recent Stanford University study showed that K-12 students frequently perform better on math, writing, and coding tasks when using AI tools. But when you take the chatbots away, those improvements tend to evaporate, leaving some students (especially those using straight-up AI chatbots rather than those fine-tuned for learning) more dependent on AI tools than truly helped by them. Another study from the Brookings Institute found that while “well-designed” AI tools used in an “overall, pedagogically sound approach” can be a boon in the classroom, an “overreliance” on AI chatbots can harm a student’s ability to learn and hinder their relationships with their teachers and fellow classmates. The AI ban for New York City schools, which calls for a one-year pause in “student-facing generative AI” for public school students through the eighth grade, is among the toughest in the nation, yet some fear it’s still not strong enough. For one thing, the current ban only encompasses a single school year, not two as many parents had hoped, the New York Times reports. There are also some key loopholes, including a provision that “centrally approved” e-books and coding programs are exempt from the AI ban, the Times notes. Of course, there have always been debates about computers in the classroom. Personally, I love that my daughter (who’s starting her first year of public high school in Manhattan, where AI in the classroom is still allowed) has been studying Scratch coding in class. But while I’m pleased she’s working with computers, I mainly want her to learn how to learn, rather than for her to learn about learning with AI. Even if it isn’t perfect, I think New York’s pushback on AI in the classroom is a step in the right direction, as well as a discussion worth having. But like all things AI, I wonder if we haven’t already passed the point of no return. More in AI this week - Aside from being more powerful than their predecessors, Claude Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 will add invisible watermarks all their text and file outputs, just as Anthropic previously promised. (PCWorld) - Speaking of Claude, here are five Claude privacy settings you shouldn’t overlook. (PCWorld) - Remember OpenClaw? The hype around that viral personal AI assistant tool (which just hit version 2.0) has largely faded, but that doesn’t obscure the fact that it ushered agentic AI into the mainstream. (PCWorld) - Love making AI podcasts with Google Notebook? You might have to settle for making fewer of them now, given that Notebook just switched to “computer-specific” usage limits. (PCWorld) - Google is taking on Canva with Google Pics, an Nano Banana-powered image creating tool that lets you create and edit images with a prompt. (TechCrunch) - There’s been more talk of an AI “kill switch,” with OpenAI reportedly telling members of Congress that it’s working on automatic shutdown systems that can pull the plug on an AI that’s gone rogue. (Reuters) Prompt of the week: The “verify the name” prompt This week’s prompt is a bit different from the others. Written by Anthropic specifically for Claude Fable 5.1, the latest and most powerful (for now) Claude model, this prompt tackles a specific Fable 5.1 quirk: its tendency to skip searches and rely on its memory during low-effort sessions. The Anthropic prompt “nudges” the model to double-check its facts using its search tool rather than making assumptions based on its training data — and indeed, it’s a prompt that would do plenty of other AI models good, especially those that run locally.

item.title: Kalshi urges targeted CFTC rules to curb prediction market manipulation risks
item.description:
Source: ReadWrite Score: 5.17
Kalshi wants federal regulators to tackle manipulation in prediction markets by going after misconduct and restricting specific traders, rather than placing sweeping limits on event contracts. In August 27 written comments, KalshiEX LLC responded to issues aired during the Commodity Futures Trading Commission’s inaugural Innovation Advisory Committee meeting on August 20. The federally regulated exchange concentrated on manipulation, so-called mention markets and questions over whether event contracts connected to corporate results might come under securities rules. Kalshi, founded in 2018 and designated by the CFTC as a contract market in November 2020, said regulators should treat manipulation much as they would on established exchanges. “The existence of manipulation and similar trading misconduct on exchanges should lead us to work harder to root out that misconduct, not to ban or restrict legitimate trading on the platform,” Kalshi said. CME Group’s Terry Duffy had questioned the rapid pace of event-contract self-certifications and warned that some products could be manipulated during the committee meeting. Kalshi responded that prediction exchanges already face CFTC anti-manipulation requirements alongside surveillance, compliance and disciplinary obligations. The company said its own monitoring has identified suspicious activity for investigation and CFTC referral, while disciplinary cases have included trades valued below $100. “The solution is to continue pursuing bad actors, not to close markets or delist contracts that innocent market participants, by their own revealed preferences, value and wish to trade,” the company said. Kalshi favors targeted CFTC safeguards for manipulation risks Another area drawing scrutiny is mention markets, which settle according to whether someone says a specified word or phrase during an event. Robinhood’s Vlad Tenev told the committee that some of these contracts could invite manipulation and raise customer-protection concerns. Kalshi acknowledged those risks while opposing a blanket ban. “Kalshi shares the view that the answer is robust guardrails rather than prohibition,” the company said. Under Kalshi’s proposed approach, the person whose words determine settlement could not trade the contract. Speechwriters, communications staff, teleprompter operators, producers and others with advance knowledge would also be excluded. Kalshi said those restrictions already apply through its rules, while screening tools introduced in June prevent known politicians, athletes and league-affiliated people from trading related markets. It wants the CFTC to set comparable minimum requirements across exchanges. On corporate event contracts, Kalshi also rejected the idea that correlation with a company’s share price automatically makes a binary contract securities-based. The exchange said these products differ from conventional options because there is no non-refundable premium or exercise right, with buyers and sellers instead taking symmetric risk. Rather than assigning every crossover product to a single regulatory bucket, Kalshi wants the CFTC and Securities and Exchange Commission to leave exchanges flexibility when contracts touch both jurisdictions. Its broader argument is that federal oversight can cover these products without creating overlapping regulatory regimes. Featured image: Canva

item.title: Bally’s finance chief exits as casino giant faces costly expansion pressures
item.description:
Source: ReadWrite Score: 5.13
Bally’s Corporation is changing finance chiefs as the casino company pours money into major developments, deals with financial pressure and fights over video gambling terminals in Chicago. Mira Mircheva told Bally’s she plans to leave her jobs as executive vice president and chief financial officer for personal reasons, according to the company’s Thursday announcement. Her resignation becomes effective September 4, but she will stay with the company until September 30 to assist during the handover. President George Papanier will temporarily handle the CFO duties in addition to serving as Bally’s president and sitting on its board. Directors are already looking for someone to fill the finance position permanently. The assignment puts a longtime gaming executive back into a familiar role. Papanier, who has more than four decades of industry experience, previously became Bally’s interim CFO in 2023. He is a certified public accountant and has overseen its land-based casino business since October 2021. Earlier, he spent February 2011 through October 2021 as Bally’s president and CEO. “On behalf of the entire Board and executive management team, I want to thank Mira for her dedication to Bally’s and we wish her great success going forward,” said Robeson Reeves, Chief Executive Officer of Bally’s Corporation. “Having spent more than two decades in key operating and financial leadership roles at Bally’s, George has been instrumental in developing our business model, asset portfolio, and growth strategy. He steps into the interim role supported by an experienced finance organization and I am confident that our reporting, controls and capital markets work will continue without disruption.” Papanier takes finance chief reins amid Bally’s multibillion-dollar casino expansion The leadership switch comes at a time when Bally’s has several expensive casino developments underway and a complex financial position to manage. For the fourth quarter of 2025, Bally’s preliminary results showed revenue reaching $746.2 million, a 28.6% increase from $580.4 million in the prior-year period. Casinos and resorts brought in $366.2 million during the quarter, with another $236.5 million coming from international online gaming. Bally’s has grown through dealmaking as well. A transaction valued at roughly $3 billion combined its International Interactive operation with Intralot, giving Bally’s a controlling 58% interest in Bally’s Intralot. Big construction commitments are also demanding capital. Bally’s plans a $4 billion casino and entertainment development in the Bronx while building its $1.7 billion permanent casino in Chicago. Chicago has brought fresh complications. In August, Bally’s said it was “resetting the pace” of some construction while challenging a potential expansion of video gambling terminals across the city. The company contends that unrestricted VGT growth would run against promises in its Host Community Agreement and leave the casino facing added uncertainty. Bally’s said the slowdown could affect some of the 1,500 union tradespeople on the project, though it still expects the permanent casino to open in early 2027. Earlier construction problems included debris reaching the Chicago River, use of an unauthorized waste hauler and engineering revisions that forced foundation changes and relocation of the hotel tower. Papanier now takes responsibility for Bally’s finance organization through those challenges while the board searches for a permanent CFO. Featured image: SCM.com via website

item.title: States cite Ninth Circuit rulings, George Santos banned from Kalshi: today in prediction market news LIVE
item.description:
Source: ReadWrite Score: 4.64
Today in prediction market news, we’re following a fresh wave of legal and regulatory developments, including Kalshi urging the Tenth Circuit to block Utah enforcement while its federal appeal plays out, and Ohio and Rhode Island pointing to recent Ninth Circuit rulings as they defend state authority over prediction markets. We’re also tracking Kalshi’s permanent ban of former Republican New York Congressman George Santos following an investigation into his trading activity, along with the platform’s call for clearer CFTC guardrails as event contract markets grow. We’ll also be following the latest on enforcement actions involving political trading, Kalshi’s allegations against North Carolina congressional candidate Laurie Buckhout, and developments across prediction markets, regulation, politics, crypto and sports event trading throughout the day. AGA says young adults have bet $5.1B on Kalshi In a statement to ReadWrite, AGA CEO Bill Miller said: “Sports betting is a form of entertainment, yet so-called ‘prediction markets’ dangerously advertise it as investing. Given that 18- to 20-year-olds are driving billions in sports betting volume on Kalshi, it is crucial that everyone recognize this distinction and understand that on ‘prediction markets,’ users are often betting against sophisticated Wall Street operations — not their peers. "Most parents and grandparents don’t realize that ‘prediction markets’ are offering a backdoor into sports betting in jurisdictions where the legal betting age is 21. This means their freshman son or daughter may be prohibited from entering a legal sportsbook but can simply pull out their phone and use Kalshi to bet on football. "This defiance of state law is a major reason why so-called ‘prediction markets’ have drawn the ire of 44 state attorneys general, state legislatures and regulators across the country.” Kalshi trader sues over $1.17M Trump-Trudeau market dispute A Kalshi trader is taking “read the fine print” to federal court. Nicolas Pernas alleges the platform wrongly resolved a Trump–Justin Trudeau market as “No,” despite terms saying it would pay “Yes” if the leaders spoke directly. Pernas claims he held 1,173,968 positions worth $1.17 million if resolved his way. The complaint also alleges Kalshi prematurely closed the market and later prevented him from withdrawing roughly $24,293 in cash. Pernas is suing for breach of contract, fraud and other claims. In prediction markets, apparently even the meaning of “meet” can end up meeting a judge. New York tells court CFTC’s Kalshi order deserves ‘no weight’ New York’s attorney general isn’t exactly impressed with the CFTC’s attempt to ride to Kalshi’s rescue. In a new filing, the state argues the regulator’s August emergency order should receive “no weight,” saying courts — not the CFTC — get the final word on whether Kalshi’s sports contracts are swaps and whether state gambling laws are preempted. New York gets particularly spicy later, questioning whether losing access to sports wagers — or betting on Taylor Swift meeting the Pope — really constitutes a market “emergency.” Its bottom line: the CFTC can’t make allegedly unlawful offerings legal by administrative decree. Crypto.com’s prediction market unit hit by executive exodus One departing executive reportedly wished colleagues the “autonomy” needed to take the operation to the next level. The shake-up arrives as prediction markets face growing regulatory scrutiny and increasingly fierce competition. For Crypto.com, which has pushed aggressively into sports event contracts, the next prediction may be who’s still sitting in the executive suite. Crypto(.)com's prediction market exchange subsidiary is quietly dealing with a mass executive exodus. “I hope you guys finally get the autonomy you need to drive this business to the next level,” wrote the latest departee.https://t.co/yooZGcYiBA Kalshi says weather markets can double as business umbrellas Kalshi has a pitch for businesses tired of blaming the weather: hedge it instead. New research from the prediction market argues its exchange-traded weather contracts could help companies offset revenue losses from rain, snow and temperature swings. One Los Angeles ice cream shop found sales fell about 20% below 70°F, while its Kalshi hedges reportedly paid $1,500 monthly — equivalent to 43% of rent. Kalshi also says its daily weather markets have demonstrated strong calibration across roughly 70,000 resolved contracts per horizon. Apparently “everyone talks about the weather” now has a financial follow-up: “but did you hedge it?” Weather poses billions in business risk. NYC subway ridership fell >1M on the heaviest snow days this winter. Less footfall = less revenue for retail, delivery, and events. Kalshi markets saw it coming; offering price discovery & hedging utility. Read: https://t.co/RtGjLjcGBh pic.twitter.com/Fl9veNWEaO Kalshi candidate learns betting on yourself has consequences Buckhout cooperated with Kalshi’s investigation and settled the case, receiving a three-year suspension and a $2,589.96 financial penalty. Buckhout has since called the trade a “dumb mistake.” Her prediction-market career may be temporarily benched, but the actual contest continues: she’s running against Democratic Rep. Don Davis in November. Kalshi serves up US Open prediction partnership Kalshi is heading to Flushing Meadows, and apparently watching the tennis wasn’t interactive enough already. The prediction market has signed a multi-year deal with the USTA to become the US Open’s first exclusive prediction market partner, starting with the 2026 tournament. Kalshi branding will appear around the grounds, with real-time market data eventually planned for tournament coverage. There are some lines it won’t cross: markets involving umpire decisions, injuries and code violations are off limits. Kalshi is also working with tennis integrity officials on data sharing and market surveillance — because nobody wants “double fault” taking on an entirely new meaning. Kalshi is now the exclusive Prediction Market Partner of the US Open. The multi-year deal is designed to deepen our understanding of tennis through the power of free markets, live price discovery, and crowd wisdom. Together with the USTA, we're also building a comprehensive… pic.twitter.com/HCFzpeIC7F Canadian regulators give sports prediction markets the cold shoulder For now, authorized dealers can facilitate only a limited selection of contracts tied to economic, environmental or financial indicators on certain U.S.-regulated exchanges. Other prediction-market categories remain under review, so Canada hasn’t closed the book entirely. But for sports contracts, regulators have made their position decidedly less than maple-syrup sweet. Les Autorités canadiennes en valeurs mobilières (ACVM) et l’Organisme canadien de réglementation des investissements (OCRI) ont publié aujourd’hui un avis conjoint afin de fournir de nouvelles indications sur les marchés de prédiction. En savoir plus: https://t.co/gPCSteKwig pic.twitter.com/UMKst6vfXH Kalshi tells CFTC: target bad actors, not markets In comments to the regulator, the exchange argued manipulation concerns should be addressed by pursuing misconduct rather than restricting legitimate event contracts. Kalshi also backed guardrails for “mention markets,” including barring speakers, speechwriters and others with advance knowledge from trading contracts they could influence. The company says similar restrictions already exist on its platform and wants minimum standards applied across exchanges. On corporate event contracts, Kalshi also urged regulators to avoid automatically treating products linked to stock-price movements as securities-based contracts. Prediction Market Update@Kalshi pushies back against calls to restrict prediction markets over manipulation concerns. In a letter to the @CFTC following its recent advisory committee meeting, Kalshi argues event contracts face the same anti-manipulation rules as traditional… pic.twitter.com/30oSSaPcTC Kalshi gives George Santos a lifetime prediction market timeout Kalshi permanently suspended the former New York congressman and ordered him to pay $71,356 after concluding he manipulated contracts tied to whether he would attend the State of the Union. Kalshi says Santos traded on an outcome he could personally influence, made misleading public statements about his plans and ultimately earned $17,839.57 from the affected markets. Santos, unsurprisingly, didn’t leave quietly, responding to his lifetime ban by questioning how long Kalshi itself would be around. The exchange also cited manipulation, fraud and cooperation-related rule violations. Hey @Kalshi thanks for the lifetime ban from your gambling platform. Let’s see how much longer you guys are around for. 💋

item.title: Kalshi permanently suspends George Santos over State of Union market trades
item.description:
Source: ReadWrite Score: 3.94
George Santos has been permanently suspended from Kalshi and ordered to pay $71,356 after the prediction market exchange concluded that he manipulated contracts tied to his own attendance at the State of the Union address. The punishment took effect August 28 and covers trading activity from February 2 through February 25, 2026. According to Kalshi’s compliance department, Santos made several large trades on whether he would attend the event, an outcome he could personally influence. Kalshi’s rules prohibit members from trading contracts when they have control or influence over the underlying event. The exchange said Santos also made public comments about his attendance plans while buying contracts tied to the same question, with some statements described as false or misleading. “The Compliance Department found that Santos made these statements with the intent to manipulate the price of the Yes or No contracts that he intended to purchase,” the notice said. The comments moved contract prices, Kalshi found. Santos ultimately earned $17,839.57 from trading in the markets covered by the disciplinary case. Santos responded on social media, stating: “Hey @Kalshi thanks for the lifetime ban from your gambling platform. Let’s see how much longer you guys are around for.” Kalshi says George Santos profited by manipulating markets he could influence The exchange cited several violations, including rules against market manipulation, fraud and trading on events a member can influence.
